docs.title: iOS background location
docs.summary: How the iPhone app lowers its location cost when the phone is not moving: the states, thresholds and Apple sources behind them, what CI proves, and the test plan for a real iPhone.

headings.text: Test plan on a real iPhone

docs.text: iOS background location How the iPhone app lowers its location cost when the phone is not moving: the states, thresholds and Apple sources behind them, what CI proves, and the test plan for a real iPhone. Status: the Dart side is unit-tested; the Objective-C side was written without a Mac and has not been compiled or run yet. The first macOS CI run is the compile proof (see What CI must show); the first iPhone day is the behavior proof. Before and after Before (up to v0.25): startUpdatingLocation with kCLLocationAccuracyBest, a 50 m distance filter and pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically = NO, all day. The adaptive cadence was Android only: the iOS plugin did not implement updateLocationRequest, and the background isolate could not reach the plugin channel at all (the plugin registered its channel only on the UI engine). So a phone lying on a desk kept the GPS-class request running around the clock. Now: the same cadence policy as Android (app/lib/services/trackingcadence.dart) decides the tier from speed, stillness, live boost and SOS, and app/lib/services/ioslocationprofile.dart maps every tier to a Core Location request. The plugin (app/packages/backgroundlocator2/ios/Classes/BackgroundLocatorPlugin.m) only applies it. States and requests Cadence tier Entered when iOS accuracy Distance filter Activity type SOS SOS burst (foreground reporter) best none other navigation boosted someone watches live best 5 m other navigation driving smoothed speed >= 3 m/s twice, or one fix >= 8 m/s best 10 m automotive navigation driving, battery < 15% as above, not charging nearest ten meters 25 m automotive navigation walking smoothed speed >= 0.8 m/s nearest ten meters 15 m (25 m below 15% battery) fitness stationary ("slow") default; registration; every native wake-up nearest ten meters 25 m other idle ("still") 10 min within 60 m of the same spot three kilometers 200 m, plus a 150 m exit region other Exit thresholds and hysteresis are the existing ones (driving ends after 60 s below 1 m/s, walking after 30 s below 0.4 m/s; details in Live tracking: the sending side). Still mode in detail: Entering. iOS delivers fixes only on movement (distance filter), so the 10 minute stillness rule needs a clock: the plugin now runs a 5 minute timer that calls the existing Dart heartbeat callback (the same /devices/heartbeat POST Android sends every 10 minutes). The tick re-evaluates the cadence, so still mode starts 10 to 15 minutes after the last move. The wake-up region. On entering still mode the plugin arms an exit-only CLCircularRegion (orbitly.still) of 150 m (or the fix's accuracy if larger) around the newest fix with an accuracy of 100 m or better. On exit the plugin, without waiting for Dart, switches back to the slow request and restarts updates so a fresh fix arrives at once. That fix carries nativereset: true; Dart then forgets the request it last applied and the idle anchor, so the phone stays out of still mode for at least another 10 minutes. Coarse fixes. At three kilometers accuracy iOS uses cell towers only. Such fixes (worse than 100 m) are not reported while still or as the first fix after a wake-up: a cell fix can be a kilometer off and would make the person jump on the family map. One exception: a coarse fix whose whole error circle lies outside the 150 m region ends still mode (backup for a region exit that never fires). No region monitoring (unsupported or a monitoring failure): still mode uses hundred-meter accuracy (Wi-Fi) instead, so the 200 m filter notices leaving. Decisions pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically stays NO. When iOS pauses updates in the background, they only resume when the app is opened again (Apple's documentation of the property), so a family member who drives off after a pause would vanish. Still mode is the controlled replacement: the same saving, with a defined wake-up. With the flag off, the activity type does not trigger pauses; it is still set so Core Location can tune its filtering (automotive while driving, fitness while walking). No CMMotionActivityManager. It would add a Motion & Fitness permission prompt and a second wake source without being needed for the decision: speed from GPS and the region exit cover moving and still. NSMotionUsageDescription stays in Info.plist because the app links Core Motion through sensorsplus (driving detection), which can need it. Significant-location-change stays on as a cheap backup wake-up and the relaunch trigger after termination. Deferred updates are not used (deprecated since iOS 13). No kCLLocationAccuracyBestForNavigation. Apple intends it for navigation apps on external power; best is enough for 1 Hz driving. allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates is set to YES only when the service is registered or resumed after a relaunch (the location background mode is declared), and back to NO when the service stops. showsBackgroundLocationIndicator stays on (registration setting, unchanged): people can see that location is in use. It is saved so a relaunch restores it. Relaunch after termination If the app is terminated while sharing, the plugin arms a termination region (at least 150 m) around the last good fix, and significant-change monitoring keeps running. When iOS relaunches the app for either event, the plugin starts the background isolate, re-applies the slow request, turns background updates back on, restarts the heartbeat and both location services. The first fix is held until the isolate reports that it is ready, then delivered with nativereset: true. The older behavior (one fix per region hop after a relaunch) is gone. SOS, places and live viewers SOS runs in the foreground reporter (its own location stream); the background request never delays it. In the background the boosted and SOS tiers are applied at once (the existing "urgent" rule of ProfileApplier). Place arrivals and departures are evaluated on the server (and on the phone for private circles) from fixes. In still mode a departure produces a fix on region exit. Apple documents region events within 3 to 5 minutes on average, so a departure can show up to a few minutes later than with the old always-on request. The architecture budget for iOS is 5 minutes from starting to move to the first live fix. Battery rationale and sources The quotes were collected on 2026-11-08 for the optimisation research notes (docs/design/RESEARCHNOTESPERFORMANCE.md on the architecture branch); this page did not re-read them. Apple's energy guide: lowest acceptable accuracy, a distance filter, and region (or visit) monitoring instead of continuous updates; significant-change monitoring runs "around the clock": https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Performance/Conceptual/EnergyGuide-iOS/LocationBestPractices.html desiredAccuracy (defaults to best): https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/desiredaccuracy pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically: a pause "ends access to location changes until the app launches again"; Apple suggests turning it off and dropping to kCLLocationAccuracyThreeKilometers in the background instead: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/pauseslocationupdatesautomatically Region monitoring (20 regions per app, radii "between 1 and 400 meters work better", events "within 3 to 5 minutes on average"): https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/monitoring-the-user-s-proximity-to-geographic-regions Significant-location-change (500 m, at most every 5 minutes, relaunches a terminated app): https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/startmonitoringsignificantlocationchanges() Background updates and the indicator: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/handling-location-updates-in-the-background App Review guideline 2.4.2 (apps must not "rapidly drain battery"): https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#hardware-compatibility What CI must show The macOS jobs are the only compile proof. In the run for this change: 1. test.yml, job ios, step "Build for the iOS Simulator (unsigned)": the step passes and its log has no error: line mentioning backgroundlocator2. Search the log for BackgroundLocatorPlugin.m, MethodCallHelper.m, Util.m, PreferencesManager.m and Globals.m: any warning: there (for example "does not conform to protocol", "conflicting return type", "undeclared selector", "incompatible pointer") must be read and fixed, even if the build passed. 2. Same job, step "Boot a simulator, install, and launch the app": passes (the plugin registers on launch without crashing). 3. ios-unsigned.yml (device build, flutter build ios --release --no-codesign): passes, same log search for the arm64 compile. 4. Optional simulator check of the switch: run the app in the simulator with location set to "Freeway Drive" (Features > Location), sign in and allow location "Always", background the app, and watch Console for backgroundlocator2: request lines (accuracy -1 = best while driving). Then set a fixed location and wait 15 minutes: expect accuracy=3000 ... still=150 and still region armed. Test plan on a real iPhone Use a TestFlight build, location "Always" with precise location on, Low Power Mode off. Note the start time and battery level for each run; Console.app (device connected, filter backgroundlocator2) shows the request lines without coordinates. 1. Still. Leave the phone at home, screen off, for 2 hours. Expect: after 10 to 15 minutes a accuracy=3000 ... still=150 line and still region armed; no location arrow in the status bar between heartbeats; "last seen" on another phone stays fresh (heartbeat every 5 minutes). Settings > Battery should list Orbitly with a low background share. 2. Walk. From still mode, walk away (300 m or more). Expect wake-up (region exit) within about 5 minutes of leaving, then accuracy=10 filter=15 once walking speed is seen; the family map follows; leaving home triggers the place departure. 3. Drive. Drive for 15 minutes. Expect accuracy=-1 filter=10 activity=2 (automotive) and a smooth track; on arrival and 10 to 15 minutes parked, still mode again. 4. Live viewer. While still, open the person on another phone. Expect a boosted request (filter=5) within seconds (live boost push) and fresh positions, then back to still after the boost. 5. Relaunch. Swipe the app away from the app switcher, then walk or drive 1 km. Expect a relaunch by significant change or the termination region (relaunched by a location event), and positions resuming without opening the app. Whether iOS relaunches a force-quit app is not settled (iOS release notes expect no relaunch); record what actually happens. 6. Reboot. Restart the phone, do not open the app, walk 1 km. Record whether positions resume. 7. Day test. One normal day; screenshot Settings > Battery (24 hours, by app) for the release notes. Budget: 3% per stationary day and 8% per mixed day attributable to Orbitly.

docs.title: API compatibility policy
docs.summary: Users do not update the app straight away, and app-store review is slow. The server therefore has to keep working for the apps people really run, not only for the newest one. This page is the…

headings.text: What the server tells an old app
Wire efficiency (feature `wirev2`, apps 0.25 and newer use it)

docs.text: API compatibility policy Users do not update the app straight away, and app-store review is slow. The server therefore has to keep working for the apps people really run, not only for the newest one. This page is the contract. Supported window The server supports the last 5 released minor versions of the app (a rolling window). When a new minor ships, the oldest one drops out. The list of released lines is compat.Releases in backend/internal/compat/compat.go. Add the new x.y.0 there in the same commit that tags a release; the window and the minimum supported version follow automatically (as of v0.20.1: 0.16 to 0.20, minimum 0.16.0). MINSUPPORTEDAPPVERSION (env, e.g. 0.16.0) pins the minimum instead. An admin can override the minimum in the admin panel (Settings, App versions). Precedence: admin override, then env, then the rolling window. Versions below the minimum are "outside the window": the server no longer promises that they work, and tells them so (below). A version 2 or more minors behind the latest release gets upgraderecommended (it still works). How an app identifies itself Every request from the app carries: Header Value X-App-Version the app's pubspec version, e.g. 0.20.1 (build suffix +45 and pre-release -rc1 are ignored) X-App-Platform android, ios or web Apps up to and including v0.20.1 send neither header. The server treats such clients as unknown: it never blocks them and never changes their responses, because it cannot tell a v0.16 from a v0.20.1. They still appear to the server through devices.appversion, which is only as good as the value sent at registration. (The app now registers with its real version; before, it sent the constant 0.1.0 unless built with a dart-define.) The server records which versions each user runs in appclientversions (migration 000200), written at most once per user, version and platform per 10 minutes, from the authenticated API groups. Retention: rows live as long as the user. What the server tells an old app Every response to a client that sent X-App-Version carries X-OpenFamily-Compat: ok recommended required, plus X-OpenFamily-Min-App-Version and X-OpenFamily-Latest-App-Version. GET /compat (public, cheap) returns {status, upgraderequired, upgraderecommended, minsupportedversion, latestversion, clientversion, message} for the version in X-App-Version (or ?v=). GET /config embeds the same object as compat. POST /locations and POST /locations/batch answer 426 with {"code":"upgraderequired","upgraderequired":true,"minsupportedversion":...} to a client below the minimum, only when the admin enabled enforcement (default off). Clients that sent no version are never refused. The app shows a banner for required, for a circle it cannot open, and a dismissible one for recommended, instead of silently showing "No location yet" or "Offline". Rules for API changes 1. Additive only inside the window. Add fields; do not rename, retype or remove one that an in-window app reads. A new field must be optional for old clients (omitempty or a default), and new request fields must be optional on the server. 2. New enum values (for example a new e2eemode) must not be sent to clients that cannot interpret them without a shim. Apps parse unknown enum values defensively (an unknown circle mode is shown as "needs a newer app", not as an empty circle). 3. New required request fields, new auth steps and changed semantics need a feature gate: add the feature to compat.Features with the first app version that supports it and branch on compat.Supports(...). 4. Removing something an in-window app uses waits until it leaves the window. Deprecate first: keep serving it, document it here, drop it after the release that moves the last user of it out of the window. 5. The contract guard enforces rule 1: backend/internal/compat/testdata/contract/<tag>.txt lists every Struct.jsontag the handlers and models declared at each release. TestContractAdditiveOnly fails if a field from an in-window release disappears. An intentional removal goes in allowedremovals.txt with the reason. Record a new release with: git archive vX.Y.Z backend/internal/handlers backend/internal/models tar -x -C /tmp/vX.Y.Z go run ./cmd/compat-contract /tmp/vX.Y.Z/backend > internal/compat/testdata/contract/vX.Y.Z.txt The guard sees named struct fields only; fields built with map[string]any are not covered, so keep those stable by review. Wire efficiency (feature wirev2, apps 0.25 and newer use it) Additive only, so apps 0.20-0.24 are unaffected: gzip responses, ETag / If-None-Match on authenticated JSON GETs, view=compact / fields= and ?since= on /family/members and /family/places, simplify / maxpoints on member history, limit / before on /audit, GET /app/bootstrap, and POSTQUERY /family/history/query. A new app checks features.wirev2 in GET /compat (or just handles 404 / a plain array) and falls back to the old requests. See API wire efficiency. Shims in place Situation Who What the server does Private (end-to-end encrypted) circle, app below 0.15.0 reports a version GET /circles appends "(update the app to open this private circle)" to the circle name (the only field every version renders) and sets updaterequired; every client gets minappversion on a private circle All circles private, app below 0.16.0 posts a plaintext location reports a version the existing 409 e2eeprivatecircle carries "Update Orbitly to share location..." Owner-approval key-log entry (action 12, feature ownerapproval) any client that does not send GET /e2ee/log?ownerapproval=1 (apps below 0.27, bridges) the entry is served redacted (hash chain still verifiable), because older verifiers reject unknown action codes; the self-approval itself is an ordinary approval entry Findings from the audit of v0.10.0 to v0.20.1 (field-level): no JSON field that a handler or model declared was removed in that range. The compatibility risks are semantic, not structural: since v0.15.0 a Private circle never returns plaintext positions to anyone (circles.Authz hides them), so an app that cannot decrypt shows its members as "No location yet"; and since v0.16.0 an account whose circles are all Private gets 409 for plaintext uploads. Both are covered by the shims above for clients that identify themselves. What is not covered Apps that predate the header are indistinguishable from each other, so no per-version shim can apply to them. The first release that sends the header starts the window for real. Old-APK behaviour is not tested against real APKs. The contract fixtures check the server's declared fields, not what each old build renders. Do a manual pass with an old APK from apk/ or the GitHub release before dropping a version from the window. The headless background location isolate does not read the package version unless built with --dart-define=OPENFAMILYAPPVERSION; those uploads send no version header (they are never refused).

docs.title: API wire efficiency
docs.summary: How the app and server keep requests small, few and reliable on mobile networks, and whether to use the HTTP QUERY method.

headings.text: 3. The HTTP QUERY method: should we use it?

docs.text: API wire efficiency How the app and server keep requests small, few and reliable on mobile networks, and whether to use the HTTP QUERY method. Goal: a phone keeps a small working set and fetches the rest on demand, cheaply on mobile networks. Everything below is additive: apps 0.20-0.24 send none of the new parameters and get exactly the responses they always got. A new app detects the server through features.wirev2 (in GET /compat and GET /app/bootstrap) and falls back to the old requests on a server without it. All numbers in this page were measured on a local test server with seeded data (one circle, six people, one person with a 24 hour trail), not on a phone and not through Cloudflare. Sizes are the JSON body in bytes; "gzip" is the size after the server's own gzip (level 1). 1. What the app calls (before) When Calls Notes Cold start / map open GET /family, /circles, /family/members[?circleid=], /family/places, /chat/unread, /config, then the WebSocket /ws/stream 5-7 sequential-ish round trips, each previously on a brand new TCP+TLS connection (see below) Resume refreshMembers() = GET /family/members + GET /family/places (places cached briefly) on every resume, even when the WebSocket is healthy; returns the whole list again Open a person's day GET /family/members/{id}/history?from&to already bucketed to 30 s and capped at 1500 points / 25 h Chat GET /circles/{id}/chat?after= catch-up + WebSocket frames already incremental Driving / trips GET /trips?limit, /trips/{id}?maxpoints=400 already paged and thinned Background location uploads (POST /locations), heartbeat unchanged Findings: 1. No connection reuse. ApiClient used the top-level http.get/post helpers, which create and close an HTTP client per request: every call paid a new TCP and TLS handshake (about 2-3 round trips of latency on 4G). Fixed: one long-lived client, so keep-alive (and HTTP/2 where the platform stack offers it) is used. 2. Responses were never compressed by the API itself (Caddy compresses when it is in front; a direct or tunnel setup did not). Fixed: gzip in the API, and zstd gzip in Caddy. 3. Full lists every time. Members include email, phone, TOTP state and account timestamps the map never shows, and the whole list is re-sent when one person moved. Fixed with view=compact and ?since= deltas. 4. Resume = full refetch even if nothing changed. Fixed generically with ETag/304 (unchanged lists cost a header-only response). 5. Cold start is 5+ requests. Fixed with GET /app/bootstrap. 6. Polling vs WebSocket: members/chat/alerts arrive over the WebSocket; REST is only used for the first snapshot, on resume and for catch-up. There is no periodic REST poll while connected (checked: the only periodic timers are the 30 s WebSocket ping, a 30 s local staleness re-evaluation and the watchdog). The WebSocket ping is an app-level 30 s frame (tiny), reconnect backoff is 1-30 s with jitter-free doubling and resets only after a connection stayed up. 7. ApiClient already decodes bodies above 128 KiB on a worker isolate, so no change was needed there. 2. What was added Feature How a client uses it Server compat story gzip send Accept-Encoding: gzip (dart:io does it automatically and decodes) only for JSON/text above 512 bytes, never WebSocket/SSE/images ETag / 304 repeat a GET with If-None-Match from the last ETag weak validator over the body for every authenticated JSON GET; ignored by clients that do not send it Compact members GET /family/members?view=compact or fields=id,name,lat,lon default response unchanged Delta GET /family/members?since=<cursor> and GET /family/places?since=<cursor> see below Bootstrap GET /app/bootstrap 404 on older servers, client falls back History thinning GET /family/members/{id}/history?...&simplify=<m>&maxpoints=<n> optional Several windows POST or QUERY /family/history/query new route Audit paging GET /audit?limit=&before= + X-Next-Cursor default is still the newest 100 Delta lists ?since=<cursor> (any non-empty value, none for the first call) switches the response to an object: {"cursor":"1760000000000-ab12cd34ef56","full":false, "items":[{"id":"...","lat":51.5}],"ids":["id1","id2"]} full:true means items is the whole list: replace local state. full:false means merge items by id and drop every local row whose id is not in ids. A deletion is the absence of the id, so there is no tombstone table to grow or expire, and a missed delete can never linger. The cursor is the snapshot time plus a short hash of the list's structure (who is in it, roles, who shares where). If the structure changed, or the cursor is older than 15 minutes, malformed or from the future, the server answers full:true. Role, membership and sharing changes have no timestamp, which is why they go through the hash instead. Members changed = updated profile, new position, new heartbeat or avatar. Places changed = places.updatedat (migration 000360, set by a trigger). Authorization is unchanged: the delta is the same list the caller may see, filtered. Other circles' people never appear in items or ids. Honest limit: the server still runs the same queries; the saving is bytes on the phone's network and JSON decoding, not database work. Chat keeps its own ?after= cursor, and alerts are already paged with limit. Bootstrap GET /app/bootstrap[?view=full] runs the existing circles, members and unread handlers as the same caller and returns them with compatibility info, the server's feature map and a wire object (etag, gzip, delta, query...). A section that fails (for example members when you have no circle yet) is null with its status in errors. Authorization lives in exactly one place because the existing handlers are reused. 3. The HTTP QUERY method: should we use it? What it is. QUERY is a safe, idempotent request method that carries its parameters in a request body. It is RFC 10008, "The HTTP QUERY Method" (Proposed Standard, IETF HTTP working group, authors Reschke, Snell, Bishop, formerly draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body). Servers advertise support with an Accept-Query header. Sources: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008.html>, <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body/>. Benefits for this app. Reads whose input does not fit a URL well: many ids, several time windows, structured filters; without abusing POST (which caches and retries as unsafe). Real risks and what we know: Layer Status Go net/http accepts any method token. Tested. chi router needs chi.RegisterMethod("QUERY") before routing. Done in main.go. Caddy reverse proxy passes unknown methods and bodies. Verified locally (below). Cloudflare (owner's domain) not verified. Cloudflare's WAF/managed rules, Bot Fight Mode or an Access policy may block or rewrite unknown methods. Test command below. Dart package:http works with a raw Request('QUERY', uri). Tested with fakes and, locally, against the real server. OkHttp / Android, iOS URLSession allow custom methods in principle (dart:io HttpClient sends the token as is); not verified on devices. Some carrier proxies and enterprise middleboxes drop unknown methods: this is why a fallback exists. Browsers QUERY is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin call costs a preflight (OPTIONS); the server allows QUERY in Access-Control-Allow-Methods. The admin web is same-origin and does not use it. Caching shared caches that understand QUERY key on the body; most do not cache it at all, so there is no caching benefit over GET with ETag here. Logging / WAF many log pipelines and WAF rules only know GET/POST. Measured benefit here: none that justifies it. Member and position reads fit in a short GET ?circleid=all&view=compact&since=; a trail is one GET per day. The only place a body helps is fetching several time windows of one person in one round trip, which POST does just as well. So the implementation is minimal and off by default: POST /family/history/query always works (it is a read). QUERY /family/history/query works only when the operator sets QUERYMETHOD=1; otherwise it answers 405 with Allow: POST. Both routes set Accept-Query: "application/json". ApiClient.query(path, body) tries QUERY, falls back to POST on 405, 501, 400, 415 or a dropped connection, and remembers the result per server for 24 hours (QueryCapability, stored in preferences). If the server says QUERY is off (wire.query:false in bootstrap) it does not probe at all. A genuine answer such as 403 is returned as is and never retried as POST. Nothing in the app calls query() yet; it is there for the first screen that needs several windows, so no screen changes were made. Test it through Cloudflare on the owner's domain (replace the token; the server needs QUERYMETHOD=1 for a 200, otherwise a 405 from the origin still proves the method passed Cloudflare, whereas a Cloudflare HTML error page or a 403/400 with server: cloudflare and no JSON body means it was blocked): curl -i -X QUERY https://life.foleyit.com/family/history/query \ H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ d '{"memberid":"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000","windows":[]}' Expected from the origin: HTTP/2 400 with {"error":"memberid and 1-8 windows are required"} (enabled) or 405 with Allow: POST, OPTIONS (disabled). Compare with the same call using -X POST. 4. Reliability in ApiClient One shared keep-alive client. Timeouts per class: 15 s for reads and normal writes, 60 s for raw-byte uploads. Retry only GET (idempotent), up to 2 times, on network errors, timeouts and 502/503/504, with jittered exponential backoff (about 125-250 ms, then 250-500 ms). POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE are never retried automatically. Simultaneous identical GETs share one request (keyed by session and URL). ApiCancelToken: a disposed screen stops waiting (the response is dropped; a request already on the wire cannot be aborted with package:http). Conditional GET cache: bounded (24 entries, 256 KiB each, 1 MiB total), cleared when a session starts or ends; never used for ?since= URLs. Token refresh logic is untouched. 5. Caddy, Cloudflare, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Caddy serves HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 on its HTTPS site automatically; keep UDP 443 open for HTTP/3. encode zstd gzip compresses JSON; the push SSE path is excluded. Responses already compressed by the API are left alone. Behind a Cloudflare Tunnel or proxy, Cloudflare terminates the client connection (HTTP/2 or 3 to the phone) and speaks HTTP/1.1 or 2 to the origin; keep-alive to the phone is Cloudflare's. Cloudflare does its own Brotli/gzip for compressible types. Not verified from here. WebSocket frames are not compressed; the 30 s application ping is a few bytes. 6. Measurements See the table at the end of this page (filled from TestWireMeasure, OFWIREMEASURE=1).

docs.title: Performance and memory on low-RAM phones
docs.summary: How the app adapts to phones with 2 GB to 16 GB of RAM: device tiers, memory-pressure handling, APK variants and size, and how to test on real phones.

headings.text: What the platform guidance says (and what we took from it)
Measured in the test VM (host heavily loaded, single run, NOT a phone)

docs.text: Performance and memory on low-RAM phones How the app adapts to phones with 2 GB to 16 GB of RAM: device tiers, memory-pressure handling, APK variants and size, and how to test on real phones. Scope: release 0.25 work to make the app comfortable on 2 GB and 3 GB phones while keeping the full app on 6 GB and up. Build size, memory tiers, memory-pressure handling, and what was deliberately not changed. Important: nothing here was measured on a phone. Numbers come from (a) a Gradle release build of the APK in Docker on a build server and (b) the Flutter test VM on that server, which is a desktop-class process with in-memory stores and no platform channels. They show relative effects and exact sizes of files, not what a 2 GB phone feels. The section "Testing on real phones" lists what to run on real hardware; it has not been run. What the platform guidance says (and what we took from it) Source Used for Android: manage app memory R8 shrinking lowers RAM as well as size; avoid package-wide keep rules; from Android 14 only TRIMMEMORYUIHIDDEN and TRIMMEMORYBACKGROUND are delivered, so those two drive the trim policy; bitmaps are the largest objects, release image caches when the UI is hidden; ActivityManager.getMemoryInfo for total/available memory; do not leave services running without need; LMK kills cached processes first Android: memory overview page dumpsys meminfo, Perfetto heap explorer, Android vitals (LMK rate) as the production signal Flutter: performance best practices build lists lazily, avoid saveLayer/Opacity/clip-heavy trees, measure in profile mode on the lowest-end device Flutter: measuring and reducing app size --analyze-size, --split-debug-info, remove unused resources, tree-shaking Android: optimize battery for background tasks batch work into one task, avoid needless wake-ups Not read in full (the fetch returned only a title or nothing useful): Apple's jetsam documentation page, Flutter's Impeller and Dart-isolate pages, and Android's location-battery page. The iOS section below therefore rests on general knowledge of jetsam (per-process limits, background apps killed first) and on Flutter's own didHaveMemoryPressure hook, not on a fresh read of Apple's text. Treat those parts as unverified. Device tiers Decided once at start-up in app/lib/services/perf/devicetier.dart from ActivityManager.MemoryInfo.totalMem (Android) or ProcessInfo.physicalMemory (iOS; Swift unverified, see below). isLowRamDevice() forces Lite. Tier Marketing RAM Reported-RAM rule Notes Lite under 4 GB (2, 3 GB) isLowRamDevice or reported total under 3500 MiB Standard 4 GB up to under 6 GB 3500 to under 5300 MiB (also: memory unknown) Full 6 GB and more (6, 8, 12, 16) 5300 MiB and up Phones report less than they are sold with (kernel, GPU and modem reserve), so the cut-offs sit below the marketing sizes: a "4 GB" phone usually reports around 3.7 GiB. The cut-offs are a judgement from typical reported values, not a measurement of any specific phone; PerfProfile.memory keeps what the phone reported (not yet shown on a screen). PerfProfile (perfprofile.dart) holds every value that scales with the tier: Setting Lite Standard Full Decoded-image cache 24 MB / 60 images 48 MB / 150 100 MB / 1000 (Flutter default) Map tiles in memory / on disk 3 MB / 25 MB 6 MB / 50 MB 10 MB / 50 MB (as before) Tile download concurrency 1 2 2 Track points kept per member (stored and in memory, Private circles) 500 2000 6000 (as before) Catch-up page size (items per request) 50 100 200 (as before) Animation scale, blurred marker shadows 0.6x, off 1x, on 1x, on "Last seen" refresh tick 60 s 30 s 30 s Keep the background isolate warm no no yes (flag; see below) On-device trip/drive/week processing never allowed allowed Everything on the Full row equals the values before tiers existed, so a 6 GB+ phone behaves as in 0.24. Two flags are declared but only partly consumed: keepBackgroundIsolateWarm has no reader yet (the background location isolate is owned by the vendored backgroundlocator2 plugin), and allowOnDeviceProcessing is the single place to ask before running heavy processing locally; the processing-lanes code still decides by consent first. Direction taken for history: the phone keeps a working set (latest fix per member plus a few hundred recent points on Lite) and older history is meant to be fetched on demand. For Plain circles the day view is built from a server request (HistoryService.fetchDay). For Private circles the server holds only ciphertext, so the phone's copy is the only readable history; shrinking the cap on Lite means older points are dropped on the next write (the cap is applied when a track is written). That is a deliberate trade for 2 GB phones and is why Standard and Full keep far more. Memory pressure memorypressure.dart (MemoryPressureGuard) reacts to Flutter's didHaveMemoryPressure and to Android onTrimMemory forwarded by MainActivity over the app.openfamily/device channel: every signal at or above RUNNINGLOW: clear the image cache and live images; UIHIDDEN (20): images only; BACKGROUND (40) and above, or the legacy RUNNINGCRITICAL: also run the registered trimmers: write out pending Private-circle points and last positions (never dropped), and free the encoded avatar photos (fetched again when needed). Trimmers are registered with addTrimmer; a trimmer that throws does not stop the others. Nothing in a trimmer may lose data. Not done: releasing the vector map's tile memory on background (the vectormaptiles layer exposes no hook; its memory cache is capped per tier instead), and dropping track lists held by individual screens (not audited screen by screen; see the leak section). Build size No APK size was measured. The Docker release builds (--analyze-size, arm64, arm, combined) were started but never finished: the host was overloaded and the Gradle step stalled, then all heavy jobs were stopped. The size claims below (for example "about 40 percent smaller" for a single-ABI APK) are therefore expectations from the native-library split, not numbers; re-run flutter build apk --release --analyze-size --target-platform android-arm64 and record the baseline. What changed in the build: R8 minify and resource shrinking were already on for release (isMinifyEnabled, isShrinkResources, with proguard-android-optimize.txt). The keep rules in proguard-rules.pro are package-wide (app.openfamily., com.google.crypto.tink., yukams.app.backgroundlocator2., GMS location). Android's guidance warns that these stop R8 from shrinking those packages. They were left alone: narrowing them without a device to run the release build on (Keystore channel, background locator callbacks, Tink) risks a crash that only shows on a phone. This is the biggest unverified opportunity. The release workflow now builds three APKs from the same source and the same versionCode: the combined orbitly-<v>.apk (arm64 + armeabi-v7a), orbitly-<v>-arm64-v8a.apk and orbitly-<v>-armeabi-v7a.apk, plus the AAB. flutter build apk --split-per-abi was not used: Flutter's Gradle plugin then adds 1000 x ABI to the version code (checked in FlutterPlugin.kt: arm 1, arm64 2), which would make an arm64 split newer than the next combined release and block updates. Building each target separately keeps one code for all three files. /app.apk and the admin download pick the combined APK first (it installs everywhere, including 32-bit systems that are common on 2 GB phones), then arm64-v8a, then armeabi-v7a (pickAPKAsset in backend/internal/apkrelease, with a test). Obtainium, which takes the first .apk of a release, may now ask which file to track; set its ABI filter or the regular expression orbitly-[0-9.]+\.apk$ for the combined one. scripts/apk-size-budget.sh <apk> compares an APK with scripts/apk-size-baseline.txt and fails above +5 percent. In CI it runs after the arm64 build as a warning only (it never fails the release). Record the first baseline from a release build with scripts/apk-size-budget.sh <apk> --record. Considered and not done: --obfuscate --split-debug-info: the app prints runtimeType names in Diagnostics and the Performance screen and in self-test messages, and obfuscation would turn them into gibberish; whether persisted enum names survive it was not verified. The size win is a small part of the Dart snapshot. Locale stripping (localeFilters): the app is English only, but library strings (for example the system biometric dialog text) are translated and would turn English on other-language phones. Deferred components: the app has no feature large enough to justify the Play-only complexity. Dependency removal: all 25 direct dependencies are imported by lib/ (checked with a grep per package). The heaviest families are the map stack (fluttermap, vectormaptiles) and cryptography (pure Dart); there is no lighter drop-in. Fonts/assets: assets/ is 200 KB in total; the app uses the Material icon font, which Flutter tree-shakes. Startup main() already reads the stored settings in parallel and defers screens. Added: PerfProfile.init() runs in that same Future.wait (one small platform call, no extra step before the first frame) so caches are sized before the first screen. The memory-pressure guard is installed right before runApp. Nothing was added to the critical path that touches storage or the network. iOS Shared in Dart: tiers, PerfProfile, image cache sizing, didHaveMemoryPressure (Flutter forwards iOS memory warnings to it). Added in Swift (ios/Runner/AppDelegate.swift): a memoryInfo method on app.openfamily/device returning ProcessInfo.physicalMemory and osprocavailablememory(). Not compiled or run here; verify on a Mac before release. The tier thresholds are the same numbers; iPhones report their physical RAM (an iPhone with 4 GB reports about 3.7 to 4 GB), so the Lite/Standard boundary on iOS is the least certain part. Battery and CPU Location reporting is already adaptive (trackingcadence.dart: stationary background reports every 60 s, idle every 3 minutes, faster only while driving). It was reviewed against Android's guidance on batching and wake-ups and not changed: the outbox already batches uploads, and the Private history writes are write-behind (one rewrite per 4 s instead of per point). The tier scales the staleness timer only. Measured in the test VM (host heavily loaded, single run, NOT a phone) memoryfootprintbenchtest.dart: 6000 points written per member, then a 300-item catch-up. Process RSS in MB: Tier Points kept Catch-up page RSS start after catch-up max RSS Lite 500 50 192 214 219 Full 6000 200 191 203 208 This does not show Lite using less memory: RSS in a long-lived VM is dominated by the harness and the garbage collector's timing, and 6000 points are well under 1 MB of Dart objects. The reliable, deterministic effect is the count of points kept and stored (500 vs 6000), and fewer items per request. Smaller pages trade more requests for lower peak per request; the table suggests no memory win at 300 items. A Standard run was lost when two runs wrote to the same file. The 50-cycle screen leak test (screenleaktest.dart, leaktracker, server settings and privacy policy screens) passes in the test VM; it ignores the image cache's own stream handles. Only those two screens are covered, not the map or chat screens. The "before vs after" comparison and the 100-member marker benchmark were not done. Reproducing Unit tests: flutter test test/perf/devicetiertest.dart (tier mapping, profile values, memory-pressure behaviour). Benchmark (one tier per process for clean numbers): flutter test test/perf/memoryfootprintbenchtest.dart --plain-name 'lite:' (prints MEMMETRIC). Testing on real phones (not run) adb shell dumpsys meminfo app.openfamily # PSS by category; run before/after 30 min of use adb shell am send-trim-memory app.openfamily BACKGROUND # then check Diagnostics / dumpsys meminfo adb shell am send-trim-memory app.openfamily RUNNINGCRITICAL adb shell cat /proc/$(adb shell pidof app.openfamily)/status grep -E "VmRSSRssAnonVmSwap" adb shell am kill app.openfamily # process death, then cold start Emulator: create an AVD with 2 GB RAM (hw.ramSize=2048) and, if available, an Android Go system image (it reports isLowRamDevice). Use adb shell dumpsys meminfo to see the total; there is no on-screen tier readout yet. Developer options: turn on "Don't keep activities" and set "Background process limit" to "At most 2 processes" to force restarts and trims. DevTools Memory view (profile build) and Perfetto (perfetto.dev, heap dump explorer) for Dart and native heap. Production signal: Android vitals "Memory usage" and the low-memory-kill rate. Success looks like: no OOM or LMK kill of the foreground app during a 30-minute session with a large Private circle on a 2 GB device, and a cold start to first frame comparable with a 6 GB phone.

docs.text: Optimisation architecture Principles, per-platform budgets, the reference architecture for adaptive background tracking, the watch and server architectures, and the measurement plan that keeps Orbitly fast and light on battery from v1.0 on. Status: architecture decision for the v1.0 release train (November 2026). The work items derived from it live in the Optimisation backlog; the sourced findings behind every number are in the Research notes. Earlier, narrower performance work is documented in Performance (UI rebuilds, request counts), API efficiency (wire format) and Performance and memory on low-RAM phones (device tiers). Nothing on this page was measured on a phone or a watch while writing it. The audit below cites code; the "Measured baselines" section lists what ran on the build host and what still has to run on hardware. 1. Principles 1. The radio and the GPS chip are the battery. CPU time matters on the watch and for smoothness, but on the phone the day's drain is decided by how many seconds GPS is powered and how many times the modem leaves idle. Every design question is first "does this wake the radio or keep GPS on?". 2. Events are the clock, not timers. Activity-recognition transitions, OS geofence exits, visits and the server's live flag decide when to sample and send. Periodic timers are the fallback, never the main path, and each one must have a stated reason and period on this page or in the backlog. 3. Send changes, not samples. A viewer needs a new position when it moved on their screen; a watch needs a new snapshot when a rendered field changed; the server needs a point when it adds information to the track. Identical or sub-threshold updates are dropped at the source. 4. Batch when nobody is watching, stream when someone is. The server already tells the phone whether a member is being watched ("live": true on POST /locations). Live means immediate 1 Hz delivery; not live means the same GPS quality stored on the phone and uploaded in one request per minute. 5. The watch renders, the phone thinks. No network, no GPS, no crypto on either watch. The phone computes everything the watch shows and sends the smallest readable snapshot, at a cadence the watch asked for. 6. Small servers are the target. The reference deployment is 2 vCPU and 2-4 GB RAM shared between the API and Postgres/Timescale. Per-fix server work is a budget (statements, pool checkouts, fsyncs), not an afterthought. 7. Budgets are measured, not believed. A budget without a script or a dashboard that reports it does not exist. Every budget below names how it is measured. 8. Cut before you optimise. When a feature's cost is out of proportion to what families get from it, the recommendation is to remove or gate it, and this page says so. 2. Target budgets Targets are for release builds on the named reference devices. "Gate" is what fails CI or blocks a release; "target" is where we want to be; "store" is the threshold at which Google Play or App Store Connect flags the app. Phone app (Flutter, Android and iOS) Budget Target Gate Store threshold Measured by Cold start, process start to first frame (TTID) <= 1.5 s mid-range Android (Pixel 6a class), <= 2.5 s on a 3 GB phone, <= 0.4 s to first frame on iPhone 12 median > 2.0 s on the reference phone Android: 5 s; iOS: Organizer launch p90 scripts/perf/startup-time.sh (adb am start -W), hidden Performance screen "startup" line, Xcode Organizer Time to usable map (cached members drawn) <= 2.5 s none yet Android reportFullyDrawn (not wired) Performance screen startup steps Frame build time while panning with 6 members p90 <= 8 ms, p99 <= 16 ms > 15% regression in PERFMETRIC rebuild counts > 50% slow frames or > 0.1% frozen frames (> 700 ms) Performance screen, flutter test PERFMETRIC lines, dumpsys gfxinfo Janky frames at the display's refresh rate <= 1% on the 60 Hz budget, <= 5% at 120 Hz none yet as above Performance screen "janky frames" Foreground RAM (PSS) <= 150 MB standard tier, <= 110 MB lite tier, <= 90 MB when backgrounded under the location service none yet Play memory vitals from Feb 2027 (1 GB background on the 4 GB tier) adb shell dumpsys meminfo app.openfamily, DevTools memory view Battery, stationary day (phone at home, app not opened) <= 3% per 24 h attributable to Orbitly soak before release App Review 2.4.2 ("rapidly drain battery") 8 h batterystats soak, Settings > Battery, iOS Organizer background battery Battery, mixed day (1 h driving, 1 h walking, 22 h still) <= 8% per 24 h; driving <= 5% per hour soak before release same same Data, background, per day (mixed day) <= 10 MB none yet 50 MB/day (Play vital) Performance screen HTTP table, Android data usage per app Requests per hour, driving, nobody watching <= 90 (one batch per minute plus heartbeats) PERFMETRIC request-count tests none Performance screen HTTP table Wakeups (AlarmManager) per hour <= 6 none > 10/h (Play vital) dumpsys batterystats alarms Partial wake locks only the location service's 30 s per-update lock none 2 h/24 h background (location-tagged locks exempt) dumpsys batterystats wakelocks APK download size, arm64 release <= 32 MB; The tiers size the image cache (24 / 48 / 100 MB), history points (500 / 2000 / 6000 per member) and tile caches. Section 4 adds "raster tile mode on lite" to that list. 304 answered with one query perfendpointstest.go (OFPERF=1) WebSocket frames per stored fix per viewer 1 (today up to one per shared circle) WS counters on the Performance screen Keepalives per idle socket 1 every 60-90 s (today 2 every 30 s) packet capture or server logs Trips segmentation, one day of one user <= 5 ms BenchmarkSegmentDay (backend/internal/trips/benchtest.go) API container GOMEMLIMIT set, no OOM kills in a week docker stats, journal Postgres tuned for the container limit (sharedbuffers ~25% of its RAM) SHOW sharedbuffers Admin web Budget Target Measured by Shell JavaScript (gzip) <= 250 KB; map chunk loaded lazily Vite build output, size-limit Lighthouse performance >= 0.9 (median of 3) Lighthouse CI Polling while a page is hidden none document.hidden checks 3. Where we stand (audit summary with evidence) The phone's reporting policy is already adaptive and well tested in Dart (app/lib/services/trackingcadence.dart: driving 1 Hz, walking 5 s, stationary foreground 10 m filter, stationary background 60 s, idle 3 min after 10 min still, low-battery back-offs; app/lib/services/locationreporter.dart and backgroundlocationservice.dart apply it). The server has a stationary-dedup path, store-and-forward with a batch endpoint, gzip, ETag and compact views (v0.25). The UI work in Performance holds up in code. The gaps are in what the OS is asked for, in how often the radio is used, and in the watch cadence: Area Finding Evidence Background upload Every accepted fix is one POST /locations; the outbox and the batch endpoint are used only after a failure. At 1 Hz driving that is 3,600 requests per hour whether or not anyone is watching. app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart:239-258, locationreporter.dart:435-466 Background HTTP The background isolate uses the top-level http.post, which opens and closes a client per call: a new TCP and TLS handshake per fix. The foreground ApiClient reuses one client. backgroundlocationservice.dart:482-495; apiclient.dart:910-933 Android location request interval = fastestInterval = maxWaitTime, so the fused provider never batches; every fix wakes the Dart isolate and takes a 30 s partial wake lock. app/packages/backgroundlocator2/android/.../provider/GoogleLocationProviderClient.kt:27-35, IsolateHolderService.kt:30,175-185 Android stationary Activity recognition drops to one balanced fix per 15 min when STILL (good), but only on API 29+ with the permission granted; otherwise the Dart profile asks for high-accuracy GPS every 60 s all day. ActivityTransitionsManager.kt:36, IsolateHolderService.kt:450-460,497-510; trackingcadence.dart:33-34 Heartbeat alarm An inexact 10-minute wake-up alarm posts a heartbeat unconditionally, even when a fix was posted seconds ago. 6 wakeups per hour against a Play threshold of 10. HeartbeatScheduler.kt:30-47; backgroundlocationservice.dart:60-81 iOS background startUpdatingLocation with the best accuracy and a 50 m filter, pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically = NO, forever. The adaptive cadence (updateLocationRequest) is Android-only; iOS never lowers accuracy while still. The exit region is armed only at termination. app/packages/backgroundlocator2/ios/Classes/BackgroundLocatorPlugin.m:157,196-220,84-95; the method is absent from ios/ Geofencing Place arrivals are computed server-side on every ingest (standard circles) and on the phone per fix (private circles). No OS geofence is used anywhere, so a parked phone must keep sampling to notice leaving. backend/internal/handlers/geofenceeval.go:93-162; app/lib/services/e2ee/privateruntime.dart:669 E2EE per fix Sealing is cheap, but each private circle writes the queue, a timestamp, the chunker and history to SharedPreferences per fix (whole-file rewrites) before the batched, jittered upload. privateruntime.dart:648-681; PrefsChannelKv at :42-85 Server per fix A moving fix costs 16-28 SQL statements across 4 or more pool checkouts: token-version lookup, circle modes, the ingest transaction (6 round trips, 3 index writes), broadcast lookup, and a geofence pass with its own transaction per candidate. Every commit fsyncs. backend/internal/middleware/ingestkey.go:125-200, handlers/location.go:112-267, geofenceeval.go:93-433; migrations 000001, 000025 Server fan-out One frame per viewer per fix, duplicated per shared circle; two keepalives (server ping and client JSON ping, both 30 s); per-socket revalidation every 30 s with 2 queries. handlers/hub.go:19-84,550-576, handlers/ws.go:240-307 Watch cadence The 5 s throttle is real, but the content hash includes a millisecond timestamp and the formatted status line, so a snapshot goes out on nearly every roster frame, always setUrgent(), and each one rewrites prefs and requests a tile and complication refresh on the watch. The phone also polls alerts and sharing state over REST every minute for the watch. app/lib/services/watch/watchsnapshot.dart:141-147,246-249, watchbridge.dart:245-274,493-526, WatchBridgePlugin.kt:141-147, wear/.../SnapshotRepository.kt:43-88 Watch link state The phone's manifest only registers MESSAGERECEIVED; peer connect/disconnect is effectively never delivered, so publishing continues up to 10 min after the watch is gone and the first snapshot after reconnect can be 10 min late. app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:143-145, WatchListenerService.kt:34-50 Phone startup The session gate awaits 5-6 serial Keystore operations and a network-first /config fetch (4 s timeout) before the shell appears; the cached config is not applied on timeout. app/lib/main.dart:249-260,288-318, services/offline/offlinecache.dart:127-146 Map rendering Vector tiles are rendered on every tier; the motion ticker runs at the display rate (120 Hz on the Fold 4) while a member drives; no per-marker RepaintBoundary around blurred shadows. widgets/openfamilymaplayers.dart:91-106, screens/mapscreen.dart:239,333-339,1441-1445, memberavatarbubble.dart:253-255 Idle timers CrashWatcher reads two prefs every 3 s for the process lifetime; FamilyService keeps the socket and its two 30 s timers running while backgrounded. services/driving/crashwatcher.dart:25-38, services/familyservice.dart:417,476-477 APK Combined APK 47.8 MB (arm64 libapp.so 11.3 MB, libflutter.so 11.2 MB, dex 4.7 MB). docs.text: Optimisation backlog Prioritised, independently assignable work items that implement the optimisation architecture, each with files, expected win, risk, size, dependencies, a done criterion and a recommended agent tier. Derived from Optimisation architecture (budgets and design) and the Research notes (sources). Ordered within each group by impact on the v1.0 store and demo quality divided by effort. Sizes: S under half a day, M one to two days, L three days or more. Tiers: Sonnet for mechanical, well-specified changes; Opus for concurrency, crypto, native Android/iOS/Kotlin/Swift or SQL with data-loss risk; Fable for architecture-level changes that touch several components. Expected wins are estimates with the assumption stated; "measured" means the done criterion includes the measurement. Concurrent workstreams (do not duplicate; build on them): driving dashboard, identity and check-in bugs, Z Fold 4 rendering, Galaxy Watch Ultra Compose performance, store readiness, demo server, CI speed. Items below that border on those say so. MUST for v1.0 OPT-01 Persistent HTTP client in the background isolate Area: background tracking (Dart). Size: S. Tier: Sonnet. Files: app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart (post, postLocation, sendLocationBatch, report), app/lib/services/e2ee/privateruntime.dart (IngestKeyChannelApi also uses top-level http.post). Why: the top-level http.post opens and closes a client per call, so every background fix pays a TCP and TLS handshake and keeps the modem out of idle longer. The foreground ApiClient already shares one client. Expected win: at 1 Hz driving, 3,600 handshakes per hour become a few reconnects; per-request latency drops by one to two round trips (100-300 ms on LTE); less radio-on time. Assumption: server and proxy keep connections alive (Caddy does by default). Risk: low. A stale connection must fall back to a new one (the http package does this on ClientException; add one retry). Dependencies: none. Done: unit test that two sequential posts reuse the same http.Client instance; Performance screen HTTP p50 for POST /locations from the background isolate recorded before and after on a phone. OPT-02 iOS: adaptive cadence and a cheap stationary mode in the native plugin Area: background tracking (iOS native, Objective-C). Size: M-L. Tier: Opus. Files: app/packages/backgroundlocator2/ios/Classes/BackgroundLocatorPlugin.m, Helpers/MethodCallHelper.m, Globals.m, lib/backgroundlocator.dart (updateLocationRequest already sends the method; iOS must handle it), app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart:125-143 (remove the Android-only assumption). Why: iOS runs startUpdatingLocation with best accuracy and pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically = NO permanently; nothing lowers accuracy while still. Apple's energy guide says to drop to kCLLocationAccuracyThreeKilometers in the background and prefer region monitoring. App Review 2.4.2 covers battery drain. Do: implement updateLocationRequest on iOS mapping the profile to desiredAccuracy, distanceFilter and activityType (.otherNavigation when fast); when the profile is stationary or idle, set 3 km accuracy, a 200 m filter, and arm a 150 m exit-only CLCircularRegion around the last fix (observeRegionForLocation exists); on region exit or a visit departure, switch back to the walking profile. Keep significant-change monitoring on. Expected win: GPS-on time while still from continuous to near zero on iOS; the dominant iOS battery item. Assumption: most of a day is still. Risk: medium: region exits arrive 3-5 min late (Apple), so the first fix after leaving is later than today; the Dart cadence must treat the first fix after a region exit as "moving" at once (driveEnterInstantSpeedMps covers driving; add a walking shortcut). Dependencies: none. Done: compiles in the iOS CI build; a simulator run with a simulated route shows the profile switch in logs; a TestFlight day on one iPhone with Settings > Battery screenshot recorded in the release notes. OPT-03 Batch uploads when nobody is watching ("live" switches streaming on) Area: background tracking (Dart) and server contract. Size: M. Tier: Opus (two isolates, outbox consistency, live/not-live race). Files: app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart (onLocationUpdate, sendAndDrain), app/lib/services/locationreporter.dart (deliver), app/lib/services/locationoutbox.dart (flush timer and a cheaper store: an append-only file or sqflite instead of a JSON blob in prefs), app/lib/services/liveboost.dart, backend/internal/handlers/locationbatch.go (return the same live flag as the single endpoint), docs/live-tracking-client.md (policy table), app/test/services/location. Why: every fix is a request today; the batch endpoint is only a failure path. See architecture section 4. Expected win: requests per hour while driving unwatched 3,600 to about 60; server statements per fix from 16-28 to 2 pipelined per point; measurable radio idle time; background data per day down by the request overhead (about 600 bytes of headers per request, 2 MB per driving hour). Assumption: viewers watch for minutes, not hours. Risk: medium: a viewer opening the map must see fresh data within seconds. The /locations/watch call from the viewer already sends a liveboost push to the subject; the first batch response with live: true must trigger an immediate post of the newest fix. Test the race where the phone switches from batch to live while a batch is in flight. Dependencies: OPT-01 (otherwise batch posts also reconnect). Done: PERFMETRIC request-count tests for a simulated 10-minute drive watched and unwatched; BenchmarkIngestBatch100 per-point cost recorded; server test that the batch response carries live. OPT-04 Heartbeat only when nothing was reported Area: background tracking (Dart). Size: S. Tier: Sonnet. Files: app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart:60-81 (onHeartbeatTick), optionally app/packages/backgroundlocator2/android/.../HeartbeatScheduler.kt:30 (interval stays 10 min). Why: the alarm's POST is unconditional; while fixes flow it only adds a request and a radio wake every 10 min. Expected win: 6 requests per hour removed whenever reports flow; Android vitals wakeups unchanged (the alarm still fires; it just does no network). Risk: none (the server refreshes lastseen on every report already). Dependencies: none. Done: unit test with a fake clock: heartbeat skipped when lastPostAt is within 10 min. OPT-05 Android: let the fused provider batch when not live Area: background tracking (Android native, Kotlin). Size: S. Tier: Opus. Files: app/packages/backgroundlocator2/android/.../provider/GoogleLocationProviderClient.kt:27-35, provider/LocationRequestOptions.kt, IsolateHolderService.kt (updateLocationRequest), lib/backgroundlocator.dart (updateLocationRequest gains maxWaitMs), app/lib/services/backgroundlocationservice.dart:125-143. Why: maxWaitTime = interval disables batching; every fix wakes the Dart isolate and takes a 30 s wake lock. Google: set the max update delay "several times larger than the interval". Do: pass maxWaitTime = 60 s for walking and driving profiles when not live (OPT-03's flag), = interval when live; move from the deprecated LocationRequest.create() to LocationRequest.Builder with setMaxUpdateDelayMillis. Expected win: isolate wakeups and wake-lock acquisitions while driving unwatched from 3,600 to 60 per hour; Dart-side CPU in the background isolate down proportionally. Risk: low-medium: batched LocationResult carries several locations; LocationParserUtil must forward all of them in order (today it takes the last). Needs flutter build apk --release to prove it compiles. Dependencies: OPT-03 for the flag (can land first with a constant). Done: Kotlin unit test for the request builder; release APK built; a logcat capture on a phone showing batched results. OPT-06 Stationary background profile without activity recognition Area: background tracking (Dart policy). Size: S. Tier: Sonnet. Files: app/lib/services/trackingcadence.dart:33-34,431-448, app/test/services/trackingcadencetest.dart, docs/live-tracking-client.md. Why: when the native STILL profile is unavailable (API < 29, permission denied, non-Google client) the Dart stationary profile asks for high-accuracy GPS every 60 s all day. Do: stationary background becomes balanced accuracy, 180 s, 0 m filter (the server dedup and the heartbeat keep liveness); idle stays 3 min balanced with a 30 m filter. Expected win: GPS fixes per hour while still from 60 to 20 on phones without activity recognition; "last seen" freshness stays under 10 min (heartbeat). Risk: low. Dependencies: none. Done: cadence unit tests updated; policy table in the docs updated. OPT-07 Watch snapshots only on meaningful change, at the cadence the watch asked for Area: watch (Dart bridge, Kotlin, Swift). Size: M. Tier: Opus (three code bases, one contract). Files: app/lib/services/watch/watchsnapshot.dart (watchContentHash, member: snap lat/lon to 50 m, bucket fixAt to the minute, drop the formatted line, send since/lastSeen timestamps), app/lib/services/watch/watchbridge.dart (minInterval 5 s when a watching command is fresh, 60 s otherwise; alerts, lastCommand, unread and sharing bypass the slow tier), wear/.../logic/Presenter.kt, wear/.../logic/Format.kt, wear/.../WearViewModel.kt and MainActivity.kt (send watching on RESUMED and every 30 s while resumed), app/ios/OrbitlyWatch/PhoneLink.swift, Format.swift, docs/design/WATCHAPPS.md, docs/design/WATCHAPPSAPPLE.md. Why: the hash includes a millisecond timestamp and a formatted status line, so almost every roster frame produces a snapshot (up to 720 per hour) that wakes the watch's listener service. Expected win: background snapshots per hour from up to 720 to 12 or fewer when idle and about 60 while someone drives; watch listener wakes, prefs writes and Bluetooth transfers down by the same factor; no minute-tick snapshots. Risk: medium: SOS and check-in results must still arrive immediately (bypass list); ages formatted on the watch must match the phone's wording (shared test vectors in docs/design/WATCHAPPS.md). Dependencies: none; coordinate with the Galaxy Watch Ultra Compose workstream on Screens.kt. Done: Dart unit test that 100 jittery frames within 50 m produce one snapshot; Kotlin unit test for the age formatter; a dumpsys activity service WearableService count on a watch for one idle hour recorded. OPT-08 Watch: urgent only when it matters, gate surface refreshes, drop REST polling Area: watch (Dart, Kotlin). Size: S-M. Tier: Sonnet (Dart and Kotlin parts are mechanical). Files: app/android/app/src/main/kotlin/.../WatchBridgePlugin.kt:141-147 (setUrgent only when the Dart side passes urgent: true), app/lib/services/watch/watchbridge.dart:227-306,500-526 (feed alerts, sharing, unread from AlertEvents, FamilyService.onSharingChanged, ChatEvents.unreadTotal instead of AlertService.list and SharingService.pauseStatus every minute; run the members pre-hash before source.read()), wear/.../data/SnapshotRepository.kt:38-88 (surface key; requestUpdate and requestUpdateAll only when it changed or 60 s passed; write the prefs copy at most once a minute), CircleTileService.kt, NearestComplicationService.kt. Expected win: about 120 HTTP requests per hour removed from the phone while a watch is connected; immediate Bluetooth syncs from 720 per hour to only user-visible events; tile and complication service binds from about 2,000 per hour to about 100. Risk: low (position staleness is bounded by OPT-07's tiers). Dependencies: OPT-07 for the tiers (can land first). Done: Dart test that an unchanged roster performs no HTTP; Kotlin test for the surface key; release Wear APK built. OPT-09 Wear OS: event-driven phone link state Area: watch (Android native). Size: S. Tier: Opus. Files: wear/app/src/main/res/values/wear.xml (declare a capability), app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:139-147 (add CAPABILITYCHANGED to the listener filter), app/android/.../WatchListenerService.kt (onCapabilityChanged drives peerChanged and the sign-out debt; remove the dead onPeerConnected path), docs/design/WATCHAPPS.md:76-78. Why: the current manifest never delivers peer events, so the phone publishes to an absent watch for up to 10 min and the first snapshot after reconnect can be 10 min late. Expected win: zero snapshots built while no watch is connected; first snapshot within seconds of reconnect. Risk: low; confirm on a device with logcat (the finding is inferred from the manifest). Dependencies: none. Done: release phone and Wear APKs built; logcat shows onCapabilityChanged on watch connect and disconnect. OPT-10 Wear OS: baseline profile and release-build verification Area: watch (Gradle, Kotlin). Size: S-M. Tier: Sonnet. Files: wear/app/build.gradle.kts (androidx.profileinstaller, a committed baseline-prof.txt covering MainActivity, WearApp, ScreenList, Snapshot.parse, tile and complication services), wear/.../ui/Screens.kt (items(rows, key = { it.id }), remember(snapshot, here) for Presenter.rows), wear/.../data/SnapshotRepository.kt and WearViewModel.kt (content flow with distinctUntilChanged, timestamp in a separate flow, 60 s age ticker). Why: Google names baseline profiles and R8 as the first Wear performance tools; the Ultra's Exynos W1000 is fast, so lag there is software. The Galaxy Watch Ultra Compose workstream owns the specific jank fixes; this item is the build-level part and the list keys. Expected win: 15-30% faster cold start (Google's range; Todoist measured 14% on Wear), fewer first-scroll jank frames; keep-alive snapshots no longer recompose every screen. Risk: low. Dependencies: none. Done: adb shell dumpsys package dexopt shows speed-profile for the Wear package on the Ultra after bg-dexopt-job; stopwatch cold start before and after recorded. OPT-11 Phone startup: nothing but the session check before the shell Area: phone app (Dart). Size: S. Tier: Sonnet. Why: the gate awaits 5-6 serial Keystore round trips and a network-first /config with a 4 s timeout; on timeout the cached style is not applied. Expected win: splash shortened by 100-400 ms on low-end phones (Keystore) and by up to 4 s on slow links; correct map style on an offline start. Risk: low (housekeeping is idempotent; background start already waits for the first frame). Dependencies: none. Done: startup request test shows the gate issues only the session check before first frame; scripts/perf/startup-time.sh median on the Fold 4 recorded.
