docs.title: Research notes: how serious apps optimise battery, latency and smoothness
docs.summary: Sourced findings (official docs, engineering blogs, WWDC and Google I/O talks) behind the optimisation architecture and backlog, grouped by platform, with the numbers that set our budgets.
docs.text: Research notes: how serious apps optimise battery, latency and smoothness Sourced findings (official docs, engineering blogs, WWDC and Google I/O talks) behind the optimisation architecture and backlog, grouped by platform, with the numbers that set our budgets. Companion pages: Optimisation architecture (what we do with these findings) and the Optimisation backlog (the work items). Collected 2026-11-08; Apple pages were read through their .md documentation endpoints and WWDC transcripts because the HTML is script-rendered. Vendor numbers (Life360, Timescale, Samsung) are marked as self-reported. 1. Background location at scale What the big apps do Life360 publishes no interval. Its support page describes an algorithm that "helps us decide when to wake up your phone and update your location to avoid leaving your GPS on", budgets "about 10% shorter battery life in a 24-hour period", and turns on "high-precision GPS" only "when the device is in transit". https://support.life360.com/hc/en-us/articles/23053716563223-Life360-and-Battery-Usage (self-reported). The CEO described the trigger: at a known place it "will shut off GPS and listen for signals that you're changing locations" (Wi-Fi set churn, cell), then "Once you're in motion, it will flip the GPS on". https://venturebeat.com/ai/life360-battery Apple Find My network: offline finding relays end-to-end encrypted BLE sightings; "Approximately every 15 minutes, the public key is replaced"; "minimal impact on battery life". No person-to-person cadence is published. https://support.apple.com/guide/security/find-my-security-sec6cbc80fd0/web Google Find Hub throttles by design: it "limits the number of times that a nearby Android device can contribute a location report" and "throttles how frequently the owner ... can request an updated location"; devices near the user's home do not contribute. https://security.googleblog.com/2024/04/find-my-device-network-security-privacy-protections.html Strava asks for high-accuracy mode and every OEM battery saver disabled; Beacon live sharing is reported at roughly 15 s updates. https://support.strava.com/hc/en-us/articles/216918967 , https://www.androidauthority.com/strava-beacon-location-sharing-2741621 Google Maps Timeline is on-device since December 2024 and publishes no cadence. https://support.google.com/maps/answer/6258979 , https://9to5google.com/2024/12/11/google-maps-on-device-timeline/ OwnTracks (open source) documents its two modes: significant mode publishes only at ">500m and at most once every 5 minutes" (iOS) or every 15 minutes with a 500 m displacement filter (Android); move mode is 100 m / 300 s on iOS and a 10 s high-power interval on Android, recommended "while charging or during trips". Friends' positions ride back in the upload response, so a backgrounded client needs no second channel. https://owntracks.org/booklet/features/location/ , https://owntracks.org/booklet/tech/http/ Traccar stores positions append-only and keeps "Last position id ... in the devices table" (a latest-row pointer), with one WebSocket carrying devices, positions, events. https://www.traccar.org/forums/topic/mass-query-last-position/ , https://www.traccar.org/traccar-api/ iOS Core Location power tools Significant-location-change: "500 meters or more ... not expect notifications more frequently than once every five minutes"; relaunches a terminated app. Apple's energy guide warns it runs "around the clock" and prefers region and visit monitoring. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/startmonitoringsignificantlocationchanges() , https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Performance/Conceptual/EnergyGuide-iOS/LocationBestPractices.html Region monitoring: "up to 20 regions at a time", radii "between 1 and 400 meters work better", delivery "within 3 to 5 minutes on average". CLMonitor (iOS 17) keeps the 20-condition cap, persists until reboot. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/startmonitoring(for:) , https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/monitoring-the-user-s-proximity-to-geographic-regions Visits (CLVisit): system-detected arrivals and departures, works with reduced accuracy, relaunches the app. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/clvisit CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates (iOS 17) pauses itself: "once the device is in stationary state for a sufficient amount of time ... trigger Automatic Pause" and resumes "without any user interaction". CLBackgroundActivitySession owns the blue indicator and "you must start the new session from the foreground". https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2023/10180/ , https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/handling-location-updates-in-the-background iOS 18 CLServiceSession: "Always authorization will only be effective when you hold one of these"; approximate location "is updated only every 15 to 20 minutes". https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10212/ Defaults that cost: desiredAccuracy defaults to kCLLocationAccuracyBest; pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically defaults to true but a pause "ends access to location changes until the app launches again" for When-In-Use apps, so Apple suggests disabling it and dropping to kCLLocationAccuracyThreeKilometers in the background instead. Deferred updates are deprecated since iOS 13. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/desiredaccuracy , https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/cllocationmanager/pauseslocationupdatesautomatically CMMotionActivityManager reports "walking, running, in a vehicle, or stationary" from the motion coprocessor. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coremotion/cmmotionactivitymanager Android Google's battery model is accuracy x frequency x latency: "Pass the largest possible value when using setIntervalMillis()"; set setMaxUpdateDelayMillis() "several times larger than the interval" so fixes arrive in batches; geofence responsiveness "five minutes or larger is recommended"; avoid PRIORITYHIGHACCURACY "for sustained background work". Worked example: 10 min interval + 60 min max delay "delivers approximately six location data points in a batch approximately every hour". https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/battery , https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/battery/optimize LocationRequest.Builder: setMaxUpdateDelayMillis (default 0, no batching), setMinUpdateDistanceMeters, setWaitForAccurateLocation. https://developers.google.com/android/reference/com/google/android/gms/location/LocationRequest.Builder Android 8+ background limits: background apps "can receive location updates only a few times each hour"; a foreground service is the way out, and on Android 11+ starting one from the background needs ACCESSBACKGROUNDLOCATION. https://developer.android.com/about/versions/oreo/background-location-limits Geofencing API: "limit of 100 per app, per device user"; minimum radius "between 100 - 150 meters"; latency "usually ... less than 2 minutes", "up to 6 minutes" when long stationary; re-register after reboot. https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/geofencing Activity Recognition Transition API: ENTER/EXIT for INVEHICLE, ONBICYCLE, RUNNING, STILL, WALKING; "The latency of event detection might vary by device." https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/location/transitions Doze: while-idle alarms "cannot fire ... more than once per nine minutes, per app"; standby buckets cap alarms (working set 10/h, frequent 2/h, rare 1/h); apps holding ACCESSBACKGROUNDLOCATION are exempt from the restricted bucket; Doze exemption is "Acceptable" for a "Safety app. Apps that keep their users and their families safe." https://developer.android.com/training/monitoring-device-state/doze-standby , https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/power/power-details , https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/appstandby Foreground service types (Android 14): foregroundServiceType="location" plus FOREGROUNDSERVICELOCATION, also declared in Play Console. https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types Exact alarms: SCHEDULEEXACTALARM is user-revocable and "not pre-granted to fresh installs of apps targeting Android 13"; inexact windows are clipped to 10 min; WorkManager periodic minimum 15 min. https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/alarms/schedule OEM killers: Samsung puts "any app which is not started in 3 days ... to sleep" by default; One UI 6 honours Android 14 foreground services. https://dontkillmyapp.com/samsung Adaptive sampling RAPS (MobiSys 2010): turn GPS on only when position uncertainty exceeds a threshold, gate on a duty-cycled accelerometer, blacklist cell signatures where GPS fails; "increase phone lifetimes by more than a factor of 3.8 over an approach where GPS is always on." https://solar.cs.ucl.ac.uk/appoptimization.github.io/publications/PKG2010 Radio baselines (old hardware, ordering still holds): GPS "approximately 400 mW", Wi-Fi 55 mW idle with ~1100 mW probe spikes; lifetimes 9 h GPS vs 40 h Wi-Fi vs 60 h GSM. https://eudl.eu/doi/10.1007/978-3-642-12607-914 A commercial activity-tiered tracker reports "less than 1% per hour" stationary at 10 min reports, "2-3% per hour" walking at 5 min, "5-6% per hour" driving with GPS every 30 s (vendor numbers). https://blog.corvusgps.com/?p=809 Urban GPS "can be off by 50 meters or more"; Uber corrects server-side with map matching and a particle filter. https://www.uber.com/blog/rethinking-gps/ Trajectory compression: Douglas-Peucker is lossy and batch; delta encoding is "lossless ... zero error and a time complexity of O(n)". https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s13369-024-08956-0.pdf 2. Wear OS Google's Wear performance guide: "Start with the most effective performance tool types: baseline profiles (including startup profiles) and the R8 code optimizer." Verify with adb shell dumpsys package dexopt showing status=speed-profile; debug builds "impose a significant performance cost". Public Wear datapoint: Todoist ~14% median startup improvement. https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/compose/performance , https://doist-dev.pages.dev/android-app-baseline-profiles Compose hygiene applies: remember expensive work, stable keys and contentType, lambda modifiers, and "Use Row or Column for small, bounded lists (1 to 10 items)". https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/performance/bestpractices Horologist UI is retired: "use the components in M3"; Wear Compose Material 3 1.5.0 stable since 27 Aug 2025. https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/compose/migrate-to-material3 , https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/wear-compose-m3 Tiles: freshness "should not be used to update your tile more frequently than once a minute, and the system may throttle"; the power guide says "Disable automatic refresh, or increase the refresh rate to 2 hours or longer" and "Don't schedule work for your tile or complication when the user isn't interacting with it". https://developer.android.com/reference/androidx/wear/tiles/TileBuilders.Tile.Builder , https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/apps/power Complications: UPDATEPERIODSECONDS minimum 300 s, 0 means push-driven via ComplicationDataSourceUpdateRequester; onComplicationRequest "should ideally just return the value with minimal computation"; use TimeDifferenceComplicationText so ages tick without pushes. https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2025/08/building-complication-data-sources-wear-os.html Ongoing Activity is for work "likely to last longer than one minute" and explicitly not for "the status of an updating app". https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/ongoing-activity Always-on: at most 15% lit pixels, minute-granular updates, "--" for live values, no animation; keepScreenOn "severely impacts battery life". https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/always-on Data Layer: payload "limited to 100 KB"; non-urgent items "might delay up to 30 minutes ... usually ... only a few minutes"; "Clients should only setUrgent() for DataItems which need to be delivered right away"; "Transmit state changes instead of configuring rapid updates"; "Only transmit state changes that update your UI"; audit with adb shell dumpsys activity service WearableService. https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/data/data-items , https://developers.google.com/android/reference/com/google/android/gms/wearable/PutDataRequest , https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/apps/power Location on the watch: "WHS is recommended for all workout tracking"; FLP on a watch at balanced power, "no more than once per minute"; power table ranks network "Very high", GPS "High", Bluetooth "Medium". https://developer.android.com/training/wearables/apps/location-detection Galaxy Watch Ultra: 590 mAh, Exynos W1000 (3 nm, 1x A78 + 4x A55, 1.4 GHz), 2 GB RAM, 480x480; "Up to 60" h with AOD, 80 h without (Samsung, self-reported). Lag on this chip is software, not hardware. https://www.samsung.com/uk/support/mobile-devices/how-does-the-galaxy-watch-ultra-and-galaxy-watch7-compare-to-their-previous-models/ , https://semiconductor.samsung.com/processor/wearable-processor/exynos-w1000/ Wear OS 5 and 6: "running a marathon consumes up to 20% less power on Wear OS 5"; Wear OS 6 "up to 10% improvement in battery life", apps targeting SDK 36 are always-on by default with updates "as infrequent as once per minute". https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2024/05/whats-new-in-wear-os-io-24.html , https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2025/05/whats-new-in-wear-os-6.html Vitals per watch model: crash 4%, ANR 5%, excessive battery 1%; ANR triggers include startForeground within 5 s and heavy work in composable bodies. https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/vitals , https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/vitals/anr 3. Apple Watch Foreground-first: "Apps on watchOS primarily run in the foreground to limit the impact on system resources." Background refresh is "approximately four tasks per hour for each app with a complication on the active watch face", shared by all complications; inside a task "a maximum of four seconds of active CPU time", "15 seconds of total time", "No networking activity is allowed". https://developer.apple.com/documentation/watchkit/background-execution , https://developer.apple.com/documentation/watchkit/wkapplicationrefreshbackgroundtask , https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2020/10049/ WatchConnectivity semantics: updateApplicationContext "replaces the previous dictionary" and is sent "when the opportunity arises"; transferUserInfo is "queued ... delivered in the order in which they were sent"; sendMessage from the watch "wakes up the corresponding iOS app in the background" but the reverse does not; isReachable on the watch is true o

docs.text: Privacy model v1: is it still end-to-end? An independent review of who can read what in Orbitly today, a plain answer to "is it still end-to-end encryption if the server is in the group", and the recommended v1.0 positioning, naming and defaults. Status: review, 2026-11-08, branch feat/privacy-model, against main at v0.25.2 plus the token-refresh hotfix. Companion: PRIVACYMODELBACKLOG.md (prioritised change requests). Background: E2EE.md, PRIVACYPROCESSING.md, E2EECHAT.md. Everything marked verified was checked in the code named next to it; nothing was run against the production server. Phone behaviour on real devices was not exercised. 1. The short answer for the owner Is it still end-to-end encryption with the server in the group? For some data, yes; for some, no; and the app currently says "yes" for all of it. Precisely: End-to-end encryption is a statement about who holds the keys, not about where the bytes travel. Data sealed under the phone key (CK) can only be opened by circle members' phones and the viewers they approved. The server never receives CK (database trigger e2eewrapguard, phone check checkWrapRecipient, sidecar alarm exit 7: verified). That part is real end-to-end encryption and it did not get weaker. A member on the server lane seals their location under the server key (SK), which the server holds. For that member's location, trips, places, events and check-ins the server is one of the ends. Cryptographically that is no different from a Normal circle: the server reads it and keeps a plaintext copy in locations. Calling that member's data "end-to-end encrypted" is false; the honest term is "encrypted in transit, readable by your server". Chat in a Private circle is always under CK (CHECK constraint e2eeitemschatphoneonly, verified), so chat stays end-to-end encrypted even for server-lane members. That is a genuine improvement over Normal circles. The server key is registered under the platform admin's own account, and server help only works in circles where that account is a live member (e2eeserverassist, migration 000220processinglanes.up.sql line 168, verified). So wherever the server helps, the person who runs the server is already in the circle and reads everyone, including "phone only" members, on their own phone. "Phone only" therefore protects against the machine (a stolen disk, a hosting company, a backup, a breach of the server software), not against the person who runs it. That is still worth a lot, but it must be said that way. Is there a point having the server as a member? Yes, but less than it looks. The features that truly need a reader that never sleeps are few (section 4). Most of what the server lane gives today (trips, driving reports, weekly summary, history, admin map, Dawarich, Home Assistant) is either already computable on phones, or needs only a non-reading server that stores ciphertext, or is an operator convenience. The server lane is the right answer for families who trust their own box and want everything to "just work" with no battery cost; it is the wrong default for a rented VPS. Are we going the right direction or backwards? The architecture is going forward: two key lines, per-member signed choice, CK never on the server, chat always phone-to-phone, transparency log. The defaults and the words went backwards in v0.24 to v0.25: a circle that is mostly server-processed still shows "End-to-end encrypted", members are switched to the server by a server-wide setting without a tap ("auto-apply"), and a few leaks undercut the phone-only promise (section 3). Fix the words and those leaks before v1.0 and the model is defensible and differentiating. Do not market "end-to-end encrypted" for a circle; market it for people who keep data on their phone and for chat in Private circles. 2. What each party can learn (truthful matrix) Legend: Reads = can read content; Meta = metadata only; No = nothing useful. "Server lane" = a member of a Private circle whose own signed lane is server (including members auto-applied). "Phone lane" = a member of a Private circle who keeps data on the phone. All "verified" items were checked in code. 2.1 Location, places, trips, events, check-ins Party Normal circle Private, server-lane member Private, phone-lane member Server operator (DB, files, process) Reads everything, history 90 days, last position kept until account deletion Reads everything the phone sends after the lane was signed: fixes, history, trips, driving, places they created, events, check-ins (SK), stored as plaintext in locations/memberpositions Meta (see 2.3). But see leaks L1 and L2 below: SOS/help/check-in coordinates and place-picker coordinates reach the server in plaintext Platform admin in the admin web Only with ADMINLOCATIONACCESS=true (audited). The switch is a UI/API rule; anyone with DB access reads regardless Same as Normal Sees "keeps data on phone" flag and counts; no data Another circle member Reads everything the circle shares Reads everything (holds CK and SK) Reads everything (holds CK). Opting out never hides you from members Member's approved web viewer / Dawarich bridge n/a (server feeds Dawarich directly) Bridge: SK only in circles with server help. Web viewer: SK and, after a warning, CK Web viewer with CK: reads. Bridge in a circle without server help holds CK and exports every member to its owner's Dawarich Network attacker (no TLS break) Meta: IPs, timing, sizes Same Same TLS-terminating proxy (Cloudflare tunnel, CDN, reverse proxy you do not run) Reads everything, plus session tokens (can act as any user) Reads plaintext? No: items are sealed. Sees tokens, SOS/check-in coordinates (L1), geocoder queries (L2), and can serve modified web-viewer JavaScript Same as server-lane, except nothing under SK exists Stolen DB dump / DB backup Everything Plaintext copies of server-lane data. SK ciphertext needs the server device key, which is not in the DB Ciphertext + metadata Stolen whole disk or VPS snapshot (incl. .env and volumes) Everything Everything above plus the server device key and OPENFAMILYDATAKEY (it sits in .env on the same disk), so also future SK items until the key is revoked; plus JWTSECRET (can mint a session for any account) Ciphertext + metadata; still cannot get CK Lost or stolen phone, powered off / before first unlock Session token in secure storage; nothing else readable Same Same; vault cannot be opened Lost or stolen phone, unlocked once since boot, then locked With app-level code execution or a forensic exploit: tokens, local trail Same, plus the Keystore can be asked to open the vault (no setUnlockedDeviceRequired since 0.24.2) Same; on-device history and parked fixes are plaintext in the app sandbox anyway Lost phone that someone can unlock Everything the owner sees Same Same Apple (APNs) Visible push text: place name and circle name by default ("A family member arrived at School", "New message in Family"); person names and chat text previews if the recipient turned names on or VERBOSEPUSH=true; device token, timing, IP Private circles: silent e2eewake with circle id only; no text Same Google No FCM, no Google Play services push. docs.title: Wear OS performance
docs.summary: What was changed to make the Orbitly watch app smoother and lighter on the battery, what is still unmeasured, and how to measure it on a real Galaxy Watch Ultra.

headings.text: What the audit found, and what changed
Things checked that were already right
How to measure on the Galaxy Watch Ultra
Status of OPT-10 (baseline profile and list keys)

docs.text: Wear OS performance What was changed to make the Orbitly watch app smoother and lighter on the battery, what is still unmeasured, and how to measure it on a real Galaxy Watch Ultra. Honesty first. No watch was available while this was written. The findings below come from reading the code and from what compiles and passes unit tests. Nothing here was timed on a device. Every "faster" claim is a design argument until you run the measurements in the last section. What the audit found, and what changed Area Before Now Reading the saved snapshot at start Synchronous disk read and JSON parse in the view model constructor, on the main thread, before the first frame Read and parsed on a background thread. The screen shows nothing for that moment instead of a wrong "Sign in on your phone" message Every push from the phone Parsed, written to disk, and the tile and complication were redrawn, even when the text was identical (also on every app resume) An identical item (same text, same login) is dropped with one string comparison. No parse, no disk write, no redraw Parsing on resume syncNow parsed on the main thread Runs on the default background dispatcher Last known location Read on the main thread on each resume Background thread Tile request Disk and parse on the main thread on the first call Built on a worker thread Complication request Same Built on the default dispatcher SOS hold button The whole list was recomposed every 50 ms while the finger was down The list recomposes only when the phase or the countdown second changes. The progress ring reads its value while drawing, so only that canvas redraws Compass Sensor kept registered while the app was in the background with the screen on; whole screen recomposed 5 times a second Registered only while the app is resumed and not in ambient mode, sampling requested at 5 Hz, unregistered on pause. Low-pass filter with a 1.5 degree dead band. The arrow reads the heading while drawing, so only the arrow redraws, and not at all when the watch is held still List rows No keys, rows rebuilt on every recomposition, second line string built per row per recomposition Stable keys (ids, made unique when the snapshot is parsed so duplicate ids cannot crash a list), rows remembered per snapshot and location, second line built once Compose stability List fields make the model classes "unstable" stabilityconfig.conf marks the immutable model classes as stable so unchanged screens are skipped Avatars Clip plus background One shape-aware background. Avatars were already initials only; there is no image loading in the app Release build Minified and resource-shrunk Also isDebuggable = false stated explicitly, androidx.profileinstaller added, a hand-written baseline profile under wear/app/src/main/baseline-prof.txt Manifest Only the watch feature GPS, compass and accelerometer declared required=false so Play does not hide the app from a watch that lacks one Things checked that were already right No polling anywhere. The app is woken only by the Wearable Data Layer when the phone writes the snapshot or connects. No foreground service and no wake lock taken by the app. WAKELOCK is declared only because AmbientLifecycleObserver requires the permission. The only continuous sensor is the rotation vector on the Direction screen, now bound to the resumed lifecycle. Ambient mode: AmbientLifecycleObserver is registered; in ambient the theme switches to black with outlined chips, the home screen shows only the nearest person, the compass sensor stops, and the vignette and scroll indicator are not drawn. The only moving thing in ambient is the system clock. Hardware buttons: no key handler is installed, so the Quick button and the power button keep their system behavior. Rotary and touch-bezel scrolling is handled by ScalingLazyColumn itself. Complication: UPDATEPERIODSECONDS = 0, content is pushed after a new snapshot. Tile: freshness interval 0, redrawn on a new snapshot and whenever the system shows it. No Application class and no dependency injection: nothing runs before the activity, so there is no Application start-up cost to remove. minSdk 30 (Wear OS 3 and up), targetSdk 35. Build result cd wear && ./gradlew --no-daemon :app:testDebugUnitTest :app:assembleRelease (in the Flutter image): 36 unit tests, 0 failures; the unsigned release APK is 3.2 MB and contains assets/dexopt/baseline.prof (7 KB) and baseline.profm, plus the profileinstaller version marker. Whether the profile actually speeds up start on the Ultra is unmeasured. Known and left alone: Android lint (non-fatal here, abortOnError = false) flags BINDLISTENER on DataLayerService as deprecated because it wakes the service for every Data Layer event of this app. Switching to filtered DATACHANGED and MESSAGERECEIVED filters would save a few wake-ups, but connect and disconnect events need the broad listener, and a wrong filter would silently stop all phone pushes, which cannot be tested without a watch. The phone side WatchBridge (app/lib/services/watch/watchbridge.dart) decides how often the watch is woken. The full rules are in Watch apps, Cadence; in short: Nothing in the snapshot changes by itself as time passes. The status line no longer carries "25 min ago" or the exact speed; the watch formats ages from fixAt and the new lineAt. Each new snapshot is compared with the last one the watch got: alerts, command answers and a new sign-in go out at once and urgent; unread and sharing within 5 s; a move of more than 100 m, a state, place or battery step at the pace of the tier; GPS jitter and newer fix times only with the keep-alive. The watch app sends visible (every 60 s while on screen), visible ambient and hidden. Visible: at most every 5 s, urgent. Ambient: meaningful changes once a minute. Hidden (default): meaningful changes at most every 2 minutes, not urgent (the Data Layer may batch them), keep-alive every 10 minutes. Alerts and the sharing pause are no longer fetched every minute; they are refreshed on live-socket events and every 10 minutes (126 requests an hour down to 18 while a watch is connected). Link state: the Wear app advertises the orbitlywatchapp capability; the phone listens for it at runtime and through WatchListenerService, so it stops building snapshots for a watch that left within seconds instead of up to 10 minutes. Measured in app/test/services/watch/watchcadencetest.dart (simulated hours, before = the previous logic on the same data): Hour Before After someone driving, watch app not open 720 snapshots, all urgent 31, 2 urgent (start-up and first roster) still family with GPS jitter 125, all urgent 7, 2 urgent still family, 4 alerts, 20 messages, a pause 125, all urgent 31, 7 urgent someone driving, watch app open 720 721 (all urgent, by design) someone driving, watch in always-on 720 61 On the watch, SurfaceGate (wear/.../logic/SurfaceGate.kt) redraws the tile and complication only when what they show changed: at most about 60 redraws in an hour of driving with the app open, instead of one per snapshot (720), and none for keep-alives. Tested in CadenceLogicTest.kt. To check it on a watch: adb shell dumpsys activity service WearableService on the phone and the watch lists the Data Layer items and their delivery; over one idle hour with the app closed expect about 6 to 7 snapshot writes. adb logcat -s WearableService shows each onDataChanged. Not measured yet. Baseline profile A baseline profile tells Android which classes and methods to compile ahead of time at install, so the first launch and the first scroll do not run in the slow interpreter. wear/app/src/main/baseline-prof.txt is hand-written and covers the app's own start-up and screen code. AGP packs it into the release APK as assets/dexopt/baseline.prof, and androidx.profileinstaller installs it on first run (and when the system does not do it itself). Compose and Wear Compose libraries ship their own profiles inside their AARs, and these are merged in. A hand-written profile is a fallback. A generated one is better because it lists exactly what ran. Generating needs a watch or a Wear emulator, which this build environment does not have; see "Generate a real profile" below. How to measure on the Galaxy Watch Ultra Connect with Wireless debugging (Developer options, ADB debugging, Debug over Wi-Fi) and adb pair / adb connect. Use the release APK; a debug build is much slower and tells you nothing. 1. Cold start time: adb shell am force-stop app.openfamily adb shell am start-activity -W -n app.openfamily/app.openfamily.wear.MainActivity Read TotalTime and WaitTime. Run it 10 times, drop the first, take the median. Do this once with the profile compiled and once without: adb shell cmd package compile -m speed-profile -f app.openfamily # with profile adb shell cmd package compile --reset app.openfamily # back to the installed state 2. Dropped frames while scrolling the People list (open it, then scroll for 10 seconds): adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo app.openfamily reset ... scroll ... adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo app.openfamily framestats Look at "Janky frames" and the 90th, 95th and 99th percentile frame times. On a 60 Hz AMOLED the budget is 16.6 ms. 3. SOS hold: the same gfxinfo while holding the SOS button for 1.5 s. Before this change the whole tree was recomposed every 50 ms; the draw-only ring should show far fewer long frames. 4. Compass: with adb shell dumpsys sensorservice check that the rotation vector has an active connection only while Direction is on screen and the screen is on (nothing after you press the power button). 5. Traces: record a Perfetto trace (adb shell perfetto -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/t.pb -t 20s sched freq idle am wm gfx view binderdriver ... or the Perfetto UI over USB/Wi-Fi), open the app, scroll, then look at the main thread for Choreographer#doFrame over 16 ms and for any JSONObject or SharedPreferences slice on the main thread (there should be none now). Android Studio's Profiler (CPU and Energy, with the watch selected) shows the same without command lines. 6. Battery: adb shell dumpsys batterystats --reset, use the watch normally for a few hours, then adb shell dumpsys batterystats app.openfamily. Expect almost nothing; if there is wake-up time, check the Data Layer push rate in adb logcat -s WearableService. 7. Large text: Settings, Display, Font size at the largest step, then open every screen once. Chips are limited to 1 to 3 lines and the list scrolls, so overflow should only clip a long name. Generate a real profile The Gradle Baseline Profile plugin needs a device. On a machine with a Wear OS emulator or a watch connected, add a com.android.test module that drives the app (open, scroll People, open a person, open Direction) with Macrobenchmark's BaselineProfileRule and run ./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile. Replace or merge the output into wear/app/src/main/baseline-prof.txt. The plugin was not added to the build here because a build that cannot run its generator would be a broken task, not a feature. Tests added wear/app/src/test/kotlin/app/openfamily/wear/PerfLogicTest.kt: duplicate-push dropping, heading filter (wrap-around at north, dead band, convergence), unique list ids after parsing, row text, oversized snapshot rejection, and the SOS hold timing in 50 ms steps. They run in ./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest in wear/. Status of OPT-10 (baseline profile and list keys) Done in the change above: androidx.profileinstaller, the hand-written baseline-prof.txt (covers the activity, view model, data and logic packages, UI package, tile and complication services), list keys on every items(...) and snapshot parsing off the main thread. Not done: a device-generated profile and the before/after cold-start numbers on the Galaxy Watch Ultra (needs a watch), and a separate content flow with a 60-second age ticker (the identical-push drop and the slower phone cadence already remove most recompositions; revisit if the device trace shows otherwise). Not done, on purpose Moving from Wear Compose Material 2 to Material 3 (ScreenScaffold, AppScaffold, EdgeButton). It is a visual redesign and needs real-watch review; the M2 Scaffold plus ScalingLazyColumn already handle round screens, the clock and the scroll indicator. Worth doing after the v1.0 demos. A tile age that updates itself. The "2 min" text is drawn when the tile is requested, and the system requests it again whenever the tile is shown.

docs.title: Performance on foldables and large, high-refresh screens
docs.summary: Rendering and layout work for the Galaxy Z Fold class of phones: what changed, what the tests lock, and how to measure on a real device.

headings.text: What was reviewed and left alone
Measuring on a real Z Fold

docs.text: Performance on foldables and large, high-refresh screens Rendering and layout work for the Galaxy Z Fold class of phones: what changed, what the tests lock, and how to measure on a real device. Nothing here was measured on a phone. There was no phone available. The changes come from reading the code and from Flutter widget tests (build and layer counts in the Flutter test VM). They prove structure (what is rebuilt, what is recreated, what is on screen), not frame times. The section "Measuring on a real Z Fold" lists what to run; it has not been run. What changed 1. Fold and unfold no longer recreate the map or the tabs. Both layout switches used to put the same widget in a different place in the tree, so Flutter threw the old one away and built a new one: AppShell swapped the bottom bar layout for the rail layout (width >= 840 dp, or landscape >= 560 dp). The banners plus the four tabs were rebuilt, which restarted the map screen: camera reset, WebSocket reconnected, location reporter recreated. LocationTabView swapped the bottom sheet layout for the two-pane layout (body width >= 720 dp, or clearly wide). The FlutterMap was recreated and re-fitted. Both now hold a GlobalKey (KeyedSubtree), which lets Flutter move the existing element to its new parent. The regression test (test/perf/foldresizetest.dart) failed before the change (tab state created twice) and passes after. 2. One layout rule. MapScreen used the window size to decide whether a sheet covers the lower map; the layout used the body size (window minus the rail). It now asks LocationTabView.isTwoPaneSize with the body's own size, so "centre the camera above the sheet" is only applied when there really is a sheet. 3. Narrower MediaQuery subscriptions. The two remaining MediaQuery.of(context) calls (chat bubble width, the add-server sheet) now use sizeOf / viewInsetsOf, so they no longer rebuild on unrelated changes. 4. Manifest. MainActivity already handled orientationscreenSizesmallestScreenSizescreenLayoutdensity... itself, so a fold does not restart the activity or the Flutter engine. Added android:resizeableActivity="true" explicitly. There is no portrait lock, no maxAspectRatio, and nothing that disables Impeller or forces software rendering (checked in the manifest, Gradle files and Dart: no EnableImpeller or software-rendering flags). The test test/perf/androidmanifestfoldabletest.dart locks this. Already in place before this work (and kept): the rail and two-pane layouts, MediaQuery.sizeOf in hot paths, the single motion Ticker for markers that stops when the tab is hidden, the saveLayer allow-list test, reduceEffects on low-tier devices, and the roster/marker repaint isolation (test/perf/). Layout rules Width Result window < 560 dp, or portrait < 840 dp Bottom navigation bar, map plus draggable sheet window >= 840 dp, or landscape >= 560 dp Navigation rail on the leading edge tab body >= 720 dp, or wider than 1.2 x its height and >= 560 dp Map beside a fixed People / Places panel Tested sizes (dp): 412x915 cover, 884x1104 inner portrait, 1104x884 inner landscape, 442x1104 and 884x552 split windows, each at text scale 1.0 and 1.3. No overflow at any of them. What was reviewed and left alone Shadows: the sheet, floating buttons and avatar markers use BoxShadow; avatar shadows are dropped on low-tier devices. Clips are hardEdge/default (no antiAliasWithSaveLayer). Opacity is used in four places for disabled states only. The test savelayeraudittest.dart fails if a new offscreen-layer widget appears. Marker motion: a single Ticker drives a motion hub; the marker layer updates through a ValueNotifier, not setState on the screen. Verified by livemotiontest.dart and markerlayertest.dart. Images: avatars are decoded at display size; chat images use cacheWidth. Startup: main() reads settings in parallel and does not await plugins before runApp. Page transitions use Flutter's FadeForwards builder. It is a framework class; no jank can be proven or disproven without a device. Measuring on a real Z Fold Build a profile build (release-like, with tooling): flutter run --profile (add --trace-skia to include raster events in the timeline; under Impeller use the DevTools Performance tab instead). Frame statistics (run after 30 s of use, reset first): adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo app.openfamily reset ...pan the map, drag the sheet, switch tabs... adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo app.openfamily framestats Look at "Janky frames" and the 90th / 95th / 99th percentile frame times. At 120 Hz the budget is 8.3 ms per frame. Emulate fold sizes on any phone or emulator: adb shell wm size 1812x2176 # inner screen portrait adb shell wm density 373 adb shell wm size reset && adb shell wm density reset The Android Studio "Resizable" and "7.6 Fold-in" emulators switch posture live; use them to fold and unfold while the map is open and check that the camera stays put. In One UI, also try the pop-up view and split-screen with the divider dragged. Perfetto: adb shell perfetto -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/t -t 20s sched freq gfx view then open it at ui.perfetto.dev and look at the app's Choreographer#doFrame slices. DevTools Performance (profile mode) shows build, layout and paint per frame; check that panning the map only repaints the marker layer. What to look at first: dragging the People sheet on the inner screen, pinch-zooming with 10+ members, switching tabs, and fold/unfold with the map open (expect no flash of loading state and no reconnect).

docs.title: Orbitly 1.0 readiness checklist
docs.summary: The master checklist for submitting Orbitly 1.0 to Google Play and the Apple App Store: what must be true, who does it, the order, and the go/no-go call.

headings.text: 1. Product blockers (must be true before any submit)
5. Manual test pass on real phones
9. What was prepared in this repository and what was not

docs.text: Orbitly 1.0 readiness checklist The master checklist for submitting Orbitly 1.0 to Google Play and the Apple App Store: what must be true, who does it, the order, and the go/no-go call. How to use it: work top to bottom, tick the boxes, and only press submit when the go/no-go section says GO. Each line says who owns it: OWNER (you, only you can do it: accounts, money, legal, signing keys), CI (a workflow does it once the owner has set the secrets), ENG (code or config in this repository) or DEMO (the demo-server workstream, see docs/release/DEMOSERVER.md). Status words: [x] done and checked in this repository, [ ] open, [?] decision or unverifiable from the build machine (needs a real phone, a Mac or a store console). Companion pages: Google Play, App Store, Store assets, Privacy policy draft, Terms draft. 0. Timeline reality check (read first) Fact Consequence for "submit within about a week" Personal Google Play developer accounts created after November 2023 must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before Production access can be requested, then Google reviews that request (the existing listing notes this in Google Play release preparation). Organization accounts do not have this rule. If the Play account is personal, production on Google Play cannot happen in a week. The week can end with the closed test running. Start the 14 days on day 1. If the account is an organization account, ignore this row. Apple App Review usually answers in 24 to 48 hours, but the first submission of an app that uses background location, push, and needs a server is the most likely to get questions. Submit to Apple early in the week and keep the demo server up and monitored the whole time. The Apple release pipeline (.github/workflows/ios-release.yml) has never run; the iOS app and Apple Watch app have never been built or run on a Mac or iPhone by the people who wrote them. Budget the first CI run as a debugging session (signing). Do it on day 1, not on day 6. Play and Apple need a reachable demo server with a demo account the whole review period (days to weeks). The demo server must be a stable, separate server, not someone's family server. 1. Product blockers (must be true before any submit) Everything here can be checked by the owner on real phones; the repository tests cover the logic but not the phone-specific behaviour. [ ] OWNER Install the exact release candidate (the signed APK from the tag, and the TestFlight build) on at least one Android phone and one iPhone and run the manual test pass below. [ ] ENG/OWNER No known crash: no open issue labelled crash; run the app for 24 hours with location sharing on and look at Android vitals / Xcode Organizer crash data from the closed test before promoting. [ ] OWNER SOS path verified end to end on a real phone: press SOS, the other member's phone shows the alert with a position; "Cancel" works; the screen says clearly that emergency services are NOT called. Test on Android and iPhone, with the app closed. [ ] OWNER Sign-in stability: leave a phone signed in for 48 hours with the screen locked and the server updated once in between; the person must not be signed out. The v0.25.2+ fix (concurrent refreshes of the same sign-in token get the same successor, no false "token theft" sign-outs, see Changelog, Unreleased) must be in the release. [ ] OWNER Background location on a locked phone for 30 minutes of walking on Android, and on iPhone (see the field test list in iOS release design, "Background execution on iOS"). On iPhone nothing runs when the phone is still and the app is suspended, so "last seen" can be old: this is a documented limitation; make sure the store text does not promise otherwise. [ ] OWNER Driving dashboard / driving report opens on Android with data; on iPhone the Driving detection settings say "Not available on iPhone yet" (documented, intended). Make sure no store screenshot shows iPhone driving sensors. [ ] ENG The app version shown in Settings > About matches the store version (see Versioning). [ ] ENG flutter analyze --no-fatal-infos has no warnings with the CI Flutter version (3.47.0), flutter test green, Go tests green (.github/workflows/test.yml green on the release commit). [ ] ENG No debug flags, no cleartext traffic, no allowBackup: audited, see Audit results. [ ] OWNER The in-app account deletion works on both platforms (Settings > Delete my account, with the password). Required by both stores. [ ] OWNER decision Chat has no "report message" or "block member" button. Apple guideline 1.2 expects a way to report objectionable content in apps with user-generated content. Options and the recommendation are in App Store, guideline 1.2. Decide before submitting to Apple. [ ] OWNER decision Ship the Apple Watch app in 1.0? It has never been compiled; the signed pipeline leaves it out by default. Recommended: not in 1.0 (add in 1.1 after one real-watch test). [ ] OWNER decision Ship the Wear OS app in 1.0? It builds in CI but has not been tried on a real watch (see Watch). Recommended: internal testing track only for 1.0, public after a real-watch test. [ ] OWNER decision USEFULLSCREENINTENT and REQUESTIGNOREBATTERYOPTIMIZATIONS in the Android manifest (see permissions audit). One of them is unused and can be removed with no behaviour change. 2. Accounts and money (OWNER) [ ] Apple Developer Program membership active (99 USD/year); Team ID noted. [ ] Google Play Console developer account active and identity verified; account type known (personal or organization, decides the 14-day closed test). [ ] D-U-N-S number if the Apple account is an organization (not needed for an individual). [ ] Two-factor sign-in on both accounts; a second person with recovery access. [ ] Tax and "paid apps" agreements are NOT needed for a free app with no purchases. (Leave the app free, no in-app purchases, no ads.) 3. Store requirements per store Google Play (details: GOOGLEPLAY.md) [ ] OWNER Decide Play App Signing enrollment BEFORE the first upload: enrollment choices. Recommended: provide the existing key so sideloaded APKs keep updating. [ ] CI Signed AAB orbitly-<version>.aab from a release tag (.github/workflows/apk.yml). [ ] ENG targetSdk meets the current Play requirement (36 with the repository Flutter, checked in the built manifest). [ ] OWNER App content declarations: privacy policy URL, ads (none), app access (demo server and account), content rating, target audience, data safety, government/financial/health (none), location permissions declaration with video, foreground service declaration with video, full-screen-intent declaration, account deletion URL. [ ] OWNER Store listing: texts in docs/release/store-listing/en-US/, graphics from store assets. [ ] OWNER Closed test: 12 testers x 14 days if the account is personal. Apple App Store (details: APPSTORE.md) [ ] OWNER App ID app.openfamily with Push Notifications (Associated Domains only if you own the demo/production host). [ ] OWNER + CI The six secrets and the variables in APPSTORE.md; a green run of "iOS release (TestFlight)". [ ] OWNER App Privacy answers entered in App Store Connect (use the table). [ ] OWNER Export compliance answered; Info.plist now sets ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption to true (see export compliance). Confirm with a lawyer or the export-control authority. [ ] OWNER Age rating questionnaire, screenshots 6.9" and 6.5" iPhone (and iPad if the app is offered on iPad), review notes with the demo account. [ ] OWNER Support URL and privacy URL live. 4. Legal pages, demo and assets [ ] OWNER Review and finalize PRIVACYPOLICY.md and TERMS.md with a lawyer (they are DRAFTS). Fill the placeholders (operator name, contact email, governing law, date), remove the draft box, run scripts/docs-check.sh --fix, deploy. Every Orbitly server then serves them at /privacy and /terms with no sign-in. [ ] OWNER Host the final privacy policy at a public URL that stays up (Play and Apple both require it). The simplest: https://<demo server>/privacy (always on) or your website. [ ] OWNER Keep the existing account deletion web page live (https://foleyit.com/delete-account.html, saved in Play Console). [ ] DEMO Demo server up with a review family, a review account without two-step sign-in, fictional people only; URL and credentials pasted into Play "App access" and Apple "Review notes" (placeholders in docs/release/store-listing/apple/reviewnotes.txt). See docs/release/DEMOSERVER.md. [ ] DEMO The demo server is on HTTPS, has APNs/push configured if you want reviewers to see an alert, and is monitored during the whole review. [ ] ENG Run scripts/store-assets.sh, review every image, replace by real device captures where STOREASSETS.md says to. Stores require truthful screenshots. [ ] OWNER Record the two Google Play permission videos (scripts in GOOGLEPLAY.md). 5. Manual test pass on real phones Do this on the exact release candidate. Two phones, two accounts, a demo or test server. 1. Install, enter the server address, create an account from an invite, accept location "Always", notifications, finish onboarding. 2. Walk or drive 10 minutes. The other phone's map follows with a delay of seconds to a minute. 3. Create a place "Home", leave and arrive: both phones get an alert. 4. Send chat text and a photo. Switch the circle to Private; chat still works; the server sees ciphertext. 5. SOS and "I'm OK" with the app closed; cancel an SOS. 6. Lock both phones for an hour; the position still updates (Android; iPhone with Always). 7. Kill the server for 5 minutes and restart it: the app recovers, nobody is signed out. 8. Change phone language/time zone, rotate the phone, dark mode. 9. Settings > Download my data, then Settings > Delete my account on a throwaway account; sign-in must then fail. 10. Uninstall and reinstall; the Android APK from the previous tag must update in place to the new tag (same signature). 6. Versioning policy There are three numbers and they must not be confused. Thing Where it lives Rule Release tag git: v1.0.0, pre-releases v1.0.0-rc.1 The single source of truth. Never move or reuse a tag. versionName (user visible) / iOS CFBundleShortVersionString derived from the tag: v1.0.0 becomes 1.0.0 (rc/beta suffix dropped for iOS) Set by CI with --build-name. versionCode (Android) / iOS CFBundleVersion derived from the tag: (major1000000 + minor1000 + patch)100 + suffix, suffix 99 for a final release, or the rc/beta number for a pre-release Set by CI with --build-number. Examples: v0.25.2 = 2500299, v1.0.0-rc.1 = 100000001, v1.0.0 = 100000099, v1.0.1 = 100010099. version: in app/pubspec.yaml 0.1.0+1 today A placeholder. CI overrides both parts on every release build, so it does not have to be edited. Only local builds without --build-name/--build-number use it (and the Wear OS app reads it for local builds). It is fine to leave it. Consequences and rules: Minor and patch must stay below 1000. Never reuse a versionCode: Play and App Store Connect both reject a repeated number. v1.0.0-rc.N builds always sort below v1.0.0 (rc number < 99), so you can test release candidates on Play internal testing and still publish v1.0.0 afterwards. Play requires the versionCode to increase for every upload on any track. The Wear OS AAB is built with the same formula, so the phone AAB and the Wear AAB get the same versionCode. If the Play Console rejects the Wear upload with "version code has already been used", rebuild the Wear bundle with a different code (Gradle property -PWEARVERSIONCODE=<number>, see wear/app/build.gradle.kts) and keep it increasing. This is untested because it needs a Play account. Server compatibility: the server keeps working for the last 5 entries of the release list in backend/internal/compat (Releases). 1.0.0 parses and sorts above 0.25.0 (checked in compat.Parse). When you cut 1.0, the owner adds "1.0.0" to that list in the release commit (this was deliberately not edited by the store-readiness work); the oldest line then drops out of the window, so tell family members on app 0.21 to update. Changelog: add the ## v1.0.0 section to the changelog before tagging; the server shows it to admins. How to release (CI does the rest): git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0. The Android workflow publishes the APKs, the AAB and SHA256SUMS.txt; the iOS workflow is started by hand with the same version number. 7. Rollout plan Google Play 1. Internal testing (up to 100 testers, no review, minutes to appear). Upload the v1.0.0-rc.1 AAB. Install via the opt-in link on the owner's phones. Check Android vitals. 2. Closed testing (needed for the 12-tester rule). Create a Google Group or email list of 12+ real people, send the opt-in link, keep them opted in 14 days, collect feedback. Fix, upload rc.2 and so on. 3. Open testing (optional, skipped by most apps). 4. Production: apply for production access (personal accounts), then create the production release from the tested AAB, start with a staged rollout (for example 20 percent) and watch crashes for two days before 100 percent. Each upload to production goes through Google review (hours to a few days; the first one with background location is longer). Apple 1. TestFlight internal (up to 100 App Store Connect users, no review): run the workflow, wait 10 to 30 minutes of processing, answer export compliance, install. 2. TestFlight external (up to 10,000 testers, needs Beta App Review of the first build, 1 to 2 days). Use the same review notes and demo account. 3. App Review: attach the tested build to version 1.0, fill App Privacy, age rating, screenshots, review notes. Choose manual release after approval so you control the moment. 4. Phased release over 7 days is available for updates (not for the very first version). 8. Go/no-go decision GO only when every line below is true. Anything else is NO-GO for that store. Condition Google Apple 1 Section 1 product blockers all ticked or explicitly accepted by the owner in writing required required 2 Release candidate installed from the store test track (not a sideloaded file) on a real phone and the manual test pass done required required 3 Demo server reachable from the public internet on HTTPS with the review account working, checked on the day of submission required required 4 Privacy policy URL, support URL and account deletion path live required required 5 Declarations and videos entered (location, foreground service, full-screen intent) required n/a 6 App Privacy, age rating and export compliance entered n/a required 7 14-day closed test completed (personal account) required n/a 8 A named person watches the stores and the demo server for the first 72 hours after release, with the previous known-good tag ready for a rollback (halt staged rollout / pull the release) required required NO-GO triggers: any crash in the release candidate that reproduces; SOS not delivered; sign-out loops; demo server down; privacy policy placeholders still in the text. 9. What was prepared in this repository a

docs.text: Google Play submission guide Everything the owner needs to put Orbitly (package app.openfamily) on Google Play: signing choice, upload, every declaration with ready-to-paste text, and the videos Google asks for. Status of the Play Console entry as of the last owner update is in Google Play release preparation (listing saved, no release uploaded). This page is the step-by-step guide to finish it. The master list is Orbitly 1.0 readiness. Ready-to-paste listing texts are in docs/release/store-listing/en-US/ (title, short and full description, release notes, category, tags, contact). Statements marked (verify) come from the author's knowledge of Google's policies, which change often, and could not be checked against the live Play Console from the build machine. Decisions for the owner at a glance Decision Recommendation 1 Play App Signing: Google-generated key or the existing key Provide the existing key (see below), otherwise sideloaded family phones must uninstall and reinstall 2 USEFULLSCREENINTENT (crash "Are you OK?" over the lock screen) Remove for 1.0 (loud heads-up notification instead); add back later with a declaration 3 REQUESTIGNOREBATTERYOPTIMIZATIONS Remove: the app never uses it (it only opens the system settings list) 4 Target audience age groups 13 and over (the Console currently also lists 6 to 12, which brings the Families policy and its location limits) 5 Ship the Wear OS app in 1.0 Internal testing only until tried on a real watch 6 Data safety: declare map-tile providers as "shared" Yes, be conservative Play App Signing: enrollment (decide before the first upload) Google Play re-signs every app it serves with an app signing key that Google holds. You sign the uploads with an upload key. You choose at the first release upload (Test and release, App integrity, App signing) and cannot undo it. The phones of your family today have the APK signed with this certificate: SHA-256: dd3f93e62dd829e4de8137b0fe8ce179a217e05761d2338c6fa7caa3b0206b03 Android only installs an update over an existing app if the signing certificate is identical. That decides everything: Choice at enrollment What users see Consequences A. Let Google generate the app signing key (default for new apps), upload with your existing keystore as the upload key The Play version is signed with a different certificate than the sideloaded APKs A phone that has the GitHub/Obtainium APK cannot update to the Play version: Android refuses ("package conflicts with an existing package"). The person must uninstall and reinstall, which deletes local app data (sign-in, local caches; the account on the server is untouched, but Private-circle keys held only on that phone are lost unless the recovery phrase is used). The reverse is also true: Play users cannot take the GitHub APK. You must run two separate update channels from then on. B. Provide the existing key as the app signing key (Console: "Export and upload a key from a Java keystore", using Google's pepk.jar) Play serves apps signed with dd3f93e6... Sideloaded APKs update from Play in place and the other way round. You hand Google a copy of the private key (encrypted for Google). Google then holds it for the life of the app. You cannot take the key back out, but you also keep your own copy. One later key upgrade is possible (for rotation after a compromise, see Play's "key upgrade"). Recommendation: B, because family members already have the sideloaded app and the whole point of the project is that those people keep updating without a reinstall. Choose A only if you decide that nobody on a sideloaded APK matters. How to do B (the Console shows the exact current wording; (verify)): 1. Play Console, create the release (see "AAB path" below), the page asks how to sign. 2. Choose "Export and upload a key from a Java keystore". The page offers the Play Encrypt Private Key tool (pepk.jar) and an encryption public key file. 3. On a machine that has the keystore (/home/dockhub/OpenFamily/private/keys/openfamily-release.jks, alias openfamily; see Android release process): java -jar pepk.jar --keystore=openfamily-release.jks --alias=openfamily \ output=orbitly-play-key.zip --include-cert --rsa-aes-encryption \ encryption-key-path=encryptionpublickey.pem It asks for the keystore and key passwords. Upload orbitly-play-key.zip. 4. Afterwards check in Console, App signing: the app signing key certificate SHA-256 must equal dd3f93e6...6b03. If it does not, stop and do not publish. 5. The upload key: the simplest correct setup is to keep using the same keystore as the upload key (the CI job signs the APK and the AAB with one key, and the sideloaded APK must stay on this key). Tradeoff: a leaked CI secret then leaks the app signing key too. If you want separation, create a second keystore for Play uploads only and teach apk.yml to sign the AAB with it (not done here; needs a CI change and a Play test). 6. Back the keystore up in two places before you hand it over (the instructions in Android release process still apply). Opt in to nothing else: leave "Play Integrity" and "Android App Bundles key upgrade" defaults as they are. AAB path The CI job .github/workflows/apk.yml builds orbitly-<version>.aab on every v tag and attaches it to the GitHub Release together with SHA256SUMS.txt. Download it from the release page, check the hash, upload it in Play Console (Test and release, Internal testing, Create new release). Do not upload the APKs to Play. Local build for a throwaway check: cd app && flutter build appbundle --release --build-name=1.0.0 --build-number=100000099 (needs android/key.properties). The Wear OS app is a separate bundle (orbitly-wear-<version>.aab from wear.yml). versionCode rules See versioning policy. In short: derived from the tag, strictly increasing, never reused. Play refuses a versionCode that was uploaded once on any track, even if the release was discarded. Test builds should be v1.0.0-rc.N tags (they sort below v1.0.0). Target API level and 64-bit The app uses Flutter's defaults (flutter.targetSdkVersion, flutter.compileSdkVersion in app/android/app/build.gradle.kts). The Flutter 3.44 image used locally resolves to compileSdk 36, targetSdk 36, minSdk 24. CI uses Flutter 3.47.0, which is the same or newer. The wear app has compileSdk 36, targetSdk 35, minSdk 30. Google's rule (verify): new apps and updates must target Android 15 (API 35) since 31 August 2025, and Android 16 (API 36) from 31 August 2026. Today (November 2026) 36 is required, which the phone app meets. The Wear OS app at 35 may be below the current requirement: recommended action is to raise targetSdk in wear/app/build.gradle.kts to 36 and run the Wear CI. This was not changed here because a target bump changes runtime behaviour and cannot be tested without a watch. Check the real value in the artifact you upload: aapt2 dump badging app-release.apk grep targetSdkVersion (for an AAB: bundletool dump manifest --bundle orbitly-1.0.0.aab grep targetSdk). The upload page of Play Console also shows a warning if the target is too low. 64-bit: Play requires a 64-bit build for every native-code app. A Flutter AAB contains arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x8664 libraries. Check: unzip -l orbitly-1.0.0.aab grep 'lib/'. The vendored plugins (backgroundlocator2, drivingnative) are Kotlin only. 16 KB page size (Android 15+ devices, required for updates targeting 36 on 64-bit libraries, verify): Flutter 3.35+ engines are 16 KB aligned. Play Console warns at upload if not. If it does, upgrade Flutter first. Audit of the Android manifest and build Read from app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml and build.gradle.kts. Item Result android:allowBackup false, plus dataExtractionRules and fullBackupContent that exclude everything. Good. usesCleartextTraffic false. Good. The app also refuses http:// server addresses. Debuggable Not set in the manifest; release builds are not debuggable. Release signing refuses to build without key.properties (no silent debug key). Minify / shrink R8 minify and resource shrink are on for release. App label and icon Orbitly, @mipmap/iclauncher. Good. Exported components MainActivity (launcher, deep links). WatchListenerService exported true: needed so Google Play services can deliver watch messages; it only matches /orbitly/cmd Wear messages and the Data Layer only delivers messages from the paired watch with the same package and signature. The widget provider and the boot receiver and IsolateHolderService are exported=false. Good. Deep links https://<any host>/join/<code> (no autoVerify, because the host is the user's own server) and openfamily://join. Play does not require verified app links. The app validates the link and only pre-fills a form. Fine. Application id app.openfamily in both the phone and the Wear app (required for the Data Layer). TODO left in build file A template comment above applicationId; harmless. Merged manifest See the next section (the build merges permissions from plugins). Permissions audit Checked on a real build: a release APK built from this tree (v0.25.x, debug-signed for the check, built by the shared build helper and inspected with aapt2 dump badging and aapt2 dump xmltree). Result: targetSdkVersion 36, compileSdkVersion 36, allowBackup=false, usesCleartextTraffic=false, no debuggable, native code arm64-v8a armeabi-v7a x8664, label Orbitly. Final merged permission list (the plugins add four to the ones written in the manifest): Permission Where it comes from Risk with Play Used for Recommendation INTERNET manifest none server connection keep USEBIOMETRIC manifest none optional app lock keep ACCESSCOARSELOCATION, ACCESSFINELOCATION manifest needs privacy policy and data safety map, sharing keep ACCESSBACKGROUNDLOCATION manifest restricted: declaration + video + review location while the app is closed (core function) keep, see declaration ACTIVITYRECOGNITION manifest runtime, low driving detection (opt-in) keep FOREGROUNDSERVICE, FOREGROUNDSERVICELOCATION manifest declaration + video (API 34+) background location service keep, see declaration POSTNOTIFICATIONS manifest low alerts and service notification keep WAKELOCK manifest none keep location service running keep RECEIVEBOOTCOMPLETED manifest none restart sharing after reboot keep REQUESTIGNOREBATTERYOPTIMIZATIONS manifest restricted use policy; unused by the code nothing (only the settings list is opened) remove (decision 3) USEFULLSCREENINTENT manifest declaration; only calling/alarm apps by default on 14+ crash "Are you OK?" over lock screen decision 2 ACCESSNETWORKSTATE, VIBRATE plugins none connectivity check, alert vibration keep USEFINGERPRINT localauth plugin none (deprecated alias) biometric lock keep app.openfamily.DYNAMICRECEIVERNOTEXPORTEDPERMISSION AndroidX none private to the app keep Not present (good): READCONTACTS, any SMS or call-log permission, QUERYALLPACKAGES, SYSTEMALERTWINDOW, SCHEDULEEXACTALARM/USEEXACTALARM, MANAGEEXTERNALSTORAGE, READMEDIA (photos use the system picker), CAMERA (the camera is used through the system camera app via the image picker, which needs no permission in the manifest as long as the app does not declare it). Nothing was removed from the manifest as part of this work. To re-check after any change: build the release APK and run aapt2 dump permissions app-release.apk. Data safety form Play asks, per data type: collected, shared, optional or required, purposes; plus security practices. Be accurate about the architecture. The developer does not receive any of this data. It is sent from the user's phone to the Orbitly server that the user's circle chose, which is run by the circle administrator (or by the owner for the demo server). Google's definition of "collect" is "transmit off the device", whoever runs the receiving server, so the types below are declared collected, and the description box explains it. Text for the free-text explanation field (paste): Orbitly is a client for a self-hosted server. Data is sent only to the server address the user enters, which is run by the user's own circle administrator. The app developer does not operate that server and receives no data. There are no analytics, advertising or crash-reporting SDKs. Private circles are end-to-end encrypted; in Normal circles the data is readable by the server operator. Data type (Play category) Collected? Shared with third parties? Required or optional Purposes Notes Precise location Yes No Optional (sharing can be paused or turned off) App functionality Also in the background, see the declaration. Approximate location Yes Yes: map tile providers (see below) Optional App functionality Derived from precise location; map requests reveal the viewed area. Name Yes No Required App functionality, Account management Display name. Email address Yes No Required App functionality, Account management Sign-in. User IDs Yes No Required App functionality, Account management Account id. Phone number Yes No Optional App functionality Own optional number, and emergency contacts typed by the user (the app never reads the address book). Address Yes No Optional App functionality Place addresses typed or searched. Photos Yes No Optional App functionality Profile photo and chat photos. Other in-app messages Yes No Optional App functionality Chat; end-to-end encrypted in Private circles, readable by the operator in Normal circles. Other user-generated content Yes No Optional App functionality SOS and check-in notes. Device or other IDs Yes No Required App functionality, Account management App-generated device id and push address. Not the advertising ID (the app does not read it). Physical activity Yes No Optional App functionality Movement type (walking, driving, still) and driving events, if the user allows motion detection. Owner to confirm: declaring it is the conservative choice. App info and performance: Diagnostics Yes No Required App functionality App version, battery level, background-restriction state shown to the circle admin as fleet health. Crash logs No n/a n/a n/a No crash SDK; the Diagnostics screen is local. Contacts (address book) No n/a n/a n/a The system contact picker returns one chosen number only; no READCONTACTS. Financial, health records, audio, files, calendar, web browsing No n/a n/a n/a Shared with third parties, in detail: map tiles are fetched by the phone directly from the tile host named by the server (by default OpenStreetMap and Esri), which sees the viewed area and the IP address. The server-side geocoder and optional SMS or push providers are chosen and configured by the server operator, not by the app; they do not receive data from the phone. Google allows an exemption for service providers acting on behalf of the developer and for user-initiated transfers; tile hosts are neither, so declare "Approximate location: shared" to be safe. Security practices: Data is encrypted in transit: Yes (HTTPS only; the app rejects HTTP). You can request that data is deleted: Yes. In the app (Settings, Delete my account)
