docs.text: Apple App Store submission guide Everything the owner needs to put Orbitly (bundle id app.openfamily) on TestFlight and the App Store: accounts, secrets, privacy answers, export compliance, review notes and screenshots. The click-by-click account setup (enrolment, certificate, profile, API key, APNs key) already exists in iOS app: readiness, signing, TestFlight; this page does not repeat it. It adds what is needed for the App Store (not only TestFlight): listing texts, App Privacy, age rating, export compliance, review notes and the workflow variables. The master list is Orbitly 1.0 readiness. Listing texts to paste are in docs/release/store-listing/apple/. Honesty note: nothing on the iOS side has ever been built, signed or run by the authors (no Mac); the first workflow run will find problems. Identifiers and capabilities Item Value Notes iPhone app bundle id app.openfamily Explicit App ID. Capabilities to tick: Push Notifications. Associated Domains only if you own the host that serves invite links (see below). Apple Watch app bundle id app.openfamily.watchkitapp Register an explicit App ID for it only if you ship the watch app in this version. No capabilities needed. Background Modes: location, remote notifications in Info.plist (UIBackgroundModes) Not an App ID capability; nothing to tick in the portal. App Groups none Not used (no widget/extension shares data). Do not add. Associated Domains optional Orbitly is self-hosted, the server host is unknown at build time, so the default entitlements have no associated domains. Invite links then fall back to the landing-page button (openfamily://) or paste/QR. If you want https://<your demo host>/join/... to open the app, enable the capability on the App ID, regenerate the profile, and set the repository variable IOSASSOCIATEDDOMAIN. Push (APNs) key .p8 for the server Separate from the CI key; see step 7 of the IOSRELEASE checklist. TestFlight and App Store builds use the production APNs host (APNSPRODUCTION=true on the server). Privacy manifest app/ios/Runner/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy Present. Does not replace the App Privacy answers below. Secrets and variables the workflow expects .github/workflows/ios-release.yml, repository Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions. The workflow's first step now checks all of them in one pass and prints, for each problem, what is wrong and how to fix it. Name Kind What it is How to create it What the check says if it is wrong IOSRELEASEENABLED variable true allows the job to run type true job is skipped IOSTEAMID variable 10-character Team ID developer.apple.com, Account, Membership details "IOSTEAMID must be the 10-character Team ID" IOSBUNDLEID variable, optional default app.openfamily only if that id is taken "not a valid bundle id" IOSASSOCIATEDDOMAIN variable, optional e.g. demo.example.com (no https://) your server host profile has no Associated Domains: signing fails IOSWATCHENABLED variable, optional leave unset see Apple Watch below setting it to true stops the job early with an explanation IOSP12BASE64 secret Apple Distribution certificate with private key as base64 Keychain Access, export as .p12, then base64 -i cert.p12 \ pbcopy "missing" or "not valid base64" IOSP12PASSWORD secret the password chosen at export chosen when exporting "missing" IOSPROVISIONINGPROFILEBASE64 secret App Store profile for app.openfamily as base64 Profiles, App Store Connect type, download, base64 -i x.mobileprovision "missing"; later steps verify team, app id (no wildcard) and production push ASCKEYID secret App Store Connect API key id Users and Access, Integrations, App Store Connect API, Team Keys, +, role App Manager "missing" ASCISSUERID secret issuer UUID at the top of that page same page "must be the issuer UUID" ASCPRIVATEKEY secret full text of the downloaded AuthKeyXXXX.p8, including the BEGIN/END lines same page, download once "must be the full text ... including the BEGIN line" Run it: Actions, "iOS release (TestFlight)", Run workflow, version 1.0.0 or 1.0.0-rc.1. The build number is derived from the version with the same formula as Android (see versioning policy). Do the first run early; signing problems are normal on a first run and each step prints what it did. The workflow uploads to TestFlight; promoting a build to the App Store is done in App Store Connect. Apple Watch Apple requires the watch app to be inside the iPhone app bundle. It is: the OrbitlyWatch target is embedded in the Runner project (companion model, watchOS 9+) and carries the iPhone's version numbers. Icons are in app/ios/OrbitlyWatch/Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset. The project wiring has never been built on a Mac. By default ios-release.yml runs python3 scripts/ios-watch-target.py disable and builds the iPhone app without the watch app (when IOSWATCHENABLED is not true). That is the recommended v1.0 path. Setting IOSWATCHENABLED=true is not wired: the signed build would also need an App ID app.openfamily.watchkitapp, its own App Store provisioning profile installed by the workflow, an extra entry under provisioningProfiles in ExportOptions.plist, and manual-signing settings for the watch target. None of this is implemented, so the workflow now stops at the first step with a message instead of failing deep inside Xcode. Plan it for 1.1 together with a test on a real watch (docs/design/WATCHAPPSAPPLE.md). If you do ship the watch app later: App Store Connect needs Apple Watch screenshots (see store assets). App Store Connect: set up the app 1. Apps, +, New App: platform iOS, name Orbitly, language English (U.S.), bundle id app.openfamily, SKU orbitly, full access. 2. Pricing: Free, all territories you want (the app has no purchases and no ads). 3. App Information: subtitle, category Lifestyle (secondary Utilities), content rights (you own or have the rights: yes), privacy policy URL (public), age rating (below). 4. Version page: description, promotional text, keywords, support URL, marketing URL, what's new, copyright: paste from docs/release/store-listing/apple/. 5. App Review Information: contact name, phone and email (a real person who can answer within a day) and the review notes from reviewnotes.txt, with the demo account filled in. Sign-in required: yes. 6. Version release: Manually release this version (recommended). TestFlight process 1. Run the workflow with 1.0.0-rc.1. Processing in App Store Connect takes 10 to 30 minutes. 2. The build shows "Missing Compliance" until you answer the encryption questions (see below). 3. Internal testing: add up to 100 App Store Connect users to a group; no Apple review. 4. External testing: add testers by email or public link (up to 10,000). The first build of a version goes through Beta App Review (1 to 2 days); give the same review notes and demo account. 5. When the release candidate is good, create the App Store version, choose the build, submit for review. The final 1.0.0 build needs its own workflow run: build numbers must increase and the rc suffix is dropped. App Privacy ("nutrition label") App Store Connect, App Privacy. Principle: Apple wants every data type that the app sends off the device and that "you or your third-party partners" can access. The server is run by circle administrators, and for the demo/review server by the owner; the conservative and honest answer is to declare everything below as collected, because the app really transmits it. The notes field lets you explain. Never answer "Data Not Collected": the app collects. Do you or your third-party partners collect data from this app? Yes. Apple category and type Linked to the user's identity Used to track Purpose Contact Info: Name Yes No App Functionality Contact Info: Email Address Yes No App Functionality Contact Info: Phone Number (own optional number; emergency contacts typed in) Yes No App Functionality Location: Precise Location Yes No App Functionality Location: Coarse Location Yes No App Functionality User Content: Photos or Videos (profile, chat) Yes No App Functionality User Content: Other User Content (chat messages, check-in and SOS notes) Yes No App Functionality Identifiers: User ID Yes No App Functionality Identifiers: Device ID (app-generated, push address) Yes No App Functionality Diagnostics: Other Diagnostic Data (app version, battery level shown as fleet health) Yes No App Functionality Data used to track you: none. There is no advertising, no third-party analytics, no data broker. App Tracking Transparency is not needed; do not add the prompt. Advertising identifier: not used. Health & Fitness, Financial, Browsing/Search history, Purchases, Sensitive Info, Usage Data: not collected. Contacts (address book): not collected: the app uses the system picker and receives one chosen number. Notes to keep consistent: PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy declares a Contacts data type and no diagnostic type; this differs from the table above. The privacy manifest is not shown to users; reconcile it when someone with Xcode (Product, Archive, Generate Privacy Report) reviews it: remove Contacts (it describes an address book the app never reads) and add OtherDiagnosticData. Not changed blind here. Location permission strings (guidelines 5.1.1 and 2.5.4) app/ios/Runner/Info.plist now contains (reviewed and clarified in this work): Key Text Why it passes review NSLocationAlwaysAndWhenInUseUsageDescription "Orbitly shares your location with the people in your circles, also while the app is closed, so they can see where you are and get arrival alerts and your SOS position. Only the members of your circles see it, and you can pause or stop sharing at any time in Orbitly." States what, who sees it, that it works in the background, and that the user controls it. NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription "Orbitly uses your location to show you on the map and, when you turn sharing on, to tell the people in your circles where you are." Specific purpose. NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription "... choose a profile photo, or a photo to send in your circle chat, from your photo library." Now covers chat photos too (the chat picks from the gallery). NSCameraUsageDescription "Orbitly uses the camera to take a photo to send in circle chat." unchanged NSFaceIDUsageDescription "Orbitly uses Face ID to unlock your private location map." unchanged NSMotionUsageDescription "Orbitly uses motion & fitness to detect when you're driving, biking, or walking." No Core Motion permission is requested on iPhone today (driving sensors are Android only), so this string is unused. Apple does not reject unused strings, but it promises something the iPhone app does not do. Recommended: remove the key until the Swift port exists. Left in place because the project documentation planned it. Guideline 5.1.1(iv) (do not force permissions): the permissions screen lets the user skip every step ("Skip anyway"), and the app works in the foreground without "Always". Guideline 2.5.4 (background services): UIBackgroundModes lists only location and remote-notification, and the review notes explain the continuous-location feature. Apple may still ask for a demo of background tracking: have a short screen recording ready. Export compliance Not legal advice. Confirm with the owner's lawyer or the export-control authority of the country of the developer. What the question is about: when you upload a build, Apple asks whether the app uses encryption, because encryption software is subject to US export rules (EAR) and rules in some other countries (France requires a declaration for non-exempt cryptography). Plain-words analysis for Orbitly: 1. Using only HTTPS (Apple's own TLS in the operating system) is exempt, and would let you answer "No non-exempt encryption". 2. Orbitly also encrypts data itself: end-to-end encryption of Private circles and chat using standard algorithms (X25519 key agreement, XChaCha20-Poly1305, HKDF, SHA-2 and Ed25519 signatures, from the Dart cryptography package, not from Apple's CryptoKit), plus Argon2 and a Secure Enclave key wrapper. Apple's questionnaire treats "standard encryption algorithms instead of, or in addition to, the operating system's encryption" as not automatically exempt. 3. In practice such an app is usually "mass market" encryption software that qualifies for a self-classification under the US rules (ECCN 5D992.c, License Exception ENC / mass-market), which means: answer Yes, it uses encryption; it qualifies for an exemption only if... then provide the documentation Apple asks for, and file a short self-classification report to the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and NSA each year by 1 February for the previous year (an email with a spreadsheet; no fee). Since the software is open source and publicly available, the "publicly available encryption source code" notification (a one-time email to BIS and NSA with the source URL) may apply instead. Which one fits is exactly the legal question to confirm. 4. France: apps with non-exempt crypto distributed in France may need a declaration (ANSSI); Apple will ask for the document or a statement. Many publishers exclude France or provide the statement. What the repository does now: Info.plist sets ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption to true (honest default). Effect: App Store Connect asks the export-compliance questions once per build/version instead of silently assuming "no". Do not change it to false unless the lawyer concludes that nothing the app does is non-exempt, because a false statement is a compliance violation, not an Apple formality. Answers in App Store Connect (typical for this app, to confirm): Does the app use encryption: Yes. Does it use encryption other than HTTPS/OS encryption (Apple's list): Yes (end-to-end encryption using standard algorithms). Is it exempt under the listed exemptions: follow the lawyer's conclusion; if self-classified, upload the documentation requested, and note the annual report date in the calendar. Sign in with Apple is not needed Guideline 4.8 requires Sign in with Apple only when an app offers third-party or social sign-in (Google, Facebook, ...). Orbitly has only its own accounts (email and password, optional passkeys and two-step sign-in) on the user's own server. So Sign in with Apple is not required and not offered. Write this in the review notes if the reviewer asks. Account deletion (guideline 5.1.1(v)) Present: Settings, Delete my account in the app (deleteaccountscreen.dart), confirmed with the password (and a two-step code if enabled), calls DELETE /me, which removes the account and its locations, devices, contacts and messages. If the person is the last admin of a circle that still has others, the app asks to hand over admin first; if they are the only member the circle is removed. "Download my data" (GET /me/export) exists too. Mention the exact path in the review notes (done in the template). Test it once on the demo server on the day of submission. User-generated content (guideline 1.2) Apps with user-generated content need: a way to filter objectionable content, a

docs.text: Store assets pipeline How to produce the screenshots, feature graphic and icons for Google Play and the App Store, what is generated and what must be captured on a real device. What scripts/store-assets.sh does scripts/store-assets.sh # needs only Docker scripts/store-assets.sh --compose-only # re-run just the layout step 1. Runs app/test/goldens/storescreenshotstest.dart in the Flutter image. It draws seven real app screens (people, places, chat, SOS, check-in, circles, private circle) at the pixel size of every store slot, using the same fictional fixtures as the user documentation screenshots: the "The Rivera Family" circle with Maria, Carlos, Sofia and Mateo (app/test/goldens/docsscreenshotstest.dart). If the demo-server work later publishes a different seed (docs/release/DEMOSERVER.md), update the fixtures in that file so the store images match what a reviewer sees after signing in to the demo account. 2. scripts/store-assets/compose.py (Pillow) puts each render on the brand background with a caption and writes the exact final pixel sizes. It also makes the 1024 x 500 feature graphic, the 512 px Play icon and the 1024 px App Store icon from assets/brand. 3. Output goes to dist/store-assets/ (git-ignored) with a generated README.md that says what to upload where. Output Pixels Slot google-play/phone/ 1080 x 1920 Phone screenshots google-play/tablet-7in/ 1200 x 1920 7-inch tablet google-play/tablet-10in/ 1600 x 2560 10-inch tablet google-play/foldable-inner-screen/ 1840 x 2208 Large screens / foldable inner display google-play/feature-graphic-1024x500.png 1024 x 500 Feature graphic google-play/icon-512.png 512 x 512 Play icon app-store/iphone-6.9in-1320x2868/ 1320 x 2868 iPhone 6.9" app-store/iphone-6.5in-1284x2778/ 1284 x 2778 iPhone 6.5" app-store/ipad-13in-2064x2752/ 2064 x 2752 iPad 13" (only if offered on iPad) app-store/app-icon-1024.png 1024 x 1024 Reference for the Xcode asset catalog Play screenshot limits (verify): PNG or JPEG, up to 8 MB, 2 to 8 images per slot, each side between 320 and 3840 px, the long side at most twice the short side. Apple: PNG or JPEG without transparency; composed images are saved as RGB. These are renders, not captures The images are drawn from the real widget tree (the same Flutter screens the app runs) in a test, with the Roboto font, fictional data, no map tiles, no status bar and no device frame. They are not screenshots of a phone. Apple (guideline 2.3.3) and Google (Metadata policy) require that screenshots show the app in actual use and do not mislead. The renders are truthful in content (same screens, same layout logic, fake people), but: recommended: capture the final set once from a real device or emulator/simulator and use the generated files only as the layout reference or a fallback; and never add features to a caption that the screen does not show; the map screen is not rendered here (it needs tiles) so a real capture of the map is the most important one to add. The existing Play listing images (assets/google-play/upload/) were made on a Mac with the older tool app/tool/storeassetscapturetest.dart; they stay valid. Capturing real screenshots Use the demo server (docs/release/DEMOSERVER.md) so every image shows fictional people. Android phone and tablet emulator (adb) create/start an emulator with the right size, e.g. Pixel 8 (1080x2400) or Pixel Tablet adb devices adb shell settings put global sysuidemoallowed 1 # optional demo mode adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command enter adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command clock -e hhmm 0941 adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command battery -e level 100 -e plugged false adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command network -e wifi show -e level 4 adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command notifications -e visible false adb exec-out screencap -p > people.png adb shell am broadcast -a com.android.systemui.demo -e command exit Play wants phone images of at least 1080 px on the short side for the best placement; use a 1080 x 2400 device and let the compose step (or an image editor) add captions, or upload uncaptioned images. Wear OS round (emulator) Wear OS 4/5 "Large Round" emulator (454 x 454) adb -e exec-out screencap -p > dist/store-assets/raw-watch/wear-people.png Pair the emulator with the phone emulator (Wear OS app in Android Studio, Device Manager) so the watch shows the demo circle. scripts/store-assets.sh --compose-only then crops each wear-.png to a centred square and writes 512 x 512 files into google-play/wear-os-512x512/. Play requires 1:1 images, at least 384 px, without a device frame. iPhone and iPad (Xcode simulator, needs a Mac) xcrun simctl list devices available # find "iPhone 16 Pro Max", "iPad Pro 13-inch (M4)" xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 16 Pro Max" xcrun simctl statusbar booted override --time 9:41 --batteryState charged --batteryLevel 100 --cellularBars 4 xcrun simctl io booted screenshot --type=png people.png # 1320 x 2868 on the 6.9" simulators xcrun simctl statusbar booted clear Install the unsigned simulator build or run from Xcode (flutter run -d <simulator>), sign in to the demo server and navigate to each screen. Device names change with Xcode versions; take the model that Apple's page lists for 6.9" and 13". Apple Watch (simulator) xcrun simctl boot "Apple Watch Series 10 (46mm)" xcrun simctl io booted screenshot --type=png dist/store-assets/raw-watch/applewatch-people.png Only needed if the watch app ships (see App Store, Apple Watch). Series 10/11 46 mm is 416 x 496; Ultra models differ; each size you provide must match an Apple slot exactly. The compose step fits the capture into 416 x 496 with black bars if the size differs; replace those by exact captures. Review checklist for every image [ ] Shows only fictional people and places; no real name, address, email or server URL. [ ] Shows features that exist in the version being submitted (no driving sensors on iPhone). [ ] Caption text is readable and in the listing language. [ ] No transparency, correct pixel size, correct order (people first). [ ] The same app version and theme the store shows in the listing.

docs.title: Orbitly Privacy Policy (DRAFT)
docs.summary: What the Orbitly app and a server running Orbitly do with your information, in plain words. DRAFT for the owner to review with a lawyer; this is not legal advice.
docs.text: Orbitly Privacy Policy (DRAFT) What the Orbitly app and a server running Orbitly do with your information, in plain words. DRAFT for the owner to review with a lawyer; this is not legal advice. DRAFT. Not legal advice. Fill in the three marked placeholders, have a lawyer review this text for your country, and remove this box before you publish it. Placeholders: [OPERATOR NAME], [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL], [LAST UPDATED DATE]. Last updated: [LAST UPDATED DATE] The short version Orbitly is software you run for your own circle (family and friends). There is no Orbitly cloud. The people who wrote the Orbitly software do not receive your location, messages, name or email, and the app contains no advertising, no analytics and no crash-reporting service. Your information is stored on the Orbitly server you connect to. That server is run by an administrator you know (often one person in your family), or by an organisation, not by the app developer. That administrator is the one responsible for your data on that server. Orbitly never sells data and never uses it for advertising. Who is who Role Who What they do You The person using the app Choose a server, a circle and what you share Server operator The person or organisation that runs the server you sign in to: [OPERATOR NAME] for the demo and review servers, whoever you were invited by for your own circle Controls the server, its database, its backups and its settings. Decides how long to keep data. Is the "data controller" for the data on that server App developer The publisher of the Orbitly app in the app stores Builds the app. Receives nothing from your use of it. Apple and Google see standard store information (see "Apple and Google") This policy covers the app and the standard server software. A server operator may add their own rules; ask them. Contact for the demo and review servers: [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL]. What the server stores The server stores what is needed to run your circle: Account: email address, display name, an optional phone number, an optional profile photo, your role (admin, member or child) and a salted password hash (Argon2id). If you turn on two-step sign-in, its secret is stored with extra protection on the server. Devices: the phone's platform and name, an app version, a push-notification address, when it was last online and its battery level. Location (if you share it): precise coordinates, time, accuracy, speed, movement type (walking, driving, still) and battery level, from your phone, also while the app is in the background if you allow "Always" or "Allow all the time". The newest position of each person is kept so a person who is offline still shows on the map. Places and alerts: places you or your circle admins create (name, point, radius), arrival and departure events, check-ins, SOS and help alerts with their notes, and short-lived links created when you share a position. Chat: messages and photos sent in a circle chat (see "End-to-end encrypted circles" for what the server can read). Emergency contacts: a name and a phone number you enter. These are used only if you use the optional text-message (SMS) alert and your server administrator switched SMS on. Driving and trips: if you allow it, trips and driving events (such as hard braking or a possible crash) are worked out on your phone or on the server. Security log: sign-ins, session changes and administrator actions, with times and network addresses. The app itself stores a sign-in token, settings and an offline queue on your phone. Secrets for end-to-end encrypted circles stay on your phone (on iPhone wrapped by a key in the Secure Enclave where available) and are not in cloud backups. End-to-end encrypted ("Private") circles A circle is either Normal or Private. In a Normal circle, positions, places, alerts and chat are stored readable on the server, so the server administrator (and whoever can access that server's database or backups) can read them. In a Private circle, positions, history, places, arrival events, the position in check-ins and SOS, chat messages and photos are encrypted on your phone and can only be opened on the phones of the circle's members. The server stores and relays ciphertext. It still sees metadata: who is in which circle, when a phone is online, how much it uploads, and network addresses. If the server operator turns on the optional "trusted server" mode, and every member of a Private circle agrees on their own phone, the server can read that circle. The circle is then labelled "Server can read" in the app. If you lose every phone and your recovery phrase, encrypted data cannot be recovered by anyone. Who can see your information Members of your circles: only what you choose to share with that circle, and you can pause or turn off sharing at any time. Server administrators: they manage accounts. By default they cannot see where people are; the server operator has a setting that allows it, and every such access is written to the security log, which circle admins can see. Emergency contacts, only when an SOS is sent and optional SMS is switched on. The text message carries a link on your own server that expires after 24 hours. Service providers the server may use, only if the operator configures them: Map tiles: your phone loads map images from a tile provider (by default OpenStreetMap and Esri). They see the part of the map you look at and your network address, not your account. Address search: when a place address is typed, the server sends that text (and the pin position) to a geocoder (by default Photon, with Nominatim and the US Census geocoder as fallbacks). No account details are sent. The operator can turn this off. Push notifications: Apple Push Notification service on iPhone; your ntfy or another UnifiedPush server on Android. Notifications do not contain coordinates; by default they do not contain the text of a message. SMS: Twilio, if the operator enabled SMS; it sees the destination number and the link. Home Assistant: only if someone in your circle creates an integration token. We do not sell, rent or share your information for advertising, and the app has no tracking (it declares "no tracking" to Apple). Apple and Google If you install the app from the App Store or Google Play, Apple or Google process your store account, purchases (there are none), device and crash information under their own policies. The app developer does not receive your location, messages or account details from them. How long information is kept Location history: 90 days by default (the server operator may choose a different period, and you can shorten it for yourself in the app). Older points are deleted automatically. Last known position: until you delete your account or leave, so an offline person still appears on the map. Alerts and share links: share links expire after 24 hours. Alerts and check-ins follow the server's retention settings. Encrypted live data on the server is held for a short live window (48 hours by default) and encrypted history for your retention setting. Security log: kept by the server operator for as long as they decide. Backups made by the operator may keep older copies until they rotate out. Your choices and rights See and export: Settings, "Download my data" produces a copy of the data the server holds about you. Delete your account: Settings, "Delete my account" deletes your account and its location history, devices, contacts and messages you sent, after you confirm with your password. (A circle's last administrator must first hand over administration; if you are the only member the circle is dissolved.) The only data kept is an append-only encryption key log that holds ids, hashes and signatures, not names or positions. If you cannot open the app, ask the server operator to delete your account. For the demo and review servers write to [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL]. Stop sharing: turn off or pause sharing, or leave a circle, at any time. Permissions can be changed in the phone's settings. Access, correction, objection, complaint: depending on where you live (for example the EU/UK GDPR or California law) you may have rights over your data. Use the in-app tools first, then ask the server operator. You may also complain to your data protection authority. Children Orbitly is meant for families and friends, not for children to use alone. A circle administrator (a parent or guardian) creates and manages "child" accounts. The operator of the server and the circle administrator are responsible for having any consent that the law of their country requires. We do not knowingly collect data from children under 13 for any purpose other than letting their own circle see them. Children cannot change places, and a parent can remove a child from a circle at any time. If you think a child's data is on a server without a parent's consent, contact that server's operator. Contacts and photos The app does not read your address book. When you add an emergency contact, the phone's own contact picker returns only the one number you choose. Photos and camera: used only if you take or attach a picture for chat or choose a profile photo; location data inside photos is removed before sending. Security Connections use HTTPS only; the app refuses plain HTTP. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, optional two-step sign-in and passkeys are available, sessions can be revoked, and Private circles are end-to-end encrypted. No system is perfect. To report a security problem, use the private advisory form on the project's GitHub page (SECURITY.md in the source) or email [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL]. Please do not publish details before it is fixed. Analytics, advertising and tracking None. The app and the server software contain no analytics, advertising, attribution or crash-reporting SDK, and the app does not use an advertising ID. The project website does not set cookies. Where your data is processed On the server you connect to, in the country where its operator hosts it. If your operator is in a different country than you, your data is transferred there by your own choice of server. Changes If this policy changes, the new text is shown at /privacy on every Orbitly server that is updated, and the date above changes. Material changes are announced in the app's release notes. Contact [OPERATOR NAME], [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL]

docs.text: Orbitly Terms of Use (DRAFT) The rules for using the Orbitly app and a server that runs Orbitly. DRAFT for the owner to review with a lawyer; this is not legal advice. DRAFT. Not legal advice. Fill in [OPERATOR NAME], [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL], [GOVERNING LAW / COUNTRY] and [LAST UPDATED DATE], have a lawyer review it, then remove this box. Last updated: [LAST UPDATED DATE] 1. What Orbitly is Orbitly lets people in a circle (family and friends) share their location, places, alerts and chat. The app talks to a server that someone you know runs. By using the app or signing in to a server you agree to these terms. If you do not agree, do not use it. 2. Who provides what The Orbitly software is open source. The operator of a server ("operator") runs that server, creates accounts, sets its rules and is responsible for the data on it. [OPERATOR NAME] operates the demo and review servers and the app listing in the stores. The operator of your own circle's server may add rules; those apply besides these terms. 3. Your account Give correct information and keep your password and recovery phrase safe. You are responsible for what happens under your account. You must be old enough to agree to these terms where you live, or have a parent or guardian set up and manage your account as a "child" account. Orbitly is not for children to use alone. Only share your location with people who know about it. Do not secretly track another adult. Using Orbitly to stalk, harass or control someone is forbidden and may be a crime. 4. Acceptable use Do not: break the law; send abusive, threatening, sexual or illegal content in chat; upload photos of people without their permission; attack, probe or overload a server; try to read data from circles you are not in; or reverse engineer protections that keep other people's data safe. Operators and circle administrators may remove content, remove members and suspend accounts. In a circle you can ask an administrator to remove a message or a member. 5. Safety features are not emergency services The SOS, Help and "possible crash" features tell your circle (and, if the operator switched SMS on, the emergency contacts you entered). They do not call emergency services. Location can be late, wrong or missing, because of the phone, battery settings, the network, the server being down or an app version problem. Do not rely on Orbitly for your safety or anyone's life. In an emergency call your local emergency number. 6. Your content and licence You keep ownership of what you post. You give the operator and the other members of your circle permission to store and show it as the app is designed to. The Orbitly software itself is licensed under its open source licence (see LICENSE in the source). 7. Privacy Our Privacy Policy explains what is stored and who can see it. 8. Availability and changes The service may be down, slow or changed at any time. Operators may stop running a server; export your data first (Settings, "Download my data"). App updates may be required to keep working with a newer server. 9. No warranty The app and server software are provided "as is" and "as available", without warranties of any kind, to the extent the law of your country allows. 10. Limit of liability To the extent the law allows, the operator, the app developer and the authors are not liable for indirect or consequential loss, loss of data, or harm from relying on location or alerts. Nothing in these terms limits liability that cannot be limited by law (for example for death or personal injury caused by negligence, or fraud). 11. Ending You can stop using Orbitly and delete your account at any time (Settings, "Delete my account"). An operator may suspend or delete an account that breaks these terms. 12. Apple and Google If you got the app from the App Store or Google Play, Apple or Google is not a party to these terms, is not responsible for the app or its support, and has no obligation to provide maintenance. Apple and its subsidiaries are third-party beneficiaries of these terms for iPhone use, and may enforce them. 13. Changes to these terms, law We may update these terms; the new version is shown at /terms on every updated server. These terms are governed by the law of [GOVERNING LAW / COUNTRY], except where your local consumer law says otherwise. 14. Contact [OPERATOR NAME], [OPERATOR CONTACT EMAIL]

docs.title: Google Play release preparation
docs.summary: Where the Google Play listing stands and what is still needed before Orbitly can go public on Google Play.
docs.text: Google Play release preparation Where the Google Play listing stands and what is still needed before Orbitly can go public on Google Play. The step-by-step guide for the 1.0 submission (signing choice, declarations, videos) is Google Play submission guide. Current status The English listing is saved in Play Console as Orbitly, with an icon, live-map feature graphic, and five phone screenshots. The short and full descriptions explicitly say a self-hosted server is required and explain how to connect to one. Public production access still requires a closed test with at least 12 continuously opted-in testers for 14 days and Google's approval of production access. Saved declarations include no ads, no advertising ID, not a government app, no financial features, and no health features. The Content ratings and Health apps declarations are actioned. The Target audience declaration includes ages 6–8, 9–12, 13–15, 16–17, and 18+, and commits to the Families policy. The developer confirmed the child-law compliance certification in Play Console. The reviewer sign-in details point to the isolated review family on https://openfamily.frankjohnette.xyz; credentials are stored only in Play Console and must never be copied into this file. Lifestyle category, support email info@foleyit.com, closed-test feedback contact info@foleyit.com, privacy policy URL https://foleyit.com/privacy.html, and account deletion URL https://foleyit.com/delete-account.html are saved. Both public legal pages now load. Data safety is saved in Publishing overview and reports that data is encrypted in transit, matching the HTTPS-only app behavior. The Play listing states that the app rejects HTTP server addresses and directs users to provide an HTTPS URL. No app release has been uploaded or published; the code and public privacy-page changes still need to ship in a release. The Alpha closed-testing track exists but is inactive and has no release. Its country targeting and tester list are not configured. Play Console currently shows 0 opted-in testers. Public production access requires at least 12 real testers continuously opted in for 14 days, followed by Google's approval of production access. Local release-preparation changes add an offline privacy policy before server setup and in Settings, explicit background-location collection and transmission disclosure, HTTPS-only networking, and signed App Bundle output in CI. These changes have not been committed, pushed, or deployed. Validation: 107 Flutter tests pass; Flutter analysis exits successfully with informational lint notices. Release build Package: app.openfamily. The current Flutter SDK targets Android API 36. Use the existing upload keystore; do not generate a replacement or expose its private key or passwords. Never upload a debug-signed build to Play. cd app flutter pub get flutter analyze --no-fatal-infos flutter test flutter build appbundle --release --build-number=NEXTUNUSEDVERSIONCODE The result is app/build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab. Keep the generic server selector: do not compile in the review server URL. The Android CI workflow now also builds a signed App Bundle and retains it as the openfamily-play-bundle-RUNNUMBER Actions artifact for manual upload. Its APK publication behavior remains unchanged. That workflow must run with the release-preparation changes before its bundle can be uploaded. This Mac currently has Flutter and signing configuration but no Android SDK. Local App Bundle generation cannot complete until the SDK is installed and its licenses are accepted. CI already provisions its Android environment. Reviewer server and accounts Use a dedicated HTTPS deployment and fictional sample data, separate from real family locations. The proposed reviewer server is https://openfamily.frankjohnette.xyz. It responds over HTTPS at /healthz and serves the Orbitly admin app; its current family list is empty. Create review-only accounts there before entering access details in Play Console. Do not use real family admin accounts for review. Create two ordinary review accounts in one isolated review family, with one designated family admin. Never give reviewers platform-admin access. Do not require payment, an expiring invite, geographic restrictions, or an unattended second factor to exercise the app. Keep the server reachable throughout review, testing, and later app updates. Enter credentials only in Play Console's private App access section. Do not commit them, put them in this document, or include them in screenshots. Reviewer instructions to complete once access exists: 1. Launch Orbitly and enter the supplied HTTPS server address. 2. Tap Connect, then Log In with the supplied review account. 3. Read the location disclosure and grant the Android permissions needed for the background-location feature being reviewed. 4. Open the family map and People to inspect the fictional review family. 5. Open Places to create a place and configure arrival/departure alerts. 6. Install/configure ntfy as documented for the review server to test notifications while Orbitly is closed. 7. Use Settings → Location sharing to stop this device reporting. 8. Use Settings → Privacy policy to read the policy, and a disposable account for the account-deletion flow. Background location declaration Declare one core feature: family arrival and departure alerts. Suggested explanation: Orbitly uses background location to detect when a consenting family member enters or leaves a saved place, such as home or school, and notify their family. The phone sends location to the user's configured Orbitly server while the app is closed or not in use. Foreground-only access cannot detect these arrivals and departures while the phone is in a pocket and the app is closed. Users can stop reporting using Location sharing in Settings or by revoking the device's location permission. Record the production Android build, showing the prominent in-app disclosure, the affirmative Allow Location action, the Android permission flow, creation of a place, and an actual arrival/departure alert while the reporting app is backgrounded. Use test devices and fictional account names; hide credentials. Upload an accessible video and provide its link in the permissions form. Static listing artwork is not a substitute for this functional demonstration. Also complete any foreground-service declaration prompted by the uploaded bundle, describing the location service and visible persistent notification. Data safety worksheet Complete the form against the exact release and actual configured services. Self-hosting does not mean no data is collected: the app transmits data off the device to its configured server. Do not claim all traffic is encrypted unless the release actually enforces HTTPS for all relevant connections. Data Where used Required/optional considerations Precise location Live map, history, alerts, check-ins Location sharing/permissions can be declined Approximate location Derived from coordinates/map viewport Review Google's precise/approximate guidance Name, email, user IDs Accounts and family membership Account name/email required Phone numbers Optional profiles/emergency contacts/SMS Optional Photos Optional profile avatar Optional Device or other IDs Device registration, push endpoints Used for app functionality Other user content Saved places, check-in/help notes Optional feature input Other data/diagnostics Battery, motion, timestamps Verify Google's category definitions Location can be viewed by same-family members and the server operator. Optional SMS and map providers must be evaluated for data sharing and Google's user-initiated/service-provider exceptions. No advertising or analytics SDK is bundled. Audit records can retain IP addresses after account deletion with user identifiers cleared; operator backups have operator-defined retention. Do not promise instant erasure of every backup. Remaining publisher decisions Build and upload a signed App Bundle; the local Android SDK is unavailable, so use CI after the release-preparation branch is pushed. Choose closed-test countries and add at least 12 real volunteer testers. Start the 14-day continuous opt-in period only after the test release is approved and available. Record a functional background-location video on the production Android build and provide its URL in the Play declaration. Complete any foreground service declaration prompted by the uploaded bundle. Review the exact release and final Play Console changes, then explicitly submit them for review. Do not publish a production release before the required closed-test period and production-access approval. Official references Personal-account testing Background location User data and privacy Account deletion Target API requirements

docs.title: Android release process (operator)
docs.summary: For the person who publishes the Android app: where the signing key lives and how the release files are built.
docs.text: Android release process (operator) For the person who publishes the Android app: where the signing key lives and how the release files are built. Signing key The release keystore lives OUTSIDE the repository: /home/dockhub/OpenFamily/private/keys/openfamily-release.jks (mode 600) /home/dockhub/OpenFamily/private/keys/key.properties (mode 600; holds the passwords and the alias openfamily) The directory is mode 700. .gitignore excludes key.properties, .jks and .keystore. Losing this keystore (or its passwords) means every installed copy can never update again: family members must uninstall and reinstall the app (losing local app data). Back it up now: 1. Copy openfamily-release.jks and key.properties to at least two places you control, e.g. an encrypted USB stick and your password manager (attach both files, or store the base64 of the jks plus the passwords). 2. Test the backup: keytool -list -keystore <copy>.jks asks for the password. 3. Never commit them, email them, or paste them in chat. Check the certificate fingerprint any time (it asks for the password): keytool -list -v -keystore openfamily-release.jks -alias openfamily grep SHA256. GitHub secrets Run scripts/android-secrets.sh owner/repo and execute the printed gh secret set commands. It prints no secret values. Secrets: ANDROIDKEYSTOREBASE64, ANDROIDKEYSTOREPASSWORD, ANDROIDKEYPASSWORD, ANDROIDKEYALIAS. Releasing git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0 The workflow .github/workflows/apk.yml runs flutter analyze and flutter test, builds the signed APK and AAB, writes SHA256SUMS.txt, and creates the GitHub Release with orbitly-<version>.apk (pre-release tags such as v0.2.0-rc.1 become GitHub pre-releases). The server's download cache (APKGITHUBREPO) picks the first .apk asset of the latest v release, which matches. versionName is the tag without v. versionCode is (major1000000 + minor1000 + patch)100 + 99 (final) or + rc number (pre-release), so newer tags always install over older ones. Do not reuse or move tags. Minor and patch must stay below 1000. A manual run (workflowdispatch) only produces downloadable workflow artifacts. Local build Put the keystore path in app/android/key.properties (storeFile is relative to app/android/app/, absolute paths work), then flutter build apk --release. Without key.properties the release build fails on purpose; for a throwaway test build pass -POPENFAMILYALLOWDEBUGSIGNING=true (never distribute it).

categories.title: Troubleshooting
categories.description: Something not working? Start with the checklist for your symptom.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.summary: Find your problem in the list, try the short checks, then follow the link for the full steps.

headings.text: Locations stop when the phone is locked or idle

docs.text: Troubleshooting Find your problem in the list, try the short checks, then follow the link for the full steps. Always start with these three commands on the server. They answer most "is it even running?" questions: docker compose ps # every service should be running / healthy curl http://localhost:8080/healthz # {"status":"ok"} docker compose logs --tail 100 api # the last lines of the server log The admin web System page lists recent warnings and errors, and Fleet shows when each phone last reported. Tip When you ask for help, say your server version (shown in the admin web footer) and paste the last lines of the log. Remove addresses and secrets first. Nobody shows on the map 1. Open the server address in the phone's browser. If it does not load, fix DNS, ports 80/443 or the VPN first (HTTPS and domain). 2. On the phone: location all the time, battery unrestricted (Battery and permissions). 3. In the circle: is Share my location on, and has the person paused sharing? 4. Private circle? The admin web cannot show it unless you are a member who approved the browser. Phones show each other. 5. Old app? With enforcement on, an unsupported app's uploads are refused (App versions). Full steps: Nobody shows on the map and the deep dive for Private circles, No locations. Locations stop when the phone is locked or idle The screen being off is normal; Android or iOS stopping the app is the problem. Allow location all the time, allow notifications, and switch off battery saving for Orbitly (Battery and permissions). Run Settings, Phone health in the app: it checks permissions, battery exemptions and connectivity. Some phone makers close apps aggressively; see what happens when Android freezes the app in Push and Reliability. The admin Fleet page shows the last time each phone reported and why it may have gone silent. Sessions: sign-in problems, lost phone Lost or stolen phone: sign in elsewhere, open Settings, Security, Active sessions, end the old session and change your password (Lost or stolen phone). New phone: sign in again; in a Private circle another of your devices must approve it, or use your recovery key. Admin web says "Access denied": only platform admins see admin pages. If REQUIREADMINMFA=true, turn on two-step sign-in in the app, then sign out and in again. Invite code refused: check it was typed exactly, has not expired and that you are on the right server (Invite and join). Backups The admin System page warns when the last backup is missing or older than 48 hours. Run ./scripts/backup.sh and copy backups/ off the machine. Prove a backup works with ./scripts/verify-backup.sh backups/<file>.dump. Back up the serverdevice volume with the database (losing it only means approving the server again). Restoring: Backups and restore, in depth Backup and restore. Notifications and push Android has built-in push and needs nothing extra, but the phone must let the app run in the background (Notifications). Optional ntfy or UnifiedPush: check the ntfy app is installed and its server is reachable (Push). iPhone alerts need Apple push to be set up by the server admin (Apple push). SOS by text message needs an SMS provider (SMS for SOS). Alerts say only "New message in a circle" unless verbose notifications are on; that is by design. Updates ./scripts/upgrade.sh makes a backup and rolls back on its own if the new version is not healthy (Updating the server). If it rolled back or left things off, restore the backups/pre-upgrade-.dump (Backups). People on an old app see "Update required": the server supports the last five app versions (App versions). A phone that says "needs update" in a Private circle must update before it shows up; a circle admin can switch the circle to Normal in one tap (Concepts). The server will not start Run docker compose run --rm api validate-config. It prints what is wrong without showing secrets. Usual causes: JWTSECRET or POSTGRESPASSWORD not set, or a database TLS setting (Self-hosting). Still stuck Open an issue at https://github.com/TheTractorHacker/orbitly/issues with the server version and the last lines of docker compose logs api. More answers: FAQ, Admin troubleshooting.
