docs.text: Maps The Android/iOS app draws its base map with vector tiles (crisp at any density) from OpenFreeMap: free, no API key, no account. Light and dark map styles follow the app theme (positron / dark). Satellite stays a raster layer. All map widgets use one shared layer, app/lib/widgets/openfamilymaplayers.dart, configured by app/lib/services/mapstyleservice.dart. Resolution order 1. Satellite toggle: raster SATELLITETILEURL (default Esri World Imagery). 2. TILEURL set to anything other than the stock OSM URL: raster tiles from that template (use {r} in the template for @2x tiles; the app then requests high-DPI tiles on dense screens). 3. MAPSTYLEURL set: vector style JSON from that URL (MapLibre style with an OpenMapTiles-schema source). 4. Default: OpenFreeMap positron (light) or dark (dark theme). If the vector style cannot be loaded (offline, server error) the app falls back to the raster TILEURL (OSM by default) and retries the style after 30 seconds. The fallback hits OSM, so avoid relying on it for heavy use. Settings are served by GET /config (tileurl, satellitetileurl, mapstyleurl) and set through .env / docker-compose.yml. All must be HTTPS. /config is public, so a key embedded in a URL is visible to every phone. Tile policy and identification The app sends User-Agent: app.openfamily ... to style and tile hosts, and userAgentPackageName='app.openfamily' on raster layers. The public OSM servers block clients that do not follow their tile usage policy and are not meant for production apps; run your own tiles or use a provider that permits app use if you ship to many users. Caching and data use Vector tiles are cached on disk (temporary directory) with a bounded size: 50 MB by default, 25 MB in reduced-data mode, 14 day TTL, plus small in-memory caches. Raster fallback tiles use fluttermap's default cache. The style JSON itself is held in memory only, so a cold start offline falls back to raster. Privacy Every tile request tells the tile host the phone's IP address, the area being viewed (tile coordinates), and the app User-Agent. With the defaults that host is tiles.openfreemap.org (and tile.openstreetmap.org for fallback, Esri for satellite). To keep that inside your own infrastructure, self-host tiles and point the app at them. Self-hosting OpenFreeMap: it publishes a self-hosting guide and scripts for serving the planet from static files behind nginx (see openfreemap.org, "Self hosting"). Then host a style JSON whose sources.openmaptiles.url points to your TileJSON and set MAPSTYLEURL=https://maps.example.com/style.json. The style also needs glyphs and sprite URLs you host. Protomaps PMTiles: serve a regional .pmtiles file with a PMTiles server (or the go-pmtiles binary) that exposes {z}/{x}/{y}.mvt, and publish a MapLibre style (Protomaps basemaps flavors differ from the OpenMapTiles schema, so check layer compatibility) with sprites and glyphs. The app's renderer expects OpenMapTiles-style layers. Raster only: any {z}/{x}/{y}.png server (including a self-hosted tileserver) works via TILEURL; this disables the vector path. Example .env: MAPSTYLEURL=https://maps.example.com/styles/liberty.json or raster only: TILEURL=https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}{r}.png You can also set the style from the admin panel (Settings, Map style). That value overrides MAPSTYLEURL, must be an https URL to a public host, can be checked with the Test button, and takes effect on the next map load with no restart. Clearing it falls back to MAPSTYLEURL (or OpenFreeMap). Address search and automatic address detection Creating or editing a place offers (a) an address filled in automatically when you drop or move the pin (reverse geocoding) and (b) autocomplete suggestions while you type an address. The app calls only your Orbitly server (GET /geocode/search, GET /geocode/reverse, signed-in users only, rate-limited per user); the server queries one geocoder provider. Default: on, using the public Photon at https://photon.komoot.io. That means the address text people type and the coordinates of places they pin are sent from your server to photon.komoot.io, which also sees your server's IP. The phone never contacts it. The server sends only a descriptive User-Agent (Orbitly/<version> (self-hosted)), forwards no user identity, tokens or client IP, caches results in memory per signed-in user (never shared, so no one can learn by response time whether someone else looked up the same address; upstream requests are never merged across users), and never logs query text or coordinates (only counts, status and latency). Lookups happen only while a user is editing a place, not for live location tracking. Settings (server environment): Variable Meaning GEOCODERURL Provider base URL. Unset = public Photon. Set to empty to disable (the app then hides search and the server answers 503). GEOCODERTYPE photon (default) or nominatim. GEOCODERLANG Default result language when the app sends none (the app sends the device language as lang; the Accept-Language header is the next fallback; en if all are empty). Photon only supports de, en, fr, it, so other languages use en there; Nominatim and Google accept any. GEOCODERALLOWPRIVATE true to allow a loopback/private-network provider (self-hosted next to the API). Otherwise private and loopback targets are refused (SSRF guard), http is refused, redirects are never followed. GEOCODERFALLBACKURL Nominatim-compatible provider asked only for explicit searches (the user pressed Search/Enter) that Photon could not match at house level. Unset = public nominatim.openstreetmap.org; empty disables. Same SSRF rules, no redirects, at most one request per second across all users (a request that would wait longer than about 2 s is answered "try again"). Never used while typing. GEOCODERCENSUSENABLED Default true. For explicit searches of US-looking street addresses that are still unmatched, also ask the US Census geocoder (geocoding.geo.census.gov, free, no key, house-number level by interpolating address ranges). GOOGLEMAPSAPIKEY Optional. Enables Google's Geocoding API as a last resort. Empty (default) = free providers only. The key stays on the server; the app never sees it. GOOGLEGEOCODINGMONTHLYCAP Most Google requests per calendar month (UTC). Default 3000; empty or invalid uses the default. Then Google is skipped silently (one log line per month). Search quality. The server normalises the query ("88rd" becomes "88 rd", "Rd" becomes "Road", a trailing "AR" becomes "Arkansas") and, if nothing is found, retries up to three times in total: the full normalised address, then without the house number, then just the locality. Hits from a relaxed attempt are marked approximate (matched: street or locality) and the app tells the user to drag the pin to the exact spot. The map centre or last known location is sent as a bias (rounded to about 100 m) so nearby places rank first. When a location is sent, search is local first: the server first asks the provider for matches inside a box of about 100 km around it (Photon bbox, Nominatim viewbox + bounded=1) and returns those when there are any; only when nothing local matches does it search worldwide (soft bias), with nearer results ordered first. Local results carry "local": true. Extra third parties. Because of the two fallbacks above, an address typed into an explicit search can also reach nominatim.openstreetmap.org (OSMF) and geocoding.geo.census.gov (US Census Bureau), always via your server and only when Photon found no exact house. They see the text, the rounded bias point and your server's IP, not any user identity. Set GEOCODERFALLBACKURL= and GEOCODERCENSUSENABLED=false to keep everything on one provider. Google Geocoding (optional, paid). Photon (OSM) and the Census geocoder miss some rural US addresses. With GOOGLEMAPSAPIKEY set, the server asks Google only when (a) the query has a house number and neither Photon nor Census found an exact house match, or (b) an explicit search found nothing at all. Never for queries under 8 characters; never for a query without a house number unless it is an explicit search with no results. While typing it additionally needs at least two comma-separated parts ("14322 Old 88 Rd, Chester"). Results are cached per user for 30 days (empty answers too), the per-user rate limit still applies, and a global monthly cap bounds spend. The cap counter is in memory: it resets at the month rollover and on every server restart. Google results are only shown to the user (never stored), and the app shows "Powered by Google" while any shown result comes from Google. The query text, a ~100 m rounded bias area and your server's IP reach Google; no user identity does. Creating a key: in Google Cloud Console create or pick a project with billing enabled, enable the Geocoding API, then create an API key under Credentials. Under "API restrictions" restrict it to the Geocoding API only. A server key cannot be restricted by app (Android/iOS/referrer restrictions do not apply to server calls), so restrict by IP address if your server has a static IP; otherwise rely on the API restriction, the monthly cap here, and a Google budget alert / quota limit on the Geocoding API. Cost: Geocoding is billed at about $5 per 1000 requests beyond Google's monthly free credit. With the default cap of 3000 the worst case is about $15 per month (less after the credit). Lower the cap to spend less. Without a key nothing changes: only the free providers are used. GET /config reports only geocoder: {"enabled", "autocomplete"}, never the URL. Self-hosting: run Photon (github.com/komoot/photon; it needs an OpenSearch index built from a Nominatim dump or the published country extracts) or Nominatim (nominatim.org) on your network and set, for example, GEOCODERURL=http://photon:2322 plus GEOCODERALLOWPRIVATE=true. The public nominatim.openstreetmap.org prohibits autocomplete: if you point a nominatim type at it, autocomplete is disabled, only explicit searches are allowed, limited to one request per second, and a startup warning is logged. Public Photon is a shared fair-use service with no uptime guarantee. Not verified in code review Visual quality and rendering performance of vector mode on real devices have not been checked; adjust layerMode / concurrency in the shared layer if older phones struggle. Daily History scrubber GET /family/members/{id}/history?from=&to= (same family only, unchanged authorization, retention and 25 h range limit) now also returns optional speedmps and batterypct on each trail point (last reported value in the 30 s bucket; omitted when unknown). The app's Daily History screen (DailyHistoryScreen, opened from a member's profile or the People list) sends the local-day window as from/to, so days follow the viewer's timezone. The scrubber works on the full (30 s bucket) trail; only drawing is downsampled. Stops are clustered client side (75 m, 5 min) and named from the server's place visits. Playback runs 60 s of day-time per real second at 1x (4x, 16x). The avatar holds position across reporting gaps over 10 minutes. Logic: app/lib/services/historyscrubber.dart.

docs.title: Reliability tools: diagnostics, silent-phone and late-arrival alerts, fleet health
docs.summary: Status: implemented and unit/DB-tested; never run on a real phone (see testing/PHYSICALDEVICES.md for the one-hour run sheet that does that).
docs.text: Reliability tools: diagnostics, silent-phone and late-arrival alerts, fleet health Status: implemented and unit/DB-tested; never run on a real phone (see testing/PHYSICALDEVICES.md for the one-hour run sheet that does that). All of it is coordinate-free metadata (timestamps, counts, OS states), so it works for Private (end-to-end encrypted) circles without the server learning anything new. In-app Diagnostics (Settings, Help, Diagnostics) Runs on the phone and explains, in plain language, why it may not be reporting. Each check is pass, warn, fail or info and most have a one-tap fix: location permission level (always vs while in use), precise location, battery optimisation and background restriction, vendor guidance and deep links (Xiaomi, Samsung, OnePlus, Huawei, Oppo; opened through DiagnosticsChannel.kt), notifications, network, server reachability and sign-in, last upload the server saw, upload queue size, push registration and last delivery, clock skew against the server, background service, and for Private circles whether the Keystore key opens. "Copy diagnostic report" produces a redacted text (no coordinates, tokens or account details; a unit test enforces it). Since 0.24.2 the Android Keystore wrapping key works while the phone is locked (iOS: after the first unlock since boot), so Private-circle fixes are sealed and sent from a locked phone like any other. Only a key that an older version created and that has not been re-wrapped yet (needs one unlock with the app opened) makes fixes wait; Diagnostics then shows a warning, otherwise "Keys available while locked". See docs/design/E2EE.md for the threat-model change. The Self-test screen exercises what can be automated: Keystore round trip, vault write/read, channel crypto round trip with tamper detection, uploading one real fix and confirming the server registered it (server clock, so a wrong phone clock cannot fake a pass), a local notification plus a server push (POST /me/diagnostics/test-push, 6 per hour), and a 5-minute background test that checks the server heard from the phone while the app was away. The app sends a coordinate-free self-report (PUT /devices/{id}/diagnostics) at most every 30 minutes when it comes to the foreground and whenever Diagnostics is opened. Server facts GET /me/diagnostics: the caller's devices (push registration and last push result, last seen, self-reported states), lastreportat, last WebSocket connect, circles with their silent-alert setting, and servertime for clock-skew measurement. GET /api/admin/fleet (platform admin): the same for every member; the admin panel shows it as Fleet health. Liveness is recorded in memberreportstate (throttled to one write per user per minute) and memberreporthours (one row per user per UTC hour, pruned after 28 days). Encrypted items expire quickly, so this is what Private circles use. Silent-phone alerts (silence.go) Per circle, off by default. A circle admin picks 2 to 72 hours (the app offers 4, 8, 12, 24, 48). A member whose phone has not talked to the server for that long and who reported in this same UTC hour on at least 3 of the last 14 days (with at least 3 active days) triggers one alert to the circle admins and to the member. It is idempotent per silence episode (silencealertstate), stops after 7 days of silence, is held back when half the circle (3 or more people) is silent at once (outage guard), sends at most 5 per circle per 10-minute pass, skips recipients in quiet hours or with "Silent phone alerts" off or who muted that member (the episode stays open so it can fire later), and honours per-member disable and snooze. Copy says "A family member's phone" unless the recipient enabled names. Paused sharing members are skipped. Limits: the "normal hours" model is by UTC hour of day, not the member's time zone; a member who turns their phone off every night at the same hour is learned correctly only if that hour is consistently silent. Late-arrival alerts (arrival.go): minimal version Opt-in per person and per saved place (Settings, Notification settings, Late-arrival alerts). Only for circles whose positions the server can read (plain circles, or trusted-server Private circles); Private circles are never evaluated and the API refuses to create a watch for them. Needs at least 5 arrivals over 42 days on the same kind of day (weekday or weekend, in the person's own offset), on at least 60% of those days, with a median absolute deviation of 30 minutes or less. Alerts at the median plus 60 minutes, for up to 3 hours after, only if the phone reported within 2 hours, the person is not at the place and has not arrived today. Hard limits: one per person/place/day, two per person per 24 hours, 20 per pass. Not done: holidays and one-off schedule changes (the median adapts after a few days), per-place thresholds, snooze (turn the toggle off), departure ("usually leaves by") alerts.

docs.title: Home Assistant integration
docs.summary: Orbitly can feed a Home Assistant (HA) you run yourself: who is home, battery, optionally GPS, places, and arrival / departure / SOS / possible-crash / trip / low-battery events. Everything is…

headings.text: What a token can learn (privacy rules)

docs.text: Home Assistant integration Orbitly can feed a Home Assistant (HA) you run yourself: who is home, battery, optionally GPS, places, and arrival / departure / SOS / possible-crash / trip / low-battery events. Everything is read-only and opt-in. Parts: Part Where Integration tokens, read API, webhook delivery server: backend/internal/handlers/ha.go, migration 000170haintegrations "Integrations" card (create / revoke tokens, webhook, test, snippets) admin panel, Settings HACS-style custom component integrations/homeassistant/customcomponents/openfamily/ (README) Quick start 1. Admin panel, Settings, Integrations: Create a token. Pick the circles HA may see and what it may read. Copy the token (shown once). 2. In HA add the Orbitly integration (see its README to install it), enter your server URL and the token. 3. Optional push: on the token open Webhook, paste the URL HA shows in the integration's Configure dialog, and put the signing secret from step 1 into that dialog. Use Send test event. Without the custom component the API is plain JSON, so a REST sensor works too (the card shows a ready-made snippet). Tokens Format ofha + 43 base64url characters (256 random bits). Only SHA-256(token) is stored. The token and the webhook signing secret are returned once, by POST /integrations/ha/tokens. Lists show a 4-character hint only. Owned by the creating user. Any adult account (admin or member, not a child account) can create tokens for circles they are a live member of; other circle ids answer a uniform 404. Max 10 active tokens per user, 10 creations per hour. Scopes (all read): presence, location (implies presence), places, events, driving. Circle scope: a non-empty list of the owner's circles. A token only sees a circle while its owner is still a live member. Authority: a token never exceeds what its owner sees as a circle member. It does not use platform-admin powers, so ADMINLOCATIONACCESS is neither needed nor bypassed: a platform admin's token sees the same circles an ordinary member would. Bound to the owner's credentials: a token stops working (401, webhook stops) when its owner changes or resets their password, uses "log out everywhere", changes two-factor settings, or becomes a child account. Create a new token afterwards. (Migration 000171: ownertokenversion.) Revocation is immediate (DELETE /integrations/ha/tokens/{id}), clears the webhook URL and secret, and the next API call is 401. lastusedat is updated at most once a minute. Audit log (GET /audit, family admins): integration.ha.tokencreated, tokenrevoked, webhookupdated (host and last 4 characters of the path only), webhooksecretrotated, webhooktest, read (at most one row per token per 15 minutes) and authfailed (at most one per address per 15 minutes). Rate limits: 120 requests/min per token (429 + Retry-After), 30 bad-token attempts per address per 15 minutes (a /64 for IPv6), 60 management calls/min, 6 test-fires/min. What a token can learn (privacy rules) Situation Result Normal circle, member shares location state, battery, speed, last seen; lat/lon/accuracy only with the location scope Member turned sharing off or paused sharing listed with state: "sharingoff", nothing else Private (E2EE) circle, no trusted server device member listed with state: "unavailableprivatecircle", locationavailable: false; no coordinates, battery, speed or timestamps, not even for the token's owner. places returns nothing for it; arrival / departure / trip / low-battery events are not produced. The circle shows state: "unavailableprivatecircle" in circles. Private circle in trusted-server mode (server holds plaintext) behaves like a normal circle Member in both a readable and a Private circle of the token located through the readable circle only SOS / crash in a Private circle the event and the sosactive flag exist (the server knows an alert was raised), with location: {available: false, reason: "unavailableprivatecircle"} and no position SOS / crash while the member paused sharing (or sharing is off in the alert's circle) event delivered, location: {available: false, reason: "sharingoff"}; a position needs a readable circle and active sharing in it Arrival / departure at a place that was deleted later shown only if the circle recorded when the event was queued is one the token reads through; otherwise hidden SOS without the location scope location: {available: false, reason: "scope"} The readability test is the same SQL used elsewhere: NOT e2eeplaintextblocked(circle) plus sharingenabled and no active sharing pause. See docs/design/E2EE.md and PRIVACY.md. API (/integrations/ha/v1, Authorization: Bearer ofha...) Route Scope Notes GET /ping any token name, scopes, circles with state GET /members presence members[]: id, name, state (home, nothome, place name, unknown, unavailableprivatecircle, sharingoff), place, batterypct, speedmps, lastseen, location (lat, lon, accuracym; location scope), driving (driving scope), sosactive / crashactive (events scope), locationavailable, unavailablereason GET /places places zones of readable circles (id, name, type, lat, lon, radiusm) GET /events?after=<id>&limit= events the pull side of the webhook (same filtering). Without after it only returns nextafter; history is never dumped Errors: 401 invalidtoken (also for revoked tokens and for user session tokens), 403 insufficientscope, 429 ratelimited / toomanyrequests. Management (session auth, owner only): GET/POST /integrations/ha/tokens, PATCH/DELETE /integrations/ha/tokens/{id}, POST /integrations/ha/tokens/{id}/test. Not available charging: the apps do not report it. SSE / WebSocket: not implemented. Use the webhook, or GET /events as the pull equivalent. Webhook delivery Event kinds: arrival, departure, sos, crash, tripstart, tripend, lowbattery (plus test). The sources are the existing tables (geofence transitions, SOS alerts, crash reports, trips) copied into a short-lived outbox without coordinates, plus the existing low-battery detector. The outbox only fills while at least one token with the events scope exists, and a webhook never receives history from before it was set. Trips are segmented after the fact, so tripstart and tripend arrive together some minutes after the drive ended (occurredat is the real time). Request: POST JSON {"id", "type", "occurredat", "member": {"id","name"}, "place"?, "location"?, "data"?} with headers X-OpenFamily-Event: arrival X-OpenFamily-Delivery: <event id> X-OpenFamily-Timestamp: <unix seconds> X-OpenFamily-Signature: v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<timestamp>.<raw body>")> Receivers must verify in constant time, reject timestamps more than 5 minutes off, and de-duplicate by event id (delivery is at-least-once). The custom component does all three. A shared test vector keeps the Go signer and the Python verifier in step (TestHAWebhookSignatureVector, testwebhookauth.py). Retry: a failed delivery (non-2xx, timeout, refused, blocked) is retried in order with exponential backoff 30 s, 1 min, 2, 4, 8 minutes (capped at 15); after 6 consecutive failures that single event is dropped and the next one is tried. The card shows the last delivery's result (HTTP status or an error class: blockedaddress, dnserror, timeout, tlserror, connectionfailed, http<code>, redirectnotfollowed, invalidurl). HA's own certificate is verified: for a LAN HA with a self-signed certificate use http:// on the LAN or a valid certificate. Target URL policy (SSRF) http / https only, no credentials, no fragment, length <= 512, valid port. Always refused: loopback, link-local (including 169.254.169.254 and fe80::/10), unspecified, multicast, broadcast, reserved ranges, known metadata addresses (100.100.100.200, fd00:ec2::254, 168.63.129.16), deprecated site-local, 6to4 and Teredo; IPv4-mapped and NAT64 forms are unwrapped first. Private LAN (RFC 1918, fc00::/7, CGNAT 100.64/10 such as Tailscale): refused unless the token's "Home Assistant is on my local network" option is on. That option can be set only by a platform administrator and only counts while the owner is still one. A public HTTPS address (for example Nabu Casa) needs nothing. Checked at save time (name resolves, every address allowed) and again at connect time on the resolved IP, so DNS rebinding after saving cannot reach a blocked address. No proxy, no redirects, 10 s timeout, response bodies are discarded (only the status code and an error class are ever stored). Trust paths: adversarial self-review Reviewed against the code as shipped. "Fixed" means a change made during this review. Path Question Finding Token at rest Does a DB read yield a usable token? No: SHA-256 of 256-bit random tokens; the plaintext exists only in the one response. A DB read does expose webhooksecret in clear (it is needed to sign): it lets an attacker forge deliveries to the HA webhook, but only with HA's secret webhook id as well; it cannot read anything. Rotate with New signing secret. Not encrypted at rest (residual risk, accepted). Token lookup timing Can the hash lookup leak a token? The lookup is by SHA-256 of the presented token through a btree index. An attacker cannot choose hash prefixes, so comparison-time differences do not help brute force. Format is checked first (cheap 401). Token in logs Can a token reach logs or audit? Only the Authorization header carries it. The router logs no headers; audit rows contain token ids, paths without query, host and last four path characters of webhook URLs, error classes. API responses to the owner mask the URL. The webhook URL is never written to the audit log in full (checked). Session vs integration token Can a user JWT call the HA API, or an ofha token the user API? No: the HA API accepts only the ofha shape and the user API only JWTs (separate middleware); both covered by TestAuthzMatrixHAAPI. Cross-family / IDOR Can A mint or use a token for B's circle? Creation requires live membership (uniform 404). A token naming a foreign circle sees nothing (membership is re-read per request). Management routes are owner-only with a uniform 404 for others, revoked or malformed ids (authz matrix with a family-B token fixture and snapshot comparison). Revoked / out-of-scope Do they stop immediately? Yes: revoked tokens 401 on the next call and their webhook URL and secret are cleared; a missing scope is 403; leaving a circle drops it from the token's view with no action. Private circle Can any path leak a position? Members: gated per circle by e2eeplaintextblocked, including the owner's own entry. Places: only readable circles. Events: re-gated at delivery; SOS positions come from alerts.lat/lon, which the SOS path already withholds for blocked circles, and are gated again. Outbox rows hold no coordinates. Tests: TestHAMembersPrivacy, TestHAServerMemberCircleDeliversCoordinates, TestHASOSPositionOnlyWhenAllowed, TestHAEventsVisibilityAndPoll. Residual: if a circle was Private and its members' earlier plaintext rows still exist from before it was switched, they are not exposed here because the gate is on circle state, not on data. SSRF Can a user make the server call internal services? Blocked classes above; dial-time guard defeats DNS rebinding and alternate IP spellings (the check is on the connected address); no redirects, no proxy; responses not reflected. Only a platform admin can open the LAN, and the public side (any public host:port) is inherent to webhooks; the failure class is shown only to the token owner. Fixed during review: also block 6to4, Teredo and site-local IPv6, and re-check that the owner is still a platform admin before each LAN delivery. Webhook replay Can a captured delivery be replayed to HA? The signature covers the timestamp; HA rejects anything more than 5 minutes old or from the future, and de-duplicates by signed event id and by delivery header (the header is unsigned, so the body id is what counts). Memory-only caches: a replay after an HA restart inside the 5 minute window is possible and would at worst re-fire one event. Signature timing Constant-time compare? The HA verifier uses hmac.comparedigest; it hashes nothing before checking the timestamp window and fails closed on a missing secret. The server never verifies incoming signatures. Amplification / DoS Can a token burn server resources? Per-token and per-address limits, GET /events scans at most 100 outbox rows per call, deliveries are limited to 25 events per target per 5 s tick, 8 targets in parallel, 10 s timeout, outbox pruned after 7 days. A permanently failing target delays its own queue only (about 15 minutes per dropped event). Rate limiters are in memory and reset on restart. Elevation Do tokens grant admin power? No: owner-level read of the chosen circles; ADMINLOCATIONACCESS is untouched. Account deletion cascades to tokens; password changes/resets, "log out everywhere", two-factor changes and a downgrade to a child account invalidate the owner's tokens (found in the second review round and fixed: tokens are bound to users.tokenversion and the adult-role check is repeated on every request and delivery). Operations Migration 000170 adds haintegrations, haevents, haeventcursors and an index on trips(endedat); the down migration drops them. The background loop (RunHAIntegrations) idles unless a token with events exists. Single-instance assumption for delivery (duplicates are possible but harmless with HA's de-duplication). Tests Go: backend/internal/handlers/haintegrationsdbtest.go (tokens, privacy gating, IDOR, scopes, rate limits, events, signed delivery with retry, SSRF) and cmd/server/authzmatrixtest.go (new routes and TestAuthzMatrixHAAPI). Need TESTDATABASEURL. Web: web/test/integrations.test.mjs. Python: integrations/homeassistant/tests.

docs.text: License compliance audit (issue #26) Date: 2026-11. Scope: repository at v0.13.3 plus this branch. Not legal advice. Conclusion 1. Project license: LICENSE is the GNU AGPL-3.0 text. NOTICE keeps the attribution to the original OpenFamily authors (https://github.com/wheresfrank/openfamily), which this project continues. scripts/license-check.sh fails CI if either is lost. 2. Vendored code: app/packages/backgroundlocator2 is a fork of an MIT-licensed plugin (Copyright 2020 REKAB, 2022 Yukams). The MIT notice is kept in the package directory and now recorded in NOTICE and docs/THIRDPARTYLICENSES.md. MIT is compatible with AGPL-3.0 as long as the notice is preserved. app/packages/drivingnative is first-party. 3. Go dependencies (16 modules): MIT, BSD-3-Clause, ISC (coder/websocket) and Apache-2.0 (pquerna/otp). All are compatible with AGPL-3.0. Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3/AGPLv3. 4. Flutter dependencies (170 locked packages): BSD-style (119), MIT (31), Apache-2.0 (11), MPL-2.0 (dbus, nm, upower, Linux-only transitive packages not in the Android/iOS builds), plus SDK-provided packages. Compatible. MPL-2.0 files remain under MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft) and MPL-2.0 section 3.3 permits combination with AGPL. 5. Admin web dependencies: production deps are MIT/ISC/BSD/Apache/dual-MIT-Apache except two; dev-only tooling (lightningcss, MPL-2.0) is not distributed in the built bundle. 6. Network source offer (AGPL section 13): the source location is stated in NOTICE, README.md and the GitHub repository. See "Open findings" for the in-product link. Open findings Finding Impact Recommendation L1 react-leaflet 4.2.1 and @react-leaflet/core 2.1.0 (admin web, production bundle) are under the Hippocratic License 2.1, an ethical-source license with use restrictions; it is not OSI-approved and, in our reading, adds restrictions the AGPL forbids when combined in one distributed work. Distribution of the built admin bundle (backend/web/dist) may not be license-compliant. Replace react-leaflet with direct Leaflet/maplibre usage (Leaflet itself is BSD-2-Clause and is already a dependency), or obtain a written exception from the authors. Needs a maintainer decision and visual regression testing; not done here. Tracked as an exception in scripts/license-exceptions.txt so CI stays green but visible. L2 No in-product link to the corresponding source for network users (AGPL section 13). A modified deployment would need to add it. Resolved in the Orbitly rebrand: the app (Settings, About) and the admin web (footer, login page, Settings, About) show the source link and the credit to the upstream OpenFamily project. Operators of modified versions must change the link constants (app/lib/brand.dart, web/src/lib/brand.ts) to their own published source. L3 Dart license detection for the inventory is heuristic (license text matching, packages without a LICENSE file are the SDK ones). Low Re-run an inventory with flutter pub deps plus manual review on major dependency changes. S1 maplibre-gl 5.24.0 had an open critical advisory (GHSA-jrc7-96c5-q579, DOM.sanitize bypass). Admin map XSS vector if untrusted HTML reaches the sanitizer. Resolved: upgraded to 6.16.0 (npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high reports 0 vulnerabilities; build and unit tests pass). The vector-style map path still wants an eyes-on check on a real style URL. govulncheck ./... on the backend (Go 1.27.3, govulncheck v1.9.0): 0 vulnerabilities affecting called code; 3 advisories in required modules whose vulnerable code is not called. Checks scripts/license-check.sh (CI job licenses in .github/workflows/security.yml) verifies: AGPL LICENSE, NOTICE attribution, vendored MIT notice, every Go module / hosted pub package / production npm package present in docs/THIRDPARTYLICENSES.md, and every npm license on the allow-list or in scripts/license-exceptions.txt.

docs.text: Current State (baseline audit, 2026-10-25) Evidence gathered by reading the tree and running the backend test suite. Anything not listed here was not verified. Stack Backend: Go (backend/, go.mod says go 1.27.3), chi router, pgx, golang-migrate, coder/websocket. 24 SQL migrations. DB: timescale/timescaledb-ha:pg16 (TimescaleDB + PostGIS image). App: Flutter (app/), Android and iOS projects present, vendored packages/backgroundlocator2. Web admin embedded in the API binary (backend/web). Deployment: Docker Compose with caddy, api, postgres, ntfy, updater services. CI: .github/workflows apk, ca-trust, pages, test, web-preview. License: AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE present). Verified Backend go test ./... passes in a golang container: cmd/server, apkrelease, auth, config, handlers, middleware, push, serverupdate, sms all ok. db, models, web have no test files. 64 Go/Dart test files exist. Flutter tests were NOT run (Flutter not installed on this host). Model facts relevant to the rebuild One family per user: users.familyid is a single nullable column. Multiple circles needs a schema change (M3). History retention is fixed at 90 days (handlers/history.go, migration 000010). Needs to be configurable (M4). Auth: email/password, optional TOTP, access 15m / refresh 720h, tokenversion for revocation, per-IP auth rate limits. WebSocket origin check uses ALLOWEDORIGIN patterns (handlers/ws.go). Push: ntfy/UnifiedPush on Android, APNs for iOS. SMS via Twilio only. Upstream references to replace (M0) go.mod module path github.com/wheresfrank/openfamily/backend. APKGITHUBREPO default wheresfrank/openfamily in docker-compose.yml and .env.example. SECURITY.md advisory URL, app/README.md, README links, serverupdate and apkrelease GitHub clients. The updater runs git fetch origin and fast-forwards, so it follows whatever origin points at. Housekeeping Directory is not a git repository (no .git), so history cannot be preserved from this copy. An empty file Test sits at the root.

docs.text: Bar Inventory — reference material for the Orbitly admin panel This file is the concrete "bar" (reference) for a gauntlet-loop build of a polished web admin panel for Orbitly, a self-hosted location sharing app for your circles. The two references are a reference live web map (map view) and Vercel's dashboard (admin panel). Method & limits. Both reference apps are behind login walls, so no authenticated screenshots could be captured directly. Material below was gathered from public sources only, via direct fetches (the websearch tool returned no results in this session, so all sources were reached by known URL, not discovered by search). Image URLs were verified hotlinkable with HTTP HEAD where noted. Nothing below is fabricated: every hex/token is quoted from a fetched public page, and where a value could not be verified it is explicitly marked "NOT VERIFIED — not found in fetched source." 1. Reference map Source reality check The reference site is Cloudflare-blocked to automated fetch (HTTP 403). The live web map at the reference site is login-gated on top of that, so no public screenshot of the actual web map was obtainable. The closest public, verified-hotlinkable reference is the App Store listing screenshots (Apple iTunes Search API, app id 384830320). These are the mobile app screens; the reference app's web map mirrors the same map styling, member bubbles, and status indicators as the mobile map. Treat these as the map-view reference, with the caveat that the web layout (side panel etc.) is not shown. No reference-app brand design-system page / public hex tokens were reachable. Brand hex values below are NOT VERIFIED and intentionally omitted rather than invented. Design inventory (inferred from App Store screens + app description) Layout (mobile map): Full-bleed map fills the screen; floating translucent cards/bars overlay the map (member strip / place cards). Member avatars shown as circular "bubbles" on the map at each member's current location. A bottom member list/strip with avatars + names. Map is the dominant surface (~70–80% of screen). Member representation: Circular avatar bubbles pinned to map positions; each member has a distinct color ring so multiple members are distinguishable at a glance. Status indicators: Driving vs. walking/stationary activity state; battery level shown per member; "last seen"/location timestamp; place-arrival status (arrived at Home/School/Work). Circle/group concept: "Circles" are the grouping unit (family circle); a circle switcher selects which group of members is visible. (Note: competitor "Family Nest" renamed Circles to "Nests" — confirms the Circle pattern is the industry norm for this category.) Places: Saved locations (Home, School, Work) drawn as pins with entry/exit alerts. Color palette: Primary brand color is a teal/cyan (visible in the app icon, artworkUrl512, a solid teal rounded-square). Exact hex NOT VERIFIED. UI chrome is light/white cards on the map. Member accent colors appear to be a small fixed palette (one distinct hue per member). Typography: System sans (mobile); no reference-app-specific typeface found. NOT VERIFIED. Motion: Live position updates (bubbles move on the map); no public motion spec found. NOT VERIFIED. Features visible across the screenshot set: Location sharing map, Place Alerts, Family Driving Summary, Individual Driver Reports, Crash Detection w/ dispatch, Pet GPS tracker, Bluetooth (Tile) tracker, Roadside Assistance. Best image URLs (all verified HTTP 200, image/jpeg, Apple CDN is1-ssl.mzstatic.com) The WxHbb.jpg suffix is a resize directive — you can request a larger render by changing the dimensions (e.g. 1242x2208bb.jpg confirmed working for the map shot, ~689 KB). Source: iTunes Search API for app id 384830320. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource221/v4/d7/6d/b2/d76db21d-672a-6fe1-8c3c-dc3627e1449b/03LocationSharing.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — THE map view: member bubbles on a full-screen map, the primary reference for the map view. Higher-res: same path with /1242x2208bb.jpg (verified 200). https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource211/v4/aa/8f/21/aa8f2155-1da5-cf5e-1361-1930e68ff963/05PLACEALERTS.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Place Alerts: saved-place pins + arrival/leave alerts UI. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource211/v4/52/57/1a/52571ad9-16f7-fe56-3e84-7bd13533fef3/06FAMILYDRIVINGSUMMARY.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Family Driving Summary: per-member driving stats cards. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource221/v4/15/bd/7f/15bd7f00-cd79-b2a5-9169-cb47097a0206/07INDIVIDUALDRIVERREPORTS.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Individual Driver Reports: detail view of one member's trip/behavior. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource221/v4/f8/38/5f/f8385f6f-7b49-f0fb-5e15-b96d97fd8f75/08CRASHDETECTIONWITHDISPATCH.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Crash Detection + emergency dispatch screen. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource221/v4/fa/f5/f8/faf5f861-48ed-26de-ac52-edcc959706a5/04PETGPSTRACKER.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Pet GPS tracker on the map (shows non-person entities as bubbles). https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource221/v4/9e/db/ec/9edbec97-4634-99b7-7f05-7d89f7030983/09BLUETOOTHTRACKER.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Bluetooth (Tile) item tracker integration. https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/PurpleSource211/v4/1d/c4/e2/1dc4e25d-571f-4fe1-11cc-446c716f8179/10ROADSIDEASSISTANCE.jpg/392x696bb.jpg — Roadside Assistance screen. App icon (teal brand mark): https://is1-ssl.mzstatic.com/image/thumb/Purple221/v4/e1/c1/63/e1c1638d-8697-c1f4-7e0b-c5cd424b3871/AppIcon-0-0-1xU007ephone-0-1-0-0-85-220.png/512x512bb.png What makes the reference map feel polished (critic checklist) 1. Map-first layout — the map dominates; chrome is translucent overlay cards, not a separate pane stealing map real estate. 2. Member bubbles with distinct per-member color rings — multiple members are instantly distinguishable; color is the primary identity device. 3. Rich status per member — activity (driving/walking/stationary), battery %, and last-seen time are surfaced on the member, not buried. 4. Places as first-class pins with arrival/leave alerts — Home/School/Work are visible on the map and trigger notifications. 5. Circle/group switcher — switching which group of members you're viewing is one tap. 6. Calm, light chrome — white/translucent cards over the map; the teal brand accent is used sparingly for primary actions/branding. 7. Live, moving bubbles — positions update in place; the map feels alive, not a static snapshot. Gaps (explicit) No verified reference-app brand hex values. (the reference site blocked; no public brand/press kit reached.) Do not invent the teal hex — confirm against the app icon or a fetched brand asset before using. No public web-map screenshot. The reference images are mobile app screens. The web map's side-panel layout is unknown from public sources; infer the member list as a side panel for the desktop build but flag it as inferred. No reference-app typeface / spacing scale found publicly. 2. Vercel — dashboard (admin panel) Source reality check The live dashboard at vercel.com/dashboard redirects to /login (auth-gated); no authenticated screenshot could be captured. However, Vercel publishes its entire design system ("Geist") publicly at vercel.com/geist/ — this is the actual system the dashboard is built from, including the color role system, full typography scale, material/elevation presets, and a component catalog that mirrors the dashboard's UI (Avatar, Badge, Button, Empty State, Skeleton, Loading Dots, Status Dot, Context Card, Tabs, Table, Command Menu, etc.). This is stronger than a screenshot for a builder and is the primary Vercel reference below. Individual dashboard docs pages (/docs/projects, /docs/getting-started-with-vercel) were fetchable but their bodies are dominated by repeated site nav and were truncated before the embedded screenshot images; specific full-page dashboard screenshot URLs could not be extracted from the docs HTML via text fetch. The Geist component examples do contain dashboard-style mockups (e.g. a /dashboard/overview path card with Hobby/Pro/Enterprise badges shown on the Colors page). Design inventory (from the public Geist design system) Foundations: Colors, Typography, Materials (elevation) — published at vercel.com/geist/colors, /geist/typography, /geist/materials. Color system (roles, not single hexes): Two backgrounds (Background 1 default, Background 2 secondary). Ten numbered color roles used consistently across components: Colors 1–3 = component backgrounds (default / hover / active) Colors 4–6 = borders (default / hover / active) Colors 7–8 = high-contrast backgrounds (e.g. upgrade prompts) Colors 9–10 = text & icons (Color 9 secondary, Color 10 primary) 10 scales total: Gray, Gray-alpha, Blue, Red, Amber, Green, Teal, Purple, Pink. P3 color used where supported. Note: raw hex values are rendered as visual swatches on the page, not as text, so they were NOT extractable from the fetched HTML. The structure (the 1–10 role ladder two backgrounds + named scales) is verified; the literal hexes are not. Don't invent them — pull them from the Geist Figma/Tailwind source or by sampling the live swatches. Typography (verified scale): Geist Sans for text, Geist Mono for code/mono labels. Classes pre-set font-size + line-height + letter-spacing + weight. Named styles actually used in the dashboard: Headings: text-heading-72 / 64 / 56 / 48 / 40 / 32 / 24 / 20 / 16 / 14 Buttons: text-button-16 (largest), text-button-14 (default), text-button-12 (tiny, in inputs) Labels (single-line, generous line-height, pairs with icons): text-label-20/18/16/14/13/12, plus mono variants text-label-14-mono / 13-mono / 12-mono; text-label-13 is tabular for numbers. Copy (multi-line, higher line-height): text-copy-24/20/18/16/14/13, text-copy-13-mono for inline code. Modifiers: <strong> inside a class gives Strong; some labels use CAPS (label-12). Materials / elevation (verified radii + shadow roles): Material encodes elevation role; pick by where the element sits in the layered hierarchy. Surface: material-base (everyday, radius 6px), material-small (slightly raised, 6px), material-medium (12px), material-large (12px). Floating: material-tooltip (lightest shadow, corner 6px, only floating element with a stem), material-menu (lift, radius 12px), material-modal (further lift, 12px), material-fullscreen (biggest lift, radius 16px). Rule: don't stack two materials on the same element; align elevation with z-index band; use the lowest elevation that still reads as raised; pair shadow with focus-visible ring. Components catalog (verified present, each at vercel.com/geist/<name>): Avatar, Badge (incl. Pill), Banner, Breadcrumbs, Browser, Button, Calendar, Checkbox, Choicebox, Clearable Input, Code Block, Collapse, Combobox, Command Menu, Context Card, Context Menu, Copy Button, Description, Destructive Action Modal, Dots Menu, Drawer, Empty State, Entity, Error, Error Card, Feedback, Fieldset, File Tree, Gauge, Grid, Input, JSON View, Keyboard Input, Label, Load More Button, Loading Dots, Menu, MiddleTruncate, Modal, Multi Select, Note, Pagination, Phone, Progress, Project Banner, Radio, Relative Time Card, Scroller, Search Input, Select, Separator, Sheet, Show more, Skeleton, Slider, Snippet, Spinner, Split Button, Status Dot, Switch, Table, Tabs, Text With Copy Button, Textarea, Theme Switcher, Toast, Toggle, Tooltip, Video. The admin-panel-relevant subset to study: Sidebar (file-tree/nav pattern via File Tree + Tabs + Menu), top bar (Search Input + Command Menu + Avatar + Theme Switcher), project list (Context Card / Entity / Table + Status Dot), empty/loading states (Empty State, Skeleton, Loading Dots, Spinner), badges (Badge / Pill for Hobby/Pro/Enterprise plan tags), buttons (Button + Split Button + Dots Menu), feedback (Toast + Note + Feedback). Aesthetic notes from the Geist intro: "high contrast, accessible color system"; the Grid is described as "a huge part of the new Vercel aesthetic" — study vercel.com/geist/grid. Typeface "specifically designed for developers and designers" (vercel.com/font). Overall feel: Black/white/gray monochrome base with a single restrained accent; very high contrast; tight, consistent spacing driven by the type+material system; near-monochrome dark dashboard with crisp 6/12/16px radii and layered, restrained shadows; developer-grade mono labels and tabular numerals for data. Best reference URLs Primary (the design system itself — these are the bar): https://vercel.com/geist/introduction — Geist overview; links to foundations + brands + components. https://vercel.com/geist/colors — color role system (Backgrounds 1–2, Colors 1–10, 10 scales); includes a dashboard-style /dashboard/overview mockup card with Hobby/Pro/Enterprise badges. https://vercel.com/geist/typography — the full verified type scale (headings/buttons/labels/copy + mono variants, tabular numerals). https://vercel.com/geist/materials — elevation presets with verified radii (6/12/16px) and shadow roles. https://vercel.com/geist/grid — the grid system Vercel calls central to its aesthetic. https://vercel.com/font — Geist Sans / Geist Mono typefaces. https://vercel.com/geist/brands — Vercel/Next/Turbo/v0/eve logo & brand assets (also "Download Brand Assets / Brand Guidelines" in the site header). Changelog (public, often shows dashboard UI in posts): https://vercel.com/changelog Docs (public, embed dashboard screenshots in body — fetchable but nav-heavy): https://vercel.com/docs/projects, https://vercel.com/docs/getting-started-with-vercel, https://vercel.com/docs/deployments. Dashboard screenshot image URLs: NOT EXTRACTED — the docs HTML embeds dashboard images, but text fetches truncated on the repeated site nav before reaching the body image tags. A logged-in screenshot of the real dashboard was not obtainable from public sources in this session. Use the Geist component examples (which render dashboard-style mockups) as the visual reference, and supplement by manually viewing the changelog/docs in a browser. What makes Vercel feel polished (critic checklist) 1. Monochrome, high-contrast base — black/white/gray with a single restrained accent; no rainbow status colors except the named semantic scales (Red/Amber/Green/Blue used sparingly for state). 2. docs.summary: The reviewed outbound clients use normal TLS verification: GitHub release/update checks, APNs, Twilio, and push clients use Go HTTP clients. Normal verification is insufficient when its root store…
docs.text: October 2026 eMudhra CA incident The reviewed outbound clients use normal TLS verification: GitHub release/update checks, APNs, Twilio, and push clients use Go HTTP clients. Normal verification is insufficient when its root store still permits the compromised CA hierarchy. This change updates trust in images; it does not establish whether any running deployment was attacked. The build disables these trust anchors by exact SHA-256 fingerprint: emSign ECC Root CA - G3: 86a1ecba089c4a8d3bbe2734c612ba341d813e043cf9e8a862cd5c57a36bbe6b emSign Root TLS CA - G3, self-signed: 7dd78d5f4f13459a83dff9abbba62edbaf6f2d102bf257fd712f4d9f2746ed8d emSign Root TLS CA - G3, cross-signed: 3094025792039a68af6e553686410bdab7c0d4a36b9084cba64202e35d6ebbdd AAA Certificate Services: d7a7a0fb5d7e2731d771e9484ebcdef71d5f0c3e0a2948782bc83ee0ea699ef4 AAA is a retired root with an alternate signing path to the compromised intermediates. Leaving it in an older distro bundle can defeat removal of just the eMudhra root. Other emSign roots and USERTrust/Sectigo roots are preserved. Valid sites that still depend on the removed hierarchies can stop connecting; their operators must move to an unaffected chain. Do not bypass verification. The script scans distribution and locally imported CA sources, disables matching configuration entries, and moves blocked certificates outside the .crt import glob. update-ca-certificates --fresh then regenerates both the bundle and hashed directory, so clients cannot fall back to an old hashed certificate. A malformed source certificate fails the build. Re-running is safe. Deployment Both the API and updater build/runtime stages apply the distrust. The backend Docker context explicitly includes the updater's shared script. Rebuild and replace BOTH services, including the updater sidecar: docker compose build --pull --no-cache api updater, then docker compose up -d --no-deps api updater from the host. Caddy, ntfy, database images, the host, and mobile-device trust stores need their own vendor updates; rebuilding these two services does not update those clients. Existing containers do not change when the PR is merged. Rebuild and redeploy. For native development, update the host/runtime CA store separately. Custom application CA options, mounted bundles, and trust-related environment overrides must be audited separately; this build does not rewrite external files. Validation Run node --test scripts/ca-trust.test.mjs (Node 22+, OpenSSL on PATH). Fixtures are public CA certificates with no private keys. Tests cover renamed and duplicate blocked certificates, local imports, idempotence, preservation of ISRG Root X1, actual OpenSSL rejection, and failure on corrupt input. CI also runs scripts/check-ca-trust.sh against built image trust stores. A package vulnerability scan alone does not prove that an application rejects a compromised chain. References Mozilla incident and alternate cross-signs eMudhra certificate repository and fingerprints Historical Mozilla-derived AAA certificate fingerprint

docs.summary: Status: stage 1 implemented on feat/circles. Stage 2 is partly done (circle-aware map and live stream, see below); the rest is listed at the end.

headings.text: Staying in sync with legacy write paths
Circle-aware map and live stream (stage 2, done)

docs.text: Multi-circle data model (GAP-001, GAP-002) Status: stage 1 implemented on feat/circles. Stage 2 is partly done (circle-aware map and live stream, see below); the rest is listed at the end. Goal: a user can belong to several circles (family, friends, ...), is admin in some and member in others, and chooses per circle whether their location is shared. The change is additive: families, users.familyid, users.role and every existing endpoint keep working unchanged for current clients. Tables (migrations 000060, 000061) circles(id, name, icon, createdby, createdat) circlemembers(circleid, userid, role adminmember, sharingenabled default true, joinedat), primary key (circleid, userid), cascades from both parents, index on userid. invitecodes.circleid (nullable FK, cascade). familyid is now nullable; a CHECK requires one of the two. How existing families map Each families row becomes one circle with the same id (name, createdat copied; createdby = oldest admin). Each user with a familyid becomes a member of the circle with that id (admin stays admin, member and child become member). Nothing that references families(id) (places, geofences, alerts, auditlog, invitecodes) is rewritten. The backfill uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so re-running is safe; the down migration drops the two tables and triggers and loses nothing legacy. Staying in sync with legacy write paths users.familyid remains the user's primary circle and the legacy endpoints still read it and users.role. Triggers keep the new tables correct without touching the legacy handlers (or other teams' code): families insert/rename/delete -> create/rename/delete the circle with that id. users insert/update of familyid or role -> upsert/delete the membership of circle familyid (self-heals a missing circle). In the other direction the circle endpoints repair the legacy pointer: removing a member, leaving, or deleting a circle moves users.familyid to the user's next family-backed circle (or NULL), and a role change in a user's primary circle also sets users.role (a legacy child stays child). So a removed member loses legacy access in the same transaction. Circles created with POST /circles have no families row; they are reachable only through circle endpoints (stage 2 will add circle-scoped places/chat to them). Roles and consent Circle role: admin (rename, invite, remove members, change roles, delete) or member. The last admin cannot leave, be removed or be demoted (409), checked inside a transaction holding the circle row lock. Sharing consent is per membership: circlemembers.sharingenabled. A member changes only their own flag with PUT /circles/{id}/sharing {"enabled": bool}; no admin can turn it on for someone else. The flag is read from the database for every live update, so turning it off stops the next update for that circle immediately. A viewer sees subject S's location only through a circle where both are members and S has sharing on. A user always sees themselves. S still appears in member lists with null location fields (wire format unchanged). The authorization helper (internal/circles) Handlers must not compare users.familyid or write membership SQL; they call: RequireMember(ctx, userID, circleID) -> membership or ErrNotFound. RequireAdmin(ctx, userID, circleID) -> ErrNotFound for outsiders, ErrForbidden for members. SharedWith(ctx, viewer, subject) -> circle ids where both are members and the subject shares (self: all own circles). SharingCircles(ctx, subject) -> circles the subject currently shares in (live fan-out). LocationVisibility(ctx, viewer, circleIDs) -> co-members and whether their location may be shown. CircleIDs(ctx, user). New(poolortx): works inside a transaction. A non-member and a non-existent or malformed circle id are indistinguishable (ErrNotFound, HTTP 404), so ids cannot be probed (IDOR / SEC-006). Platform-admin cross-family views are a separate, audited path and are unchanged. Endpoints (handlers/circles.go) POST /circles, GET /circles, PATCH /circles/{id}, DELETE /circles/{id}, GET /circles/{id}/members, DELETE /circles/{id}/members/{userid} (me allowed), PATCH /circles/{id}/members/{userid}, PUT /circles/{id}/sharing, POSTGET /circles/{id}/invites, DELETE /circles/{id}/invites/{inviteid}, POST /circles/join {code}. At most 25 circles per user. Choices: DELETE /circles/{id} is refused with 409 if it is the only circle of any member, unless ?force=true; it never deletes the legacy families row or its places/geofences. Invites reuse invitecodes; for a family-backed circle familyid is also set, so the code still works in legacy join/register. A code for a non-family circle is rejected by the legacy flow (not consumed) and only redeemable via POST /circles/join. Invite roles are admin or member. Live read path The hub keeps its maps but a socket now subscribes to all of its user's circles (registerCircles). broadcastLocation/broadcastPresence fan out to SharingCircles(owner) plus the owner's own sockets, once per socket. Removal, leave, circle delete and join call subscribeUser/unsubscribeUser so the socket set changes at once; the existing 30 s revalidation also re-syncs subscriptions from the database as a backstop and closes a socket whose user has no circle. members snapshot (WebSocket) and GET /family/members use LocationVisibility and blank location fields for non-sharing members. For a user with one circle and default sharing, output is identical to before. Stage 1 limitations child is not a circle role (maps to member); users.role stays authoritative for legacy checks. A multi-circle user's WebSocket members snapshot is the union of their circles (no circle id on the wire yet). Account deletion can leave a circle without an admin (promote the oldest member in stage 2). The legacy registration flow cannot redeem codes of non-family circles. Circle-aware map and live stream (stage 2, done) Wire protocol (GET /ws/stream, additive; legacy clients unchanged): Connect with ?circleid=<uuid> (one circle) or ?circleid=all to opt in to circle-labelled frames; an unknown, malformed or foreign id is a plain 404 before the upgrade. Without the parameter the socket is "legacy": every frame is as before (one unlabelled copy per update, snapshot of all co-members). Client -> server {"type":"subscribe","circleid":"<uuid>all"} switches an open socket (also opts in). The membership is checked against the database. Success: {"type":"subscribed","circleid":...} then a fresh members snapshot scoped to that circle. Failure: {"type":"error","code":"circlenotfound"} and the previous subscription stays. Aware clients get members with circleid (all or the id); location and presence frames carry circleid. A subject who shares in several circles is delivered once per circle (viewer and subject both members, subject sharing on), so the client can filter; an aware socket narrowed to one circle only receives that circle's frames. A subject always receives their own updates, labelled per own circle. New frames for aware sockets: sharing {circleid,userid,enabled} when a member changes their flag, and circleremoved {circleid} when the hub drops that circle from the socket (removed, left, deleted). A narrowed socket then falls back to all; a socket left with no circle is closed, as before. The 30 s revalidation still re-syncs subscriptions and closes revoked sockets. Each member in members (and in GET /family/members) carries circleids (circles shared with the caller in scope) and sharingcircleids (where that member shares). GET /family/members?circleid=<uuid>all: membership-checked, 404 for outsiders and malformed ids; without it the legacy primary circle. adminws is unchanged (platform admins keep the unlabelled global stream). App: the circle pill selects a circle (or "All circles" when in two or more), persisted in shared preferences; the roster, map markers, People list and socket are scoped to it, with a "Sharing paused" banner (and Resume) when the user turned sharing off in the selected circle. A deleted or left circle falls back to the primary one; stale frames from a previous selection are ignored. With one circle nothing is scoped or shown differently. Stage 2 (remaining) - exact files Convert from familyid to a circle id taken from the request and checked with internal/circles: handlers/place.go (List/Create/Update/Delete place + admin list), handlers/geofence.go, handlers/geofenceeval.go (+ migration relaxing places.familyid / geofences.familyid FK to circles, adding circleid). handlers/history.go (GetMemberHistory still checks same familyid, ignores sharing), handlers/locationrequest.go (family check, sharing), handlers/family.go GetFamilyMemberAvatar, ws.go broadcastAvatarUpdate. handlers/alerts.go, handlers/contacts.go, handlers/audit.go (family-scoped fan-out and audit view). handlers/admin.go, adminusers.go, adminws.go (move/assign/delete family must call circle repair). handlers/auth.go Register / invites.go consumeInviteCode (circle invite at registration), profile.go DeleteMe (last-admin handling). ~~Add circle id to WebSocket frames~~ (done above); ws.go broadcastAvatarUpdate is still family-scoped. Places, geofences and history per circle (a later issue), tracking history retention per circle, chat (GAP-005), notification settings (GAP-006). Temporary circles (migration 000114) circles.expiresat (nullable; NULL = permanent) and circles.endedat (set when an admin ends the circle early). A circle is live while endedat IS NULL AND (expiresat IS NULL OR expiresat > now()). Expiry is enforced in SQL on every read, so correctness needs no job: Every internal/circles helper reads the view livecirclemembers (circlemembers joined to live circles), so RequireMember/RequireAdmin, CircleIDs, SharedWith, SharingCircles, OwnAndSharingCircles, LocationVisibility, MemberCircles and CoMembers treat an expired circle as non-existent (404 to members and outsiders alike). That covers chat, check-ins, trips, watch/live boost, sharing pauses and WS subscriptions. Chat unread/push, crash alerts, live shares and member edit use the view too. Joining by invite code and the legacy code redeem path refuse codes of a non-live circle; creating invites needs a live circle (admin check). GET /circles omits non-live circles and returns expiresat; WS member snapshots carry circleexpires (circle id -> expiry, temporary only). API: POST /circles accepts durationhours (1-720) or expiresat (1 hour to 30 days from now). PATCH /circles/{id} (admin) accepts extendhours, expiresat, or end: true; only temporary circles can be extended or ended. A circle that lapsed naturally can be extended by its admin during the grace period (RequireGraceAdmin); one ended early cannot be revived. Cleanup: RunCirclePurge (every 10 min) drops hub subscriptions of lapsed circles and deletes circles 7 days after they ended/expired (members, invites, chat and check-in rows cascade). No expiry reminder push is sent: there is no existing scheduled-notification hook to attach one to.

docs.title: Dawarich export integration
docs.summary: Issue: #29 asked for a design document first (opt-in, secure credentials, dedup, retention behaviour). The integration was subsequently built (backend/internal/handlers/dawarich.go, migration…
docs.text: Dawarich export integration Issue: #29 asked for a design document first (opt-in, secure credentials, dedup, retention behaviour). The integration was subsequently built (backend/internal/handlers/dawarich.go, migration 000105dawarichsync, per-user mapping added later). This document records the design as built, checks it against the issue's four requirements, and lists the gaps that still need a decision. Dawarich is a self-hosted location-history viewer (https://dawarich.app); Orbitly pushes points to its POST /api/v1/points. Behaviour Direction: one-way push from Orbitly to Dawarich; nothing is read back. Configuration (admin only): PUT /api/admin/dawarich stores baseurl, optional localurl (LAN fallback tried only when the public address is unreachable), the API key, enabled, sendunmapped, and backfilldays. Per-user mappings (dawarichusermap) give a member their own Dawarich account/key. Transport: a background loop (RunDawarichSync, every minute) pushes batches of up to 500 points (max 20 batches per round) as GeoJSON locations with timestamp, accuracy, altitude, speed, battery, device name and device id, authenticated with Authorization: Bearer <key>. Credentials: API keys are sealed with a key derived from the server secret (auth.SealSecret, purpose dawarich-api-key) and never returned by the API (apikeyset boolean only). Stored errors and logs drop the request URL (scrubDawarichErr) so keys in URLs do not leak. Dedup: a per-device cursor (dawarichcursor.lastts, advanced with GREATEST) means each point is sent once, in timestamp order; the cursor moves only after Dawarich accepted the batch, so a failed batch is retried (at-least-once; Dawarich also dedups identical timestamp+coordinates on its side). Disabling or deleting the settings/mapping clears the cursor. Retention behaviour: sync starts at since (now, or now minus backfilldays when the admin chooses a backfill); older history is never pushed implicitly. Deleting points in Orbitly does not delete them in Dawarich, and disabling sync does not recall already-sent data; this is intentional (Dawarich is the user's own archive) and must be stated to users. Check against the issue Requirement Status Opt-in Yes at the server level: off by default, admin must configure and enable. Secure credentials Yes: encrypted at rest, write-only through the API, scrubbed errors. Dedup Yes: per-device cursor, at-least-once with destination-side dedup. Retention behaviour Defined above (one-way, no deletion propagation) Explicit user authorization Gap. The admin enables export for members (sendunmapped, per-user mapping). A member does not consent in-app. Design reviewed before implementation Not met historically (built first); this document is the retrospective review. Open decisions (need the maintainer) 1. Member consent: require each member to accept (in-app toggle, default off, visible "my location is exported to <host>" indicator) before their points are sent; make sendunmapped default to off. Recommended: yes, since members' location leaves the system the family agreed to. 2. Deletion propagation: document only (recommended), or call Dawarich's delete API on account deletion. 3. E2EE: the server-side sync reads only the plaintext locations table and so skips Private circles by construction (test: TestE2EEDawarichServerSyncSkipsPrivateCircles). Private circles reach Dawarich through backend/cmd/e2ee-bridge, a separate program the user runs off the server host as an approved read-only service device member (see E2EE.md, phase 3, and the bridge README). The bridge has its own Dawarich config (URL, main key, sendunmapped, per-user keys keyed by Orbitly user id), uses the same GeoJSON mapping and its own de-duplication, and its host can read the circle. A person who is in both a Private and a normal circle keeps being exported by the server for the normal circle, as before. Trusted-server mode (opt-in, see E2EE.md "Trusted-server mode"): when the owner enables it and every member of a Private circle allows the Orbitly server to read it, the server decrypts that circle's positions in a sidecar and stores them in the normal locations table, so the built-in server-side Dawarich sync works again for that circle with no bridge (test: TestServerIngestStoresVerifiedPositions runs nextDawarichBatch against server-decrypted points). The server then holds plaintext and so does the Dawarich it forwards to; this is only sensible when Dawarich is on the same trusted network. Circles without an approved server device are still skipped by the built-in sync. The separate e2ee-bridge (Dawarich mode) keeps working unchanged; a person exported by both would be duplicated, so use one of the two per circle. 4. Tests: there are no Go tests for dawarich.go; add handler tests with an httptest Dawarich server (cursor advance on success, no advance on 5xx, key never in responses/errors) before changing behaviour.
