docs.text: ADR: End-to-end encryption ("Private circle") Status: ACCEPTED (supersedes the earlier "Proposed" text of this file, which recommended against E2EE). Issue: #34. Phase 1 (keys and verification) and phase 2 (the encrypted channel) are implemented. Phase 3 (web viewer and Dawarich bridge as approved read-only device members) is implemented; see "Phase 3" below. Chat, media and phone-side trips are still future. An optional trusted-server mode (the Orbitly server as an approved member device, owner's decision) is described in "Trusted-server mode" below. Decision The maintainer adopted end-to-end encryption so that the server can no longer read member locations in circles that opt in. It is delivered in phases and opt-in per circle ("Private circle"): Phase Scope State 1 Cryptographic foundation and verification UX: device identity keys, circle key epochs, wrapped keys, key transparency log, recovery, safety numbers, server-record check, admin/CLI tooling. No location data moves. implemented 2 Live fixes, history, places, arrival/departure events and SOS positions move into the encrypted channel; place evaluation runs on the phones. Server-side trips, driving report and weekly summary are unavailable in a Private circle. implemented; phone background behaviour not yet verified on devices (see phase-2 section) 3 Web viewer and Dawarich bridge as approved read-only device members (API contract below). implemented (browser viewer, e2ee-bridge, phone approval screen); not yet exercised against a live Dawarich or on a physical phone 3b Optional trusted-server mode: the Orbitly server as an approved, per-member-consented device so the server can read (and store plaintext for) a circle again. Off by default. implemented; not exercised on a physical phone or a live deployment (see "Trusted-server mode") 4 Media (chat photos); encrypted chat; phone-side trips. encrypted chat and its photos: implemented, see E2EECHAT.md; phone-side trips: future Existing circles keep working exactly as today. A circle switched to Private mode only gets keys in phase 1. The toggle is OFF by default, admin-only, and the UI says honestly what changes now and what will be unavailable later. Threat model In scope (the server is the adversary, the members are not): Adversary Outcome with Private circles (after phase 2) Server breach (RCE, SQL injection) Attacker gets ciphertext, public keys and metadata, not positions Stolen database or backup Same Curious operator Same; the operator can still add a malicious public key (see "Honest limits") Compelled operator Can hand over ciphertext and metadata only Network attacker TLS as before; ciphertext additionally Out of scope: a hostile circle member (members are trusted by design and hold the circle key), a compromised phone (malware with the user's session reads the same data the user can), traffic analysis by the network, and denial of service by the server. What does NOT work in a Private circle (phase 2) and how it is handled Feature Why it needs plaintext today In a Private circle Place arrival/departure alerts (geofence.go, placepresence.go) SQL evaluation of fixes against places Computed on the sender's phone; it sends an encrypted "arrived at Home" event. Places are distributed encrypted. Server only relays. Live map, history, day view server serves rows Phones decrypt; history is stored as ciphertext and decrypted on the phone Trips, driving reports, crash scoring, weekly summary server segments and aggregates fixes Computed on-device and shared as encrypted summaries, or documented as unavailable. Server-side trips/driving/weekly summary are unavailable for Private circles SOS with position server pushes last position Position travels in the encrypted payload. The server does not store it and the SMS/Twilio fallback cannot be told it; SOS in a Private circle must say so in the UI. The wake-up push has no position. Known gap (PRIVACYMODELV1 L1): the app still includes the coordinates in the plaintext alert request, which the server discards, so a malicious server or a TLS-terminating proxy can see them (backlog B3) Admin map and device last-known positions operator reads positions Unavailable for Private circles (by design), except circles in trusted-server mode (below), where the server holds the plaintext it ingested. Admin panel still lists accounts, devices, keys Dawarich export server forwards points Server-side sync skips Private circles (it reads only the plaintext table). Use the e2ee-bridge (phase 3), a service device member that you run off the server host. Exception: with the opt-in trusted-server mode (below) the built-in sync works again for the circles whose members all consented Server geocoded place names and address search server reverse-geocodes Intended: geocoding moves to the phone (or an on-device lookup) so the server never learns an address. Known gap (PRIVACYMODELV1 L2): the place picker still asks the server to reverse-geocode the pin and to search typed addresses (backlog B4) Push text naming a place or person server composes the text Server sends a content-free wake-up; the app decrypts and raises a LOCAL notification Downgrade rule (implemented in phase 2, see "Enforcement"): circles.e2eemode = 'private' is the switch. The server refuses or drops plaintext positions and places for a Private circle, a database trigger backs that up, and phones never fall back to plaintext after a failed seal. Cryptographic design (frozen wire formats) Library choice: the Dart package cryptography (pure Dart: Ed25519, X25519, XChaCha20-Poly1305, HKDF-SHA256, Argon2id, SHA-2) plus bip39 (wordlist and checksum). sodiumlibs/libsodium would be faster and more widely audited, but it adds a native build (FFI and prebuilt binaries per ABI) and could not be proven to compile in the available environment within the work budget; cryptography builds everywhere, is widely used, and payloads here are tens of bytes where speed is irrelevant. Going native later is a drop-in (cryptographyflutter accelerates the same API, or a libsodium backend can replace E2ee) because both sides are pinned by cross-language test vectors. On the server, Go's standard crypto/ed25519, crypto/ecdh, and golang.org/x/crypto (chacha20poly1305, hkdf, argon2). All strings are ASCII; identifiers are lower-case UUIDs (36 bytes); integers are big-endian. Every hashed or signed message starts with its own NUL-terminated domain string, so one signature or hash can never be replayed as another. Keys Identity seed: 32 random bytes generated on the phone. ed25519seed = HKDF-SHA256(seed, salt=none, info="OFE2EE1-IDENTITY-ED25519"), x25519secret = HKDF-SHA256(seed, salt=none, info="OFE2EE1-IDENTITY-X25519"). One Ed25519 signing key and one X25519 agreement key per device. The seed lives only in the Keystore-protected vault (below). Device id: random v4 UUID chosen by the phone (it is inside signed messages, so the server cannot rename a key). Circle key: 32 random bytes per circle per epoch (epoch >= 1, strictly increasing), generated on an admin's phone. Recovery identity: derived from the 24-word phrase (see Recovery); registered as kind = 'recovery'. Fingerprint, digits, safety number fingerprint = SHA-256("OFE2EE1-FP\0" ed25519pub x25519pub) (32 bytes, stored as hex). Digits (12 groups of 5, Signal style): D = SHA-512("OFE2EE1-DIGITS\0" fingerprint); group i = big-endian uint40 of D[5i..5i+5] mod 100000. Short form: first 8 fingerprint bytes as four upper-case hex groups (5CA3 7A50 B2A2 396A). A glance aid only. userDigest = SHA-256("OFE2EE1-USER\0" userid sorted distinct fingerprints). Safety number between two users: SHA-512("OFE2EE1-SAFETY\0" min(userDigestA,userDigestB) max(...)) rendered as 12x5 digits. Symmetric; changes if either person's key set changes. Registration binding and the transparency-log action message binding = Ed25519(sk, "OFE2EE1-BIND\0" userid deviceid ed25519pub x25519pub) proves possession and binds both keys and the id to the account. Every state change is a log action signed by the acting device key: "OFE2EE1-LOGACT\0" action(1) userid actordeviceid circleidzeros subjectidzeros epoch(4) ref(32)zeros. Actions: 1 register (cross-signed), 2 rotate, 3 revoke, 4 recovery registered, 5 enable, 6 epoch, 7 disable, 8 reset (new root), 9 approve, 10/11 processing pref/policy (PRIVACYPROCESSING.md), 12 owner approval on/off (see "Owner approval"). ref is the new key's fingerprint, the revoked key's fingerprint, or, for enable/epoch, the key commitment (below). Sealed-box wrap of a circle key wrappedkey = 0x01 epk(32) nonce(24) ciphertext(32) tag(16) (105 bytes). epk is a fresh ephemeral X25519 key; shared = X25519(esk, recipientx25519pub) (an all-zero result is refused); key = HKDF-SHA256(shared, salt = epk recipientpub, info = "OFE2EE1-WRAP-KEY\0"); XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a random 24-byte nonce and AAD = "OFE2EE1-WRAP-AAD\0" circleid epoch recipientdeviceid wrapperdeviceid. The wrapper signs "OFE2EE1-WRAP-SIG\0" (circle, epoch, recipient, wrapper) wrappedkey. The AAD binds circle, epoch and both devices, so a wrap cannot be replayed to another circle/epoch/device (rollback and substitution fail authentication). Key commitment (epoch integrity) commitment = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = circlekey, salt = circleid epoch(4 BE), info = "OFE2EE1-KEY-COMMIT\0", 32 bytes). The publishing admin signs it as the ref of the enable/epoch log action. The server returns, per epoch, the signed record (publisher user/device/key, commitment, signature) in the circle state; every phone verifies that signature and, after unwrapping, recomputes the commitment from the key and rejects the key on any mismatch (fail closed if there is no record). A bogus or substituted wrap therefore can never be accepted, whoever managed to store it. (The v1 formats were never released, so this changed the meaning of ref for actions 5/6 in place and the vectors were regenerated.) Circle payload format (for phase 2) payload = 0x01 epoch(4) nonce(24) ciphertext tag(16); key = HKDF-SHA256(circlekey, salt = circleid epoch, info = "OFE2EE1-MSG-KEY\0" purpose); AAD = "OFE2EE1-MSG-AAD\0" circleid epoch senderdeviceid len(purpose) purpose. purpose ("loc", "place", "event", ...) gives key separation. Plaintext is padded first (length(2) data zeros to buckets of 256, 512, 1024, 4096, then multiples of 4096 bytes) to hide payload size inside a bucket. Nonces are random per message (24 bytes: no practical collision); a nonce is never reused with a key, and wrap/seal helpers take an explicit nonce only for test vectors. Test vectors backend/internal/e2ee/testdata/vectors.json is generated by Go (UPDATEVECTORS=1 go test ./internal/e2ee) and read by the Dart tests (app/test/services/e2ee/e2eecryptotest.dart). It covers identity derivation, fingerprints, digits, the safety number, the binding signature, a wrap (AAD, blob, signature), a sealed payload, padding, a log action with its chained entry hash, and the recovery phrase (a fixed BIP39 phrase to the exact seed and recovery key fingerprints, with and without passphrase). Server model (phase 1) Migration 000150e2ee (idempotent, with a down file): tables devicekeys, circlekeywraps, deviceapprovals, e2eelog; columns circles.e2eemode ('off''private', default off), e2eeepoch, e2eerekeyrequired, e2eeupdatedat; triggers. The server stores public keys and ciphertext only; no endpoint accepts a private key, recovery phrase or plaintext circle key. Route Who Purpose POST /e2ee/devices self register a key (root, cross-signed, reset, or kind=recovery) POST /e2ee/devices/{id}/rotate, DELETE /e2ee/devices/{id} self rotate (old key signs), revoke GET /e2ee/me self the server's record of my keys (incl. revoked) GET /e2ee/users/{userid}/devices self or co-member active keys; others get 404 GET /circles/{id}/e2ee, /pending, /wraps?deviceid= circle member state with approval flags; queue of devices lacking a wrap (ciphertext/public data only); my own wraps POST /circles/{id}/e2ee/enable, /epoch, /disable, /approvals circle admin enable (epoch = current+1), publish next epoch, disable, approve a replacement key POST /circles/{id}/e2ee/wraps epoch publisher, or anyone for their OWN other keys add or replace wraps for epoch <= current GET /e2ee/log?after=N any user the transparency log (redacted for unrelated people) GET /api/admin/e2ee/keys platform admin public keys and circle epochs Enforced by the server (migrations 000150 and 000151): authentication, rate limits (register 10/h, rotate 5/h, wraps 30/min, admin ops 20/h, reads 120/min), key length/weak-key checks (small-order Ed25519 and low-order X25519 points), binding signature, log-action signature of an active key of the caller, wrap signature by the wrapper's registered key, wrapper = caller, recipient = transitively approved active key of a live circle member (below), only the epoch's publisher (the user recorded in that epoch's signed enable/epoch log entry) may wrap a key for other members; anyone may wrap only to their own other keys (new phone, recovery identity), a later wrap from the publisher or the owner replaces an earlier one (a bad first submission cannot block the real one), strictly increasing epoch (current+1 only; the counter is kept when a circle is switched off), admin-only epoch operations, IDOR-safe lookups (404 for non-members), one active recovery key per user, max 10 active device keys, immutable log (UPDATE/DELETE blocked by trigger). Triggers: removing a member deletes that member's wraps and sets e2eerekeyrequired; revoking a key deletes its wraps and sets the flag in all the owner's private circles. The server cannot re-key itself (it holds no key): an admin phone publishes the next epoch. Audit log entries: e2ee.deviceregistereddeviceresetrecoveryregistereddevicerotateddevicerevokedenabledepochbumpeddisabledwrapsaddeddeviceapprovedrekeyrequired. Operator tools: server e2ee-fingerprints [--all] (each user's key fingerprints, circles and epochs) and server e2ee-log-head (verifies the whole log, hashes and signatures, prints the head); admin panel page "Encryption keys". Key distribution, approval, rotation 1. First key of an account is a root, trust-on-first-use. For a joiner the invite link/QR carries the inviter's key fingerprint and circle id in the URL fragment (never sent to the server by a browser), so the new phone checks the keys the server returns against a value that never came from the server (mismatch = loud alarm; match = inviter pinned as verified). 2. A second phone of the same account is cross-signed by an existing device (manual copy/paste codes, server not involved) or by the recovery key. Others see the chain (registeredbydeviceid, signature) and verify it. 3. A replacement root key (reset, e.g. a lost phone without backup) is not cross-signed. The server accepts it but refuses to store any wrap for it in a circle until a circle admin of another user approves it for that circle (or, only where the circle's creator switched it on, the creator

docs.text: Encrypted chat (design and status) Chat in a Private circle is sealed on the sender's phone and opened on the members' phones. The server relays ciphertext only. Chat is never processed by the server: it is sealed under the phone key line (CK) only, never wrapped to the server device, never read by the sidecar, even when a member's processing lane is server (PRIVACYPROCESSING.md, key lines and lanes). Code: server backend/internal/handlers/e2eechannel.go, chat.go, e2eechatblob.go, migration 000250chate2ee; app app/lib/services/chat/ and app/lib/services/e2ee/private.dart. 1. Decision: a purpose on the existing relay Chat is the channel purpose chat on the e2eeitems relay (the purpose was reserved from the start, bucket now 8192). Reasons: ordering by relay id, idempotency by (circle, device, seq), TTL, acknowledgement-free pull with a cursor, the WebSocket e2eeitem frame, the silent wake-up push, the key epoch/rollback rules and the sender signature all exist and are tested. A separate table would duplicate all of it. The cost is that edits and deletes are items too (the server cannot tell a message from an edit), see "unread". Item format is the existing v1 phone-line item: AEAD(CK epoch key) over the padded envelope 1 seq ts Ed25519 signature of the sender device body. The signature covers circle, epoch, device, purpose, seq, time and body. The body is JSON (below). Nothing about chat is new cryptography. 2. Message types (the sealed JSON body) k Fields Meaning msg id (client uuid), t text (1 to 2000 chars), optional img A message. The message key is (author, id); the author is the VERIFIED owner of the signing device, never a field in the JSON. edit id, t Replaces the text of the SENDER's own message id. Version = the item's signed time, then relay id. del id, a (author user id) Tombstone. Honoured when the signer is the author (a equals the signer) or a CURRENT circle admin. read not implemented Read markers inside the encrypted stream are out of scope (see "metadata"). Reactions and typing indicators do not exist in plaintext chat either, so they are not added. Attachments (photos). Plaintext chat has photos, so encrypted chat has them: the phone re-encodes the image (EXIF dropped, 5 MiB limit), encrypts it with a fresh random 32 byte key (XChaCha20-Poly1305, 24 byte nonce, format 0x01 nonce ct tag, AAD "OFE2EE3-BLOB\0" circleid) and uploads the bytes with POST /circles/{id}/e2ee/blobs (an opaque row in e2eeblobs, members only, circle bound, expires with the chat). The message carries img = {b: blob id, k: base64 key, m: mime, s: size}. The key is therefore only inside the sealed message. A blob the server holds is just random bytes. 3. Authentication, replay, edit and delete authorization Who sent it. The signature is by the sender's device key; the receiver maps the device to a person through the verified key log and the member list. A member who shares CK still cannot post "as" someone else. Duplicates and replay. The receiver's per-device window drops a repeated (device, seq); the store is idempotent by (author, id); the relay deduplicates on (circle, device, seq). A replayed old edit cannot revert a newer one (an edit applies only if its (signed time, relay id) is newer than the one already applied). Wrong circle or wrong epoch fails the AEAD or the signature. A tampered byte fails the AEAD. Edit. Only the author's own (author, id) can be edited: an edit from anyone else addresses (signer, id) and so touches nothing of the author's. Delete. The author may delete their own message. A circle admin may delete anyone's: the del carries a, and a receiver honours it only if the signer is a or an admin in its CURRENT member list. This is the same rule the plaintext server enforces ("sender or admin"). It is enforced by every client, not by the server (the server cannot read it). A forged tombstone from a non-admin is ignored. A tombstone that arrives before its message is kept and suppresses the message when it arrives; a deleted message is removed from the phone's store (only a tombstone stays). Honest limit. A deletion removes the message from phones that receive the tombstone. A phone that was offline for longer than the relay keeps tombstones (30 days) shows the message until it is deleted by hand; a phone that already copied the text can of course keep it. 4. Who can read what: epochs, joining, removal Chat uses the circle key epoch exactly as locations do. A member removed from the circle triggers a new epoch which is never wrapped to them: they cannot open any message sealed after the removal, and they lose relay access at once. New member. A new member receives the current epoch key. They can read chat sealed under that epoch that is still on the relay (up to the TTL), then everything new. Messages sealed under older epochs are not readable (they hold no key for them). An admin who wants a strict "only after joining" cut makes a new epoch (the existing "new key" action) before inviting. This is a property of the epoch model, not something the chat layer can add. New phone of an existing member. An approved new device gets the epoch wraps the existing device or the recovery key wraps to it, and then replays the relay (cursor 0) so it recovers up to the TTL of chat. Older history is not on the server; it is only on phones that already had it. There is no phone-to-phone history transfer in this release. Retention. The relay deletes chat ciphertext after 30 days (E2EECHATTTLDAYS, 1 to 365; longer than the 48 h of live locations). Phones keep their own history locally (last 5000 messages per circle). Attachments expire a day after the chat TTL. The phone store is not backed up to the cloud; a reinstall loses history older than the relay window. 5. What the server still sees (metadata) The server sees: that a chat item exists, the circle, the sending DEVICE (and so, from its key records, the person), the minute it arrived, and a size bucket (256 .. 8192 bytes), and that someone uploaded an attachment of a given size. It does not see text, edits, deletes, attachment content, who deleted what, or whether an item is a message, an edit or a delete. It sees which chat item id each member has marked as read in the server cursor (only to compute the badge, below). 6. Server rules chat is accepted on keyline = 'phone' only. Handler code chatphoneonly, a CHECK constraint (e2eeitemschatphoneonly) and the e2eeitemguard trigger reject anything else. e2eepurgeuserservercopies therefore never has chat to delete. A requiredserver circle does not block chat from a member who has not signed the server lane (like check-ins and events, chat is exempt). The sidecar/bridge pulls purpose=fix,history on the server line only and discards every other purpose; the pull with a server-kind device is forced to the server line. Tests assert that no chat is served to it. Plaintext chat in a private circle. POST /circles/{id}/chat, PATCH and the photo upload answer 409 {"code":"chatencrypted"} with the text "Chat in this circle is end-to-end encrypted. Update Orbitly to send and read new messages." An old app shows that message. A database trigger (chatplaintextguard) refuses plaintext rows in a private circle as a backstop. Non-private circles are unchanged. Listing and deleting old plaintext stay available. Old history. Messages written before the circle turned private stay in chatmessages and GET /circles/{id}/chat still lists them with "encrypted": true on the response; the app shows them under a divider "Sent before encryption" and marks them. A circle admin can erase them with DELETE /circles/{id}/chat/history (audit-logged chat.historydeleted); the app offers this as "Delete old unencrypted messages". Unread badge from metadata. GET /chat/unread adds, per circle, the count of chat items from OTHER people's devices with id after the caller's server cursor. The cursor moves with POST /circles/{id}/chat/read {"itemid": n} (clamped to the newest chat item, never moves back). The server count includes edits and deletes (it cannot tell them apart), so it can be too high. The app therefore shows its own exact count (decrypted messages from others newer than the local read position) and uses the server count only as a fallback. Live. The batch handler broadcasts the existing e2eeitem frame (cipher only) and a silent e2eewake data push (rate limit 1 per circle per 2 s for chat). It contains no text and no name. 7. Notifications For a Private circle the server sends no visible chat push and no text. The wake-up push is silent; the receiving phone pulls, decrypts and raises the notification locally ("<name>: <text>", or "<name> sent a photo"). Wake-ups are best effort (on iOS the OS may delay or drop a silent push); the unread badge and the open chat catch up on every app open, resume and socket reconnect. A circle may mute a person as before. 8. App behaviour Chat screen is shared; a repository (ChatService) has a plaintext implementation (ApiChatService) and an encrypted one (EncryptedChatService); a router picks per circle by its mode. Banner: "Encrypted. Only people in this circle can read this." States: "Waiting for the circle key" (no epoch key yet; items are kept and retried after a key sync), "<name> needs to update to read encrypted chat" (a member whose phone lacks chate2ee; shown from the member list), "Sent before encryption" (old plaintext), "Sending / Not sent. Retry". Send: optimistic; sealed immediately and put into the sealed upload queue (idempotent by (circle, device, seq) and by the message id), retried across restarts. Queue facts of PRIVACYPROCESSING 19.1 apply: two isolates can race on the queue in a narrow window, which the queue's own version check and the idempotency absorb; the chat store uses the same versioned read-modify-write with a read-back check and applies every item idempotently. Messages older than the queue's 48 h limit that were never delivered are dropped from the queue and shown as "Not sent". Receive: live frame, silent wake and catch-up poll all go through the same receiver (dedupe window, signature check, rollback rules). A crash between "seen" and "stored" can lose one message on that phone (it is still on the relay but the receiver treats it as seen); this narrow window is the same as for every other purpose. Old apps: a member whose app predates this cannot read or send in a Private circle's chat (it has always been unable to read Private circle locations either); they see the 409 text above. 9. Not in this release Read receipts ("Seen by") in encrypted chat, reactions, typing indicators, phone-to-phone history transfer for a new device, cloud backup of chat history, search across circles.

docs.text: iOS app: readiness, signing, TestFlight and release decision Issue: #52. Status: everything below was written without a Mac and without an Apple account. No Swift, Objective-C, Xcode project, plist or workflow change on this page has ever been compiled, run, signed or uploaded. Dart code and the Go backend are tested in CI on Linux; the native iOS side is "carefully written, unverified". Signed distribution is BLOCKED until the owner has an Apple Developer Program account (99 USD/year) and a Mac or the GitHub macOS runner has run the workflow once. Read Verification status before trusting any line here. Decision Use TestFlight for family members' iPhones: invite by email or link, automatic updates, no UDID handling, the same signed archive can later go to the App Store. Alternatives (ad hoc, public App Store, free-account sideloading) are in the table at the end. Settings > Driving detection shows "Not available on iPhone yet"; the background hook, crash watcher and opt-in sync do nothing on iOS, so the server is never told the user opted in to sensors that cannot run; the Core Motion permission step is not offered. Background execution on iOS: how the Dart code behaves Verified by reading the code, not by running it. Background isolate. backgroundlocator2 starts a headless FlutterEngine and runs the Dart callbacks onLocationUpdate / onHeartbeatTick in it. AppDelegate.swift registers GeneratedPluginRegistrant on that engine (so sharedpreferences, fluttersecurestorage, batteryplus work) and now also registers the app.openfamily/keystore channel on it, so the isolate can use the Secure Enclave wrapping key to seal location for Private circles. If the channel were missing, SecureVault would see "unavailable" and the sealing code would park fixes instead of sending plaintext (existing safety behaviour). Credentials in the background are in the Keychain with firstunlockthisdevice (BackgroundCredentialStore), readable while the phone is locked after the first unlock. Before the first unlock after a reboot nothing can be read; location callbacks then skip silently. Location triggers. Continuous updates while the process lives, with the request following the TrackingCadence tier (iOS has no interval: accuracy and distance filter only; still phones drop to cell-only accuracy plus a 150 m exit region, see iOS background location); significant-location-change (about 500 m, cell-tower based) relaunches a killed app; a 150 m exit region is armed when the app terminates. Results are bursty, not a steady cadence. No workmanager, no BGTaskScheduler. Nothing in the app registers a BGTask, and UIBackgroundModes deliberately lists only location and remote-notification (no fetch, no processing, which would invite App Review questions without a feature behind them). Periodic work is not possible; wake-ups come from location events and pushes. Silent push. The backend sends content-available pushes with apns-push-type: background for commands and the content-free E2EE wake-up. AppDelegate.application(: didReceiveRemoteNotification:fetchCompletionHandler:) forwards the of payload to Dart. Apple does not guarantee delivery: heavy throttling (a few per hour), none after a force-quit, none in Low Power Mode. E2EE correctness never depends on them: the app pulls on open, and live location keeps flowing over the location background mode. Unverified: all of it. The first device test must cover: lock the phone for 30 minutes while walking; kill the app from the app switcher (expect no relaunch: documented iOS rule); reboot and walk 600 m (expect a relaunch through significant changes); send a location-refresh command and an E2EE wake-up and time them. UIBackgroundModes: location, remote-notification (kept; see above). Runner.entitlements: aps-environment from the build setting APSENVIRONMENT (development for Debug/Profile, production for Release). Associated Domains are not in the default entitlements on purpose: the host differs per self-hosted server, and an entitlement the App ID lacks breaks signing. The workflow adds applinks:<domain> when the repository variable IOSASSOCIATEDDOMAIN is set. fixed: Flutter/Debug.xcconfig and Release.xcconfig did not include the CocoaPods configuration (Pods-Runner..xcconfig), so the pods (geolocator, backgroundlocator2, ...) would not link on a real build. docs.text: Offline resilience: what Orbitly does when the server is down Status: the cache, the store-and-forward queues, the reachability probe and the status chip are implemented and unit tested; nothing here has been run on a real phone or a real flaky network (see section 9). The fallback relay (section 5b) is not built and the reasons are written down below. Owner request: "If a server ever goes offline, the app is still functional, because no matter if it is end-to-end encryption or not, we want people to be able to see one another. We can have it stored locally on their phones, and once it is ready, it can push out to their server." 1. Short version The phone is the source of truth for what it knows. It remembers the last answer of the server (circles, people and their last positions, places, recent chat, notifications, trips) and shows it at once, with a small chip saying the server cannot be reached. Everything a person does while the server is out of reach (location fixes, check-ins, SOS and help alerts, chat messages) is saved on the phone and sent, in order and exactly once, when the server answers again. An SOS that cannot be delivered says so plainly ("SOS not sent yet"), keeps trying, and offers to open the phone's own messaging app with the emergency contacts and the last position, which needs no data connection and no Orbitly server. What cannot work without a server: new positions of other people. They are produced on other phones and only a server (or some relay) can carry them. Section 5 evaluates the options for that. 2. What users see and do not see when the server is down Thing While the server is down Opening the app Opens straight to the map from the saved snapshot. It does not wait on the network for more than 4 seconds, and never signs anyone out because the network failed. People on the map Everyone's last known position, each with its real age ("last seen 3 h ago"), in normal and Private circles. No new movement of others. Your own position Keeps being recorded and queued (12 h / 720 fixes in normal circles, 48 h / 2000 items in Private ones; oldest fixes go first). They arrive in order afterwards, so history has no hole. Places, circles, trips, notifications The last copy. Creating or editing a place in a normal circle needs the server (Private circle places are local and work). Chat Reading: the newest messages of each circle. Writing: the message appears as "waiting to send", is stored on the phone and sent in order. Photos need the server. Check-in, Help alert Saved and shown as "Not sent yet"; sent automatically later, once. SOS "SOS not sent yet", retried in the background, SOS first in the queue, "Text my emergency contacts" through the phone's own SMS, "Call emergency services". Never dropped. Settings Last known values show. Changes that were made through the queue are replayed; some screens still need the server and say so. Sign-in with a password, joining a circle by code, adding a device, key approval Need the server. A phone that is already signed in stays signed in. Live location of others, driving alerts of others, server push Not available (no server to produce them). 3. Audit: what the code did before this change Found by reading the code and confirmed with failing tests (fake HTTP client that refuses, times out or answers 5xx). Defect Effect Fix 1 LocationOutbox.drain counted every failed send as a strike; 8 failures dropped the points. A 2-hour outage with the map screen reconnecting every few minutes silently threw away the backlog. A failure only strikes when the server refused the batch for good (4xx); offline, timeouts, 5xx and rate limits never strike. 2 SealedQueue.bump dropped a whole batch after 20 failed uploads, including 5xx; prune dropped check-ins and chat after 48 h and displaced them when the queue was full. A deploy or an outage of a few minutes during frequent flushes lost sealed chat/check-ins in Private circles. Server trouble never counts; chat, check-ins, places and events are never dropped (only live fixes/history/results are bounded). 3 SOS: a failed send returned to the idle button with an error text. The SOS was lost; the person had to remember to press again. Queue + "not sent yet" state + SMS fallback + retry (section 4). 4 Check-in and Help alert: error text only. Lost. Queue, idempotent replay. 5 Plain-circle chat: the draft stayed in the box, history was an error card. No reading, no writing. Last page cached; send queued with a client id (the server already deduplicated on it). 6 Map: fetchMembers failing showed a full-screen error card and never started the socket. Empty screen at start without network. Roster cache (positions encrypted at rest), stale-while-revalidate, chip. 7 Chat/circles/trips asked GET /api/profile only to learn "who am I". Whole screen failed offline. Profile cached. 8 Start-up awaited the session refresh and the config for the full 15 s request timeout. A blank splash on Wi-Fi without internet. Capped at 4 s, then opens on the snapshot (the refresh keeps running and still stores a new token pair). 9 Any transport exception that was not ClientException (TLS handshake, reset) escaped as a raw exception; a 200 with a cut-off body threw FormatException. Uncaught errors in screens; cache fallback not used. All map to an offline ApiException(0). 10 Nothing told the user the server was unreachable, there was no probe separate from requests, no count of waiting updates. "Is it me or the server?" ServerReachability + chip + Diagnostics count. 11 LocationOutbox.drain sent one batch (100) per trigger. A 720-fix backlog needed 8 separate triggers. drainAll (max 12 batches, 400 ms apart). Checked and found already good (kept, tests added where useful): token refresh treats network errors and 5xx as "keep the session" (refreshkeepssessiontest.dart), only 400/401/403 from the refresh endpoint end it; the live socket reconnects with exponential backoff (1 s to 30 s), an inbound-silence watchdog and OS connectivity events; the Private runtime already persisted last positions (v0.24) and a sealed upload queue with (circle, device, seq) idempotency; the chat engine for Private circles is already local-first. 4. How it works 4.1 Reachability (services/offline/serverreachability.dart) One object knows "can I reach the server". Every request reports in for free (noteResponse(status) / noteFailure() from ApiClient.rawSend). A failure does not flip the chip: it schedules one confirming probe (GET /healthz, no auth, 5 s timeout, 2 s later). Only a failed probe says unreachable. While unreachable, probes follow exponential backoff with jitter (3 s, doubling, capped at 5 min, 50 to 100 % of the delay), so there is no tight loop and a family's phones do not return on the same second. Wi-Fi/cellular events (debounced 800 ms) and the Try again button probe at once. A 502/503/504 counts as "down" (a proxy in front of a dead server), any other status, including 4xx and 500, proves the server is there. When a probe succeeds the recovery hooks flush every queue. 4.2 Cache (services/offline/offlinecache.dart) JSON documents in the Keystore-wrapped vault (the one that holds the circle keys), under offline/v1/. Each document is at most 256 KB, open-ended groups (trips by date range) keep the newest 30. A locked phone or invalidated key means "no cache right now", never a crash; nothing falls back to a plain file. Cleared on sign-out. Documents cached: server config, profile, family, circles, roster per scope (kept current from live frames, written at most every 30 s), places, emergency contacts (for the SMS fallback), recent chat per circle, check-in inbox, trips, trip details and summaries. The helper OfflineCache.fetch returns the live answer and remembers it, or the last copy when the failure is an offline failure (timeout, refused, 408/429/5xx); a 403/404 or a dead session is never hidden by the cache. 4.3 Store-and-forward (services/offline/offlinequeue.dart, existing LocationOutbox, existing SealedQueue) Queue Holds Storage Bounds Never dropped OfflineQueue SOS, Help alert, check-in, plain-circle chat, soft items (settings: newest per key) vault (falls back to app preferences only if the vault refuses, so an SOS is never lost to a locked phone) 1000 protected items (a new one is refused, not swapped for an older one); soft items 300 / 7 days, oldest first SOS, check-ins, chat LocationOutbox normal-circle location fixes app preferences (plain, as before; 12 h / 720) 720 / 12 h, oldest first not applicable, fixes are the expendable kind SealedQueue Private-circle sealed items (fixes, check-in positions, chat, events, places) existing Private store (already ciphertext) 2000 items; fixes and results go first, 48 h for fixes/history/results chat, check-ins, events, places Replay is in order (SOS first), single flight, stops at the first transport failure and keeps everything. Idempotency: every queued request carries a client id; the server stores a replay once (chat already did; this change adds it for SOS, Help and check-ins: migration 000340, and a replay answers 200 with the stored object and does not count against the cooldown). Items the server refuses for good (4xx) move aside into a bounded "rejected" list that Diagnostics counts. A 429 on an SOS means the family was just notified, so it counts as delivered. An SOS or check-in sent late carries "(sent late, pressed at 14:02)" in its note so nobody mistakes it for live. Private circles keep sealing locally while offline: sealing needs only the circle key in the vault, so check-in/SOS positions and chat are sealed when the person acts and wait as ciphertext. (The Keystore-locked-phone behaviour belongs to another change and is untouched.) 4.4 The chip and Diagnostics SyncStatusChip (top of the map): Server unreachable. Showing last known. Will sync when it is back. with Try again and "N updates waiting"; Syncing…; Up to date for 3 seconds after a recovery, then nothing. Diagnostics shows "Updates waiting" (positions, messages, check-ins, sealed items together) with Send now. 5. Seeing each other without the server: options What cannot be done by any cache: show new movement of someone else while the server is down. For that, a path from their phone to yours is needed. Four options: (a) Cache only: BUILT, always on Cost: small. Risk: low. Users see the last known position with its age, can queue messages and alerts. They do not see live movement. This is the baseline and it is enough for "the server is rebooting" and "the home server has no internet for an evening". (b) Fallback relay (a second server URL per circle): NOT BUILT, evaluated Idea: Private-circle items are already end-to-end encrypted and opaque, so a second dumb relay could carry them; the app keeps an ordered list of base URLs per circle and fails over. What would have to be true: Protocol. The items themselves port well: (circle, device, seq) is a globally unique id, so duplicates across relays dedupe on seq; signatures are in the item, so a relay does not have to be trusted for authenticity. The pull cursor is a relay-local id, so the client would need one cursor per relay. The key epoch is the hard part: epochs are set by membership changes that go through the main server. During an outage no new member joins and no key rotates; items sealed under an older epoch keep working, items under a newer one stall until the key reaches a phone. Trust. A relay sees what the main server sees in a Private circle: ciphertext, sizes, purposes, timing, who is a member. Nothing more. A second Orbitly server would also need the circle, the member list and the registered device keys, plus an account or token per phone, i.e. replicating membership and authentication, otherwise it can neither authorize uploads nor rate limit abuse. That is a distributed-systems project (membership replication, token acceptance, conflict resolution), not a settings entry. Normal circles. Positions there are plaintext to the server by design. Sending them to a second server just doubles the exposure. Not recommended; normal circles should simply wait for their server. Cost. Client: relay list per circle, per-relay cursors, health per relay, retry policy, UI (Backup server setting). Server: a relay mode with its own accounts or signed-upload auth. Weeks, plus a new attack surface (unauthenticated upload). Decision: do not build now. It is neither small nor safe enough. If the owner wants this, build the "dumb relay" of (d) first, which has no accounts. (c) Nearby phone to phone (Bluetooth / Wi-Fi Direct, Nearby Connections): NOT BUILT, recommended against Works only when the phones are physically close, i.e. when people can see each other anyway. It does not help with "my mother is at work and the server is down". Android Nearby Connections needs Google Play Services (absent on GrapheneOS/LineageOS-without-gapps, which this audience likes); iOS uses a different framework (MultipeerConnectivity) with no wire compatibility. Two implementations, background restrictions on both, new permissions (BLUETOOTHSCAN/ADVERTISE/CONNECT, NEARBYWIFIDEVICES), battery cost for continuous advertising. Would be a plausible later addition for "meet at the festival without mobile data". Not trivial, so not now. (d) Push relay through UnifiedPush / ntfy topics: NOT BUILT, the most promising future path The sealed fix item is at most 1 KB (maxBucket), chat 8 KB; an ntfy message can carry 4 KB. A topic name derived from the circle key (HKDF(circle key, "relay-topic"), 128 bit) is unguessable, so the relay needs no accounts: whoever knows the topic can publish and read, and everything inside is ciphertext with per-device signatures. That is the "minimal relay" of (b) without the replication problem. The app already ships UnifiedPush and a direct push service, so the receiving side exists in part. Open points: ntfy retention is short (hours, configurable), so this is delivery of recent items, not storage; ordering and dedupe use the existing seq; the relay (public ntfy.sh or the family's own) learns timing and volume per topic; a leaked topic lets anyone flood it (signatures stop forgery, not spam); only Private circles qualify. Recommendation: prototype behind an "experimental, Private circles only" switch after the baseline here has been used on real phones. It is a week of work plus a threat-model note, not an afternoon. What we recommend 1. Ship (a) now (this change). 2. Learn from real use how often servers are unreachable. 3. If live positions during outages matter, build (d) for Private circles first. Do (b) only if (d) proves insufficient. Skip (c). 6. Server side GET /healthz already existed; the app now uses it as the reachability probe (5 s timeout, no auth, separate from login). Migration 000340 adds clientid to alerts and checkins with unique partial indexes (userid, clientid); POST /alerts/sos, /alerts/help, /alerts/check-in and POST /checkins accept an optional clientid (max 64 chara

docs.text: Privacy model backlog (v1.0 and after) Prioritised change requests from the privacy-model review, with files, risk, size and whether each is a MUST for the v1.0 store submission. Source: PRIVACYMODELV1.md (matrix, claim audit, red team). Size: S (under a day), M (1 to 3 days), L (a week or more). Risk = risk of the change itself. "MUST" = must land before submitting v1.0 to the App Store and Google Play, because a store reviewer, a journalist or a family member could otherwise show that a privacy claim is false. Already done on this branch Map badge and circle switcher no longer say "End-to-end encrypted" for a Private circle with server help on ("Private, server helps some" / "Private + server"; legacy circles "Server can read"). PrivateCircleBadge.serverAssist, locationtabview.dart, test in app/test/widgets/privatecirclewidgetstest.dart. Circle settings subtitle and info no longer say "only members can read" when server help is on. The turn-on dialog no longer says chat is not end-to-end encrypted. The in-app privacy policy no longer says locations are never end-to-end encrypted. MUST for v1.0 ID Change Files Risk Size B1 Per-member truth in the circle header. Replace the remaining circle-level claims with the real state: "Private: 2 of 3 keep data on their phone. The server can read Blake." Use the verified lanes (LanesService/ProcessingSnapshot), not the unsigned serverassist flag, for the names; the badge fixed here is the minimum. Also the member row: "Server can read" / "Only circle phones can read" widgets/privatecirclewidgets.dart, locationtabview.dart, processingwidgets.dart (LaneChip labels), encryptionkeysscreen.dart Low M B2 Auto-apply is consent-by-default: make it honest and bound to a signed decision. (a) Notice text must say the server can now read the person's location, trips and driving data, and who that includes (server owner, backups); show it as a blocking sheet the first time, not only a dismissible card. docs.text: ADR: Per-member privacy and where data is processed (server-assisted vs phone-only) Status: ACCEPTED; phase 1 (crypto, section 17) and phase 2 (server, section 18) are implemented; phases 3 to 7 are open. Extends docs/design/E2EE.md (phases 1 to 3 and "Trusted-server mode"). Audience: the maintainer, and the agents that will implement the phases in section 13. Everything below was checked against E2EE.md, backend/internal/handlers/e2eeservermember.go, backend/internal/handlers/e2eechannel.go, migrations up to 000186, and app/lib/services/e2ee/. Where something was not verified it is marked (unverified). 1. Context and owner requirements 1. On the phone every feature stays: driving reports, trips, history, places, summaries. Features that need a server in a normal circle must still work in some form on the phone. 2. The server stays a real server that stores and processes data (admin map, trips, weekly summary, Dawarich sync, push). 3. A member can opt out of sending their data to the server (circle > Encryption keys, or personal settings) while the circle's end-to-end encryption between phones continues. 4. The opt-out must warn honestly: processing then happens on the member's phone (battery, CPU, data) and some features are limited to what a phone can compute. 5. If a circle wants no server processing at all, evaluate (a) each phone computes its own stats and shares results as E2EE items, (b) members' phones split or rotate the work, (c) one elected "main processor" phone, and recommend one. 6. Only the circle admin edits circle-wide settings. A clear roles model: who changes the circle's server-processing default, who changes a member's personal opt-out. 2. The problem in today's design Trusted-server mode (E2EE.md, e2eeservermember() in migration 000165) makes the server a device member that holds the circle key. It is all-or-nothing: the server may read a circle only while every live member has a signed consent row. Consequences: There is exactly one key line per circle epoch (the circle key). Whoever holds it reads every member's items. Holding it for "the consenting members" is impossible: one member who does not consent closes the circle for everyone (Residual risks, "Consent is all-or-nothing per circle"). Therefore a per-member opt-out cannot be done by simply skipping the consent: the opted-out member's items would still be sealed under the key the server holds. The data has to live under a key the server never holds, and the choice has to be made by the author's phone, not by a server flag, an admin or a session token. 3. Decision (summary) 1. Two key lines per Private circle, both held by all members' phones: Phone key CK (the existing circle key and its epochs). Never wrapped to a server-kind device. Items sealed under it are phone-only. Server key SK (new, own generation counter). Wrapped to all members' phones and, when the circle has server assistance enabled, to the pinned server device. Items sealed under it are server-assisted. 2. The sender's phone decides, item by item, which line it seals under, from its own signed preference. The sender's preference governs everything the sender authors (fixes, events, history, check-ins, and places and results they create). The server cannot change it, an admin cannot change it, and an old app that knows nothing of SK seals under CK (fail-safe default = private). 3. Consent is per member, not per circle. The existing signed server consent now means "my phone seals my items under SK". No consent row means phone-only. A member without consent no longer closes the circle. 4. Circle admin controls circle-wide policy: whether server assistance exists for the circle at all, and the default shown to new members. Each member controls their own lane, and only their phone can sign it. An admin cannot opt a member in. (Children: open question Q3.) 5. Phone-only data is processed on the author's phone and published as E2EE result items (option (a)). Rotation of load between phones (b) and an elected processor (c) are rejected as primary designs (section 9). An optional, never-required "always-on hub" device is allowed later as pure acceleration. 6. Graceful degradation is explicit data: every member row, every result and every screen carries processing: server phone and the UI shows which, so a missing server trip is shown as "computed on Alex's phone" or "not available (Alex keeps data on their phone and this phone cannot compute it yet)", never as an empty screen. 4. Threat model and what each mode protects Adversaries (same list as E2EE.md, plus the new ones this ADR creates): Adversary Standard circle Private, phones only Private, server-assisted: member who opted IN Same circle: member who opted OUT Server DB breach / stolen backup plaintext positions ciphertext + public keys + metadata plaintext copies (locations, memberpositions) plus ciphertext whose key may sit in the sidecar volume ciphertext + metadata only Curious / compelled operator reads everything metadata only reads everything of this member metadata only Compromised server host (root) everything metadata only; can add a malicious public key (limit already in E2EE.md) everything of opted-in members, and the sidecar volume (SK) metadata only, provided phones never wrap CK to a server-kind or unapproved key Network observer TLS TLS + ciphertext same same Hostile or compromised member sees all sees all (holds CK and SK) sees all sees all. Opt-out does not hide data from other members. If member A runs a bridge or a viewer, A can export what A's keys decrypt, including B's phone-only items Platform admin (operator) admin map none admin map for opted-in members only nothing Circle admin can see members same as member same same; cannot read more than any member, cannot flip B's lane What the opt-out does not protect, stated in the product text: Metadata the server always sees: that B uploads, upload times (minute), item sizes (bucketed), purposes (fix, event, checkin, history), the item's key line (phone or server), push tokens, IP addresses. Adaptive upload cadence reveals "moving vs still". Not hidden in any mode. Other circles. Positions are per user, not per circle (E2EE.md, "multi-circle rule"). If B also sits in a Standard circle, B's phone still uploads plaintext for that circle. The opt-out is per Private circle; the screen must say "you are also in a normal circle, which still sends your position to the server". Data already copied. Server plaintext copies made before the opt-out, trips already built, notifications already sent, backups, data exported to Dawarich. Only the tagged locations rows and the sealed ciphertext can be deleted (section 8). Members. A member already holds the keys (E2EE.md out of scope: hostile member). A malicious server with write access to the DB can still withhold wraps, items or consents (availability), and can show a false "processed by server" badge. It cannot make B's phone seal under SK; the badge is derived by phones from verified item headers and the signed log, not from a server flag. What server-assisted really means: for the opted-in members the server is a trusted party that can read everything and keeps plaintext at rest. That is the point of that mode (E2EE.md says the same). E2EE between phones continues in both modes, but the confidentiality against the server exists only for phone-only items. 5. Cryptographic design (new frozen formats; vectors required, Go and Dart) 5.1 Key lines CK / circles.e2eeepoch: unchanged semantics. Rotates on member removal or key revocation (existing triggers). SK / circles.e2eeservergen (new, starts at 1 when server assistance is first enabled): 32 random bytes made by an admin phone, wrapped with the existing sealed-box wrap (E2EE.md, "Sealed-box wrap") to every approved member device and the recovery keys. The wrap AAD gains the line: "OFE2EE3-WRAP-AAD\0" line(1) circleid gen recipientdeviceid wrapperdeviceid, so a CK wrap can never be replayed as an SK wrap. Domain separation: the HKDF subkey for items is derived per (key, circle, line, gen, purpose); the info string starts OFE2EE3-. SK rotates on the same triggers as CK (member removed, key revoked, consent withdrawn by the last server member) and whenever server assistance is turned off then on. It is rotated by an admin phone (publisher rule unchanged). A key commitment for SK is published like the existing epoch commitment, so every member provably holds the same SK (a wrapper cannot hand different members different keys). 5.2 Item format v2 payload = 0x02 line(1: 0x00 phone, 0x01 server) gen(4 BE) nonce(24) ct tag(16) sig = Ed25519(sender DEVICE key, "OFE2EE3-ITEM\0" circleid line gen(4) deviceid len(purpose)(1) purpose seq(8) tsms(8) body) AAD = "OFE2EE3-ITEM-AAD\0" circleid line gen deviceid purpose v1 items (header 0x01) keep their meaning: line = phone, gen = epoch, except in a migrated legacy trusted-server circle (section 11). line and gen are in the signature and the AAD: the server cannot relabel an item, and a wrong label simply fails to decrypt. Padding buckets, seq, replay window, epoch-rollback rule: unchanged, applied per (line): the rollback rule is tracked per line (a newer SK gen does not outdate CK and vice versa). The server validates the header exactly as for v1 (length, bucket, declared == header), additionally line in {phone, server} and, for server, that the circle has server assistance on and gen <= e2eeservergen. It stores keyline in the row. This is routing metadata, not trust: the sidecar only opens keyline='server' rows and can only open them if they really are sealed under SK. 5.3 Signed policy entries (transparency log) Two new immutable log actions, signed by an active key of the actor like every other action: Action Signed by Meaning processingpolicy circle admin {circle, serverassist: onoff, defaultfornew: serverphone, skgen, commitment} processingpref the member {circle, user, lane: serverphone, effectiveseq} (this is also the per-member consent: message below) Consent message (supersedes OFE2EE1-SERVERCONSENT; the old vector stays valid for legacy rows): "OFE2EE3-PROCESSING\0" circle user lane skgen serverdeviceid serverfingerprint nonce. lane = server requires the pinned server fingerprint (so consent names the exact server key); lane = phone needs no server key. Withdrawal is a new entry (lane=phone), not a delete, so the log shows when a member switched. Phones verify, per sender, that items with line=server come from a member whose latest valid pref is server (or from before a pref change by signed time); an item sealed under SK by someone who is phone-only is accepted but flagged (a hostile member could do it; it is not a server-attack). The UI badge "server-processed" comes from this check. 5.4 Who may wrap what (hard rules, enforced by triggers and by phones) 1. CK is never wrapped to kind='server'. Server-side trigger rejects it; phones never create it (recipients(line=phone) excludes server). Today's code wraps the circle key to the server device in processPending/recipients when allowedServerKey holds; this must change to the SK line only (phase 3 below). 2. SK is wrapped to the server device only if all hold: admin processingpolicy on, the pinned key is active and approved, its wrap is made by a phone, and at least one member has lane=server (so an SK held by the server with no consenting author is never created for nothing). 3. SK must be independent of every CK. Phones and the sidecar MUST refuse an SK whose 32 bytes equal any CK epoch key they hold, or whose phone-line-domain commitment (KeyCommitment, the v1 OFE2EE1-KEY-COMMIT derivation) equals the commitment of any CK epoch, and raise a visible alert in the key log screen. An admin phone that reused a CK as SK would silently hand the server the phone key through the server line; the server cannot detect this (it never sees key bytes), so the check is on the key holders. 4. service devices (the standalone Dawarich bridge) get SK by default and CK only by the explicit decision of their owner's phone; web viewers get both (they are the owner's own eyes). Each gets an "includes phone-only data of everybody" warning (section 7). 6. Data model sketch (migration 000187processinglanes, idempotent, with down file) ALTER TABLE circles ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS serverassist BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE, -- admin policy, mirrors the signed log entry ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS serverassistdefault TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'phone' CHECK (serverassistdefault IN ('phone','server')), ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS e2eeservergen INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; line on wraps and items; existing rows are the phone line ALTER TABLE circlekeywraps ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS keyline TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'phone' CHECK (keyline IN ('phone','server')); PK/unique of circlekeywraps extended with keyline (recreate index; keep old name for rollback) ALTER TABLE e2eeitems ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS keyline TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'phone' CHECK (keyline IN ('phone','server')); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS e2eeitemscircleline ON e2eeitems (circleid, keyline, id); per member lane; replaces "no row = blocks the whole circle" with "no row = phone" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS e2eeprocessingpref ( circleid UUID NOT NULL, userid UUID NOT NULL, lane TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (lane IN ('phone','server')), skgen INTEGER NOT NULL, serverdeviceid UUID, approverdeviceid UUID NOT NULL, signature BYTEA NOT NULL, signedat TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, updatedat TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (circleid, userid)); e2eeserverconsents is kept (legacy rows are read as lane='server'); a view or data migration unions them. client capabilities so an admin cannot enable SK while a member's app cannot read it ALTER TABLE devicekeys ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS caps TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'; -- e.g. {'lanes2'} triggers refuse a CK wrap whose recipient kind = 'server' (keyline='phone') refuse an SK wrap to 'server' unless e2eeserverassist(circle) AND >=1 pref lane='server' member removal / key revoke: delete wraps (existing) and set e2eerekeyrequired for BOTH lines server assist turned off: delete SK wraps of the server key and all e2eeprocessingpref rows with lane='server' functions e2eeserverassist(circle) = private AND serverassist AND pinned key approved AND holds CURRENT SK gen wrap e2eememberserverok(circle, user) = e2eeserverassist AND pref(user).lane='server' AND signature chain valid (re-verified in Go) e2eeplaintextblocked(circle) unchanged shape, but per-user for ingest: blocked unless e2eememberserverok e2eeservermember(circle) stays as a compatibility alias for e2eeserverassist so existing handlers keep compiling; handlers that guarded "may the server hold plaintext for this circle" become per user (e2eememberserverok): ingest, server geofence, circles.Authz visibility queries, SOS position rule, purge. Server-side marking of processed vs phone-only data: e2eeitems.keyline (routing) and, for plaintext tables, the existing source='e

Code: app/lib/services/processing/ (pure Dart, no Flutter imports, safe in a background isolate). Tests: app/test/processing/. Shared fixtures produced by the real Go code: testdata/processing/.json. Go fixture generators: backend/internal/trips/processingfixturestest.go, backend/internal/handlers/processingfixturestest.go. 1. What the server computes today (source of truth) Output the app consumes Server code Where the logic lives Trips + stops (GET /trips, trip rows: startedat, endedat, distancem, maxspeedmps, avgspeedmps, mode, speedsource, start/end lat/lon, pointcount) backend/internal/trips/segment.go (Clean, Segment), legs.go (buildLegs, classify) Go, pure Driving events (speeding, hardbrake, rapidaccel; kind, startedat, endedat, magnitude, lat, lon) backend/internal/trips/events.go (DetectEvents, attachEvents) Go, pure; thresholds from env DRIVING (defaults 35.76 m/s, 30 s, 3.5, 3.5 m/s^2) phoneuse events phone sensor upload (handlers/tripssensor.go); never derived from GPS the phone already produces them (driving/phoneusetracker.dart) Effective events SQL view tripeventseffective: a GPS event is hidden if a sensor event of the same kind starts within 4 s SQL Driving report (GET /trips/report: totals, per member counts, previous period, days[], recenttrips[]) handlers/tripsreport.go, tripsreportdays.go, computeReportPeriod SQL aggregation + Go glue Weekly summary (GET /trips/weekly-summary, current/previous per member, safetyscore) and the Sunday push handlers/weeklysummary.go (weekStats, weeklySafetyScore, weeklyDue) SQL aggregation + Go score Not present on the server at all: a hard "driving score" other than the weekly safetyscore; a per-drive score; "places visited"/stay detection beyond the generic Stop list (stops are unnamed, no geocoding, no place matching on the server). The drive/week result bodies sketched in PRIVACYPROCESSING.md 8.4 (score, places, topplaces, km, drivemin) therefore have no server definition to reproduce; this spike pins what exists (see 5). Algorithm summary (all thresholds pinned in processingparams.dart) Clean: drop invalid positions (NaN, out of range, exactly 0,0), accuracy > 100 m, duplicate and out-of-order timestamps (never re-sorted), and "teleports" (implied speed > 90 m/s within a 10 min gap; the third consecutive teleport re-anchors). Segment: a stop is a dwell of at least 3 min inside max(50 m, accuracy) of an anchor fix. Departure needs two consecutive fixes outside the radius with implied speed of at least 1 m/s, then walks back to the last still-looking fix. A trip ends when the device stays inside the radius of a candidate fix for 3 min, or at a gap over 10 min. Movement under 250 m or 2 min is not a trip. In-progress trips are held back (FinalizeOpen=false) or closed (true). Legs: per step speed is the device speed (capped at 90) if reported else haversine/dt. Steps under 5 m (or jitter under 20 m while the device reports below 1 m/s) add no distance. Steps are labelled fast (>= 4.5 m/s), slow (>= 1), still; legs shorter than 2 min or 150 m merge into a neighbour; mode from the 90th percentile of moving speeds (>= 5.5 driving, <= 2.5 walking, else other). Events (driving legs only): speeding = fixes above the limit for >= 30 s (gaps over 15 s split episodes); hard brake / rapid accel = acceleration between fixes 0.5 to 4 s apart, both accuracy <= 30 m, magnitude >= threshold and <= 12 m/s^2 (larger is a GPS jump), the vehicle at >= 5 m/s before braking / after accelerating; adjacent intervals of one kind merge. Weekly: stats per member over [from,to) on startedat: driving trips only (count, sum distance, sum duration, max of maxspeedmps), events counted by their own startedat. safetyscore = clamp(round(100 - 5 n / max(km,10) 100), 0, 100) with n = hardbrake + rapidaccel + speeding + phoneuse; absent when no drives; the phone count enters the score even when hidden from the JSON (as on the server). The report period is the local Monday-start week or calendar month in a fixed UTC offset; the Sunday-18:00-UTC "due" week is weeklyDue. 2. The Dart implementation File Role processingparams.dart TripParams, EventParams, all constants, kProcessingAlgorithmVersion = 1 fix.dart Fix, haversine, stepSpeed, streaming FixCleaner, RFC 3339 helpers tripsegmenter.dart TripSegmenter (streaming), buildLegs, segmentFixes (batch convenience) drivingevents.dart detectEvents, effectiveEvents (the SQL view rule) drivingreport.dart computeWeekStat, weeklySafetyScore, computeReportPeriod, weeklyDue, weeklyMemberJson, reportMemberJson processing.dart barrel Output JSON shapes equal the server's field names (trip row without id/userid, event objects, weekStat, report members[] element, days[], recenttrips[]), so existing models (tripreport.dart, weeklysummaryservice.dart) parse them unchanged. Wrapping them into the sealed trip/drive/week result items is phase 5. Streaming design: TripSegmenter is a resumable state machine that follows the Go control flow step for step (stationary phase, moving phase, one fix of lookahead). add(fix) is O(1) amortised except at trip end (builds legs/events once over that trip's fixes). takeNew() returns finalized trips/stops. Memory is bounded by the retained fixes: from the start of the current stop through the current trip. A stationary period longer than maxStopFixes (2048) is folded into running sums (exact centroid and point count). Deterministic: no clocks, no randomness, no I/O. The caller owns persistence of what it needs to resume (see 6). 3. Fidelity The Go fixtures are produced by running the actual Go Segment, attachEvents, DetectEvents, weeklySafetyScore, computeReportPeriod, weeklyDue. For the SQL aggregations the Go test contains a transcription of the queries (it cannot call SQL without a database); equality with the real SQL is not proven by these tests (see 7). Matches exactly (asserted) Number, order, mode, speedsource, pointcount, timestamps (microsecond integers), open flag of every trip and stop; event kinds, counts and start/end instants. Cleaner statistics (Used, OutOfOrder, Duplicate, LowAccuracy, Teleport, InvalidPosition), inprogress, safeuntil. Safety score (all cases), report periods (week and month, offsets -480..+840 min, errors), weeklyDue, per-day buckets, recent trips and event counts. Chunked streaming with takeNew() between fixes equals the batch result; forcing the long-stop fold (maxStopFixes = 40) does not change any output. Tolerated differences (documented, asserted) Floating point: distances, speeds, magnitudes, coordinates compared with abs <= 1e-6 + 1e-9 expected. Reason: Go and Dart use different libm implementations of sin/cos/asin; observed differences are at the last bits. A threshold comparison that lands exactly on the boundary could in principle flip; none occurred in the fixtures. Times: Go keeps nanoseconds, Dart microseconds. Phone fixes are millisecond precision, so no effect. The server can hold fixes from several devices of one user and interleave them; a phone only has its own device. That is a difference of input, not of algorithm. The server's tripeventseffective also honours dismissedat / passenger marks (tripeventsvisible); the phone has no such state in this spike. Differences by design (not reproducible on the phone) Server Params/EventParams env overrides (DRIVING) are compile-time defaults here; the thresholds actually used must be carried in the result (the server already returns them in thresholds). The server re-segments with a 10 min overlap watermark and a 20000-point cap per pass; the phone streams. With the same fixes the output is identical, with different batching it is also identical (tested), but a phone that missed fixes while the OS killed it will simply have gaps, as the server would for a device that did not report. Only the stationary fold (above 2048 fixes in one stop) can deviate: if the walk-back for a departure needed to go behind the folded region (a sustained >= 1 m/s reported speed inside a 50 m radius for more than 64 fixes). Not observed; documented, not asserted. 4. CPU and memory (Dart VM micro-benchmarks only) There are no battery measurements in this document, and none were possible. The numbers below come from app/test/processing/processingbenchmarktest.dart, run with flutter test (two runs agreed within about 30 percent; figures are from the last run; Dart VM, JIT, x86-64 Linux desktop in a Docker container, shared host with load average above 30, no release/AOT build, no Android/iOS runtime). They bound the algorithmic cost per fix. They say nothing about energy: wake-ups, radio, GPS duty cycle, storage writes and sealing cost dominate battery on a phone and were not measured. A mid-range ARM phone is typically several times slower than a desktop core; treat the figures as an order of magnitude, not a prediction. Scenario Fixes Result One week, 2 drives/day at 2 s sampling, 60 s sampling otherwise 22,260 123 ms total for the whole week, mean 5.6 us/fix, p99 5 us/fix, worst single add 23.5 ms (the call that closes a trip: builds legs and events for ~900 fixes), peak buffer 1,322 fixes Worst case 1 Hz for 24 h (86,400 fixes, 2 drives) 86,400 32 ms total, 0.38 us/fix, peak buffer 3,369 fixes (a 30 min drive at 1 Hz plus context) Weekly aggregation of 1,000 trips + 3,000 events n/a 6.4 ms Resident memory delta during the week run n/a about 9.5 MiB (includes the 22k test fixes and JIT), so not a clean measurement of the segmenter Reading: processing cost per fix is microseconds, i.e. below the cost of receiving a fix from the OS. Buffered fixes are bounded by the longest stop (folded beyond 2,048) or the longest trip (a 10 h drive at 1 Hz would hold 36,000 fixes, roughly 3 MB). No work is proportional to total history, so the segmenter can run on every fix in the existing background isolate or in batches whenever the app wakes. Events and legs are computed once per trip, not per fix. 5. What the phone result items can reproduce, and what they cannot trip: yes (all server fields). from/to names and polyline are not part of the server trip row either (names come from geocoding, off by default for phone-only members; a polyline needs retention of raw fixes, not done by this code). drive: events yes (speeding, hard brake, rapid accel from GPS exactly as the server; phoneuse from the existing sensor stream via effectiveEvents). A per-drive score and phoneuses have no server definition; the only score on the server is the weekly safetyscore implemented here. Do not invent a per-drive score without an owner decision. week: drives, distancem, durations, topspeedmps, events, safetyscore exact. trips/km/drivemin are derived trivially. places/topplaces have no server algorithm (stops are unnamed centroids); the phone could match ProcessedStops to the circle's own places, which is new design, not parity. Not computable on a phone: anything needing other members' raw fixes, reverse geocoding, map matching, the Sunday push for a phone that is off. 6. Integration notes for phase 5 Persist, per device, only the unfinished state: the segmenter has no serialization yet. The simplest safe resume, same as the server's watermark, is to keep the raw fixes from the start of the last finalized stop (SegmentResult.safeUntilUs, minus ~10 min) and replay them into a fresh TripSegmenter; replay is deterministic. A snapshot/restore API is left out on purpose to avoid a second source of bugs. Feed it the same fixes that are sealed and uploaded (the chunk the phone already holds), time-ordered; out-of-order fixes are rejected exactly as on the server. Run in the background isolate; hand takeNew() output to the result-item sealing code. Result items are idempotent per trip startedat (the server upserts on (userid, startedat)): newest wins. Emit a result item only when takeNew() returns something; one upload per trip and one per week, as 8.4 assumed. 7. Unverified, and device measurements the owner must do Not verified here: The SQL aggregations were transcribed into Go for the fixtures; equivalence to the live SQL on Timescale/Postgres was not run (no database was started). A one-off check against a seeded database is recommended before relying on report parity. tripeventsvisible / dismissed events and passenger marks are not modelled. Behaviour on real tracks (the fixtures are synthetic, deterministic scenarios: commute with hard brake / rapid accel / speeding, derived speed, walking, walk-drive-walk, GPS garbage, gaps, in-progress, two drives with a pause, stop-and-go, 12 h stationary, jitter then drive, 30 s sparse sampling). The server's own tests use the same style. Recorded real tracks, once the owner has exported some, should be added as fixtures with the Go generator. ARM/AOT performance and anything about battery, thermal state, background execution limits. Device measurements the owner must do (mid-range Android and an iPhone, release builds, screen off, normal use for at least 24 h each, paired with a control phone running the same app with processing disabled): 1. Battery drain per hour and per day with processing on vs off (Android dumpsys batterystats / Battery Historian; iOS Xcode Energy gauge or MetricKit), for a typical day (2 drives) and a heavy day (4 h driving at 1 Hz). 2. CPU time of the background isolate per fix and per closed trip (AOT release, Timeline/dart:developer markers), and peak RSS during a 10 h drive at 1 Hz. 3. Wake-up count and whether iOS suspends the isolate between fixes (does the segmenter see every fix, or does TripSegmenter get bursts after resume?). The algorithm is burst-safe; only completeness of fixes matters. 4. Fix density the platform really delivers when moving and when still (the events need 0.5 to 4 s spacing; at the app's usual 10 to 60 s spacing hard-brake/accel events are under-counted, same as the server, see docs/driving.md). 5. Write amplification: size and frequency of result uploads and of the persisted replay window. 6. Compare phone-produced trips with the server's for the same real day on a server-assisted test member (both lanes active) and file the differences. 8. How to regenerate / run Go: regenerate shared fixtures (only when the Go algorithm intentionally changes) cd backend && UPDATEPROCESSINGFIXTURES=1 go test ./internal/trips ./internal/handlers -run 'TestProcessing' Go: verify committed fixtures are current (runs in normal CI) cd backend && go test ./internal/trips ./internal/handlers -run 'TestProcessing' Dart cd app && flutter analyze lib/services/processing test/processing && flutter test test/processing A change to any threshold or branch in backend/internal/trips fails the Go fixture test (stale file) until the fixtures are regenerated, which in turn fails the Dart tests until the port is updated: that is the drift guard.
